modules.title: Programming Foundations
modules.description: Core programming concepts: variables, control flow, functions, and data structures

lessons.title: Variables and Types
lessons.goal: Write Python programs that store values in variables, choose the right primitive type, and predict what an expression evaluates to without running it.
lessons.takeaway: A value has a type, a name and a lifetime; choosing names and types deliberately makes the rest of the program obvious.

sections.heading: A variable is a named box
body: A variable gives a value a name so you can reuse it later. In Python you create one with a single equals sign: name = value. The name goes on the left, the value on the right — the equals sign here means "bind this name to this value", not "assert they are equal".

Names are case-sensitive: total and Total are different variables. Good names are lowercase with underscores, like order_total or retry_count. A name that describes what the value holds will save you hours of staring at code in three months.
You can rebind a name at any time. price = 10 followed by price = 12 is two separate assignments; the second simply makes price point at a new value.

sections.heading: The four primitive types you will use constantly
body: int holds whole numbers: 0, 42, -7. float holds numbers with a fractional part: 3.14, 0.0, 1e6. str holds text, always wrapped in quotes: "hello" or 'hello'. bool holds exactly two values: True and False.

Mixing types is the source of many beginner bugs. "2" + "3" is the string "23", not 5. 2 + 3 is 5. And "2" + 3 is a TypeError — Python will not guess whether you meant text or numbers. That refusal is a feature: Python makes you resolve ambiguity explicitly with int(), float(), or str().
Use type(x) when you are unsure what a value is. Useful while learning; unnecessary in code that is already correct.

sections.heading: Expressions evaluate to values
body: An expression is any piece of code that produces a value: 2 + 3 produces 5; user_name.upper() produces a string; count is already a value. Assignments and function calls are how programs move values from one place to another.
Operators follow precedence you would expect from math — * and / before + and -, with parentheses to override it. When in doubt, add parentheses; they cost nothing and remove doubt.
Printing with print(...) is how you make values visible. This is the closest thing to a debugger the language offers out of the box, and professionals use it constantly.

lessons.task: Write a script that stores a product name (str), a unit price (float), a quantity (int), and an in-stock flag (bool). Print a single line: "<name> x<quantity> = <total>". Then, deliberately trigger a TypeError by adding the price to a message string, read the traceback, and explain it in a comment.

quiz.question:
What does the following print?

count = 2
count = count + 1
print(count)
choices: count + 1
A TypeError
quiz.explanation: The right-hand side count + 1 evaluates first using the current value (2), giving 3; the assignment rebinds count to 3. The old value is simply no longer referenced.

outcomes: Create a Python file and run it from a terminal with an explicit interpreter.
Store values in variables and format readable output with f-strings.
Use a traceback to find the line where a program failed.
lessons.mental_model: Running a script is like following a recipe: the interpreter reads one step at a time, and the traceback points to the step where the kitchen caught fire.
worked_example: A learner writes price = "0.50", quantity = 3, and total = price * quantity. Python repeats the text three times because price is a string. They change the value to float(price), print f"Total: {total:.2f}", and the output becomes 1.50. The lesson is not the arithmetic; it is checking the type before trusting the result.
common_mistakes: Forgetting quotation marks around text, which produces a NameError for each bare word.
Joining a string and a number with + instead of using an f-string or str().
Changing several lines at once after an error, so you cannot tell which change fixed it.

key_terms.definition: A text file containing Python instructions that an interpreter runs from top to bottom.
The program (python3 on most systems) that reads and executes Python code.
A name that refers to a value so the rest of the program can reuse it.
A string prefixed with f that inserts expressions inside braces.
The report Python prints when an error stops the program, including the failing line and call path.

checkpoint.question: What is the difference between the name of a variable and the value it refers to?
checkpoint.answer: A variable is a name that refers to a value; the value has a type.

checkpoint.question: Why does "3" * 2 produce "33" instead of 6?
checkpoint.answer: Multiplication repeats a string when one operand is text, so convert it with float() first.

checkpoint.question: Which part of a traceback tells you where to look first?
checkpoint.answer: Read the final error line, then the line number in the traceback.

checkpoint.question: Why is it useful to change only one thing after an error?
checkpoint.answer: Changing one thing at a time lets you know which change fixed the error.

checkpoint.question: What does the :.2f format specifier do?
checkpoint.answer: It formats a number with two digits after the decimal point for display.

lessons.title: Control Flow
lessons.goal: Write programs that make decisions with if/elif/else and repeat work with for and while loops, choosing the construct that fits the problem.
lessons.takeaway: Use branches for decisions and loops for repetition; every loop must visibly move toward its stopping condition.

sections.heading: Decisions with if, elif and else
body: if condition: runs a block only when the condition is truthy. elif adds more branches, and else is the fallback. Conditions use comparison operators (==, !=, <, <=, >, >=) and combine with and, or, not.

Python has no switch statement for general use — long chains of elif are idiomatic. Keep the conditions mutually exclusive and order them from most to least likely when performance matters, or by logic when clarity does.
A common trap: = assigns, == compares. Writing if x = 5 is a SyntaxError in Python, which is unusually kind of it. In other languages the same mistake compiles and quietly corrupts state.

sections.heading: Repeating work with for
body: for item in iterable: walks each element of a sequence. for i in range(5) gives you 0..4. range(2, 10, 2) gives 2, 4, 6, 8 — start, stop (exclusive), step.
Looping over a list directly, for name in names:, is preferable to indexing when you do not need the index. When you do need both, use enumerate(names) to get (index, name) pairs.

break exits the loop early; continue skips to the next iteration. Use both deliberately and sparingly — deeply nested loops with breaks can be harder to reason about than a well-named helper function.

sections.heading: while for unknown durations
body: while condition: repeats as long as the condition holds. It is the right tool when you do not know how many iterations you need — reading input until the user types "quit", retrying a request until it succeeds, or converging on a numeric answer.

The eternal danger is the infinite loop: the condition never becomes false. Always ask yourself "what changes each iteration, and does it move toward the end?" If you cannot answer, use a for loop with a bounded range instead.
Loop-and-filter and loop-and-accumulate patterns cover most real code: select items matching a predicate, or fold a sequence into one value (sum, max, count-of-matches).

lessons.task: Write a program that reads a list of daily step counts and prints (1) how many days exceed 8,000 steps, (2) the longest run of consecutive qualifying days, and (3) stops at the first day with zero steps and prints a warning. Use if/elif/else and one loop with break.

quiz.question: What does range(2, 10, 3) produce?
quiz.explanation: range(start, stop, step) starts at 2, steps by 3, and excludes 10 — so 2, 5, 8. The stop value is never included.

outcomes: Create lists and dictionaries and access values by position or key.
Use a loop to transform every item in a collection.
Use .get() and validation to avoid a KeyError on missing fields.
lessons.mental_model: A list is a queue of parcels; a dictionary is the address label on each parcel. A loop is the courier who visits every parcel once.
worked_example: Mira receives a model catalogue as a list of dictionaries. One provider is missing a price, so a direct row["price"] crashes the whole report. She changes it to row.get("price"), skips rows with no price, and counts the skipped rows. The output now tells the reader how many rows were priced instead of silently averaging over an empty list.
common_mistakes: Using a list where a key lookup is needed, then searching the list on every request.
Assuming a dictionary key exists and crashing an entire batch when one record is incomplete.
Mutating a list while looping over it, which skips items or duplicates work.

key_terms.definition: An ordered, mutable collection written with square brackets.
A mutable mapping from keys to values written with curly braces.
The error raised when code asks a dictionary for a key it does not contain.
Processing each item in a collection, usually with a for loop.
A compact expression that builds a list or dictionary from an iterable.

checkpoint.question: When is a list a better choice than a dictionary?
checkpoint.answer: A list preserves order and allows duplicates; a dictionary looks up values by key.

checkpoint.question: What happens when two records have the same name in a dictionary comprehension?
checkpoint.answer: The later record overwrites the earlier value for that key.

checkpoint.question: Why does .get() return None instead of raising KeyError?
checkpoint.answer: It returns the supplied default (or None) instead of raising an exception.

checkpoint.question: How would you count skipped records in a loop?
checkpoint.answer: Increment a counter in the branch where the record is skipped.

checkpoint.question: Why does a zero average over an empty list hide a data problem?
checkpoint.answer: It can mean every row was malformed, so the report should show counts or fail.

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.goal: Decompose a program into small, total, named functions with parameters and return values, and explain what each one does without reading its body.
lessons.takeaway: A function is a named contract: meaningful inputs, one clear job and a predictable output beat duplicated code every time.

sections.heading: A function is a reusable, named piece of logic
body: def name(parameters): defines a function; return hands a value back to the caller. A function without return returns None — legal, but almost never what you want when a value is expected.

Parameters are placeholders; arguments are what the caller passes. Positional arguments arrive in order; keyword arguments arrive by name and make call sites self-describing: search(query="rust", limit=10).
Good functions do one thing. If you can describe what a function does with "and", it probably wants to be two functions.

sections.heading: Scope: what a function can see
body: Names assigned inside a function are local to it and vanish when it returns. Names at module level are visible everywhere in the module. Reading a module-level name from inside a function is fine; assigning to it without the global keyword does not change the outer name — it creates a local one.
Minimize what a function touches beyond its parameters and return value. A function that depends only on its inputs is trivially testable: feed it inputs, check output, done.
That property — same input, same output, no hidden dependencies — is called purity. You do not need to make everything pure, but you will thank yourself for making most of it so.

sections.heading: Docstrings and small compositions
body: A one-line docstring under def tells the next reader (and your future self) the contract: what goes in, what comes out, and what the function assumes. Keep it factual — describe behaviour, not implementation.

Compose small functions rather than writing one large one: cleaned = normalize(text); tokens = tokenize(cleaned); counts = count_words(tokens). Each step is independently checkable and independently reusable.
Recursion is a function calling itself and is elegant for tree-shaped problems; iteration is usually the clearer choice for sequences. Know both; reach for recursion deliberately.

lessons.task: Refactor a 40-line script you wrote for sf.00.02 into three functions: qualifies(day_steps) -> bool, longest_streak(days) -> int, summary(days) -> str. Add a one-line docstring to each. Confirm the output is identical before and after.

quiz.question:
What is the output of the following?

def add(a, b):
    a = a + b
    return a

x = 5
y = add(x, 3)
print(x, y)
quiz.explanation: a is a local name for the parameter; rebinding it inside the function does not affect the caller’s x. x stays 5; y receives the returned 8.

outcomes: Define a function with parameters and a return value.
Validate inputs and raise a clear error when the contract is broken.
Call a function from a script and test it with several inputs.
lessons.mental_model: A function is a vending machine: you put in clearly labelled inputs, it validates them, and it returns one predictable output. Printing is not the same as returning.
worked_example: A support script calculates refunds inline in three places. One copy forgets to validate negative amounts, so a refund of -20 becomes a charge. The team extracts refund_total(amount, fee) with validation and a return value, then replaces all three copies with calls to it. The tests now cover one contract instead of three copies.
common_mistakes: Printing inside a calculation function so callers cannot reuse the result.
Using a mutable default such as items=[] and then appending to it across calls.
Returning None on invalid input, forcing every caller to remember a special case.

key_terms.definition: A named block of code that accepts inputs and can return a result.
A name in a function definition that receives an argument when the function is called.
The result a function hands back to its caller with return.
An exception raised when a value has the right type but an unacceptable value.
A default argument such as [] or {} that is created once and shared across calls.

checkpoint.question: What does return do that print does not?
checkpoint.answer: Returning hands a value back to the caller; printing only shows it on screen.

checkpoint.question: Why is a mutable default argument dangerous?
checkpoint.answer: The default list is created once and shared, so changes leak into later calls.

checkpoint.question: When should a function raise an exception instead of returning None?
checkpoint.answer: Raise when the caller violated a contract or the result would be invalid; return None when absence is an expected state.

checkpoint.question: Why are type hints not enough to validate runtime input?
checkpoint.answer: Type hints are metadata for tools and readers, not runtime checks.

checkpoint.question: What is a pure function, and why is it easier to test?
checkpoint.answer: A pure function depends only on its inputs and returns a value without side effects.

lessons.title: Data Structures
lessons.goal: Choose between list, tuple, dict and set for a given problem, and use indexing, slicing, keys and membership tests correctly.
lessons.takeaway: Data structures encode how you will use data; pick by access pattern first and micro-optimise later.

sections.heading: Lists: ordered, mutable sequences
body: A list holds an ordered collection of anything: numbers, strings, objects, other lists. Index with zero-based positions: items[0] is the first element, items[-1] the last. Slices items[1:4] give elements 1 through 3 (stop is exclusive).
Lists grow and shrink: append, insert, extend, pop, remove. Sorting with sorted(items) returns a new list; items.sort() sorts in place. Know which one you are calling.

Lists are the default container for sequences whose shape is not fixed. If you find yourself tracking a fixed set of named attributes with positional indices, you want a dict or a small class instead.

sections.heading: Dicts: look values up by key
body: A dict maps keys to values: user = {"name": "Ada", "role": "engineer"}. Keys must be hashable (strings, numbers, tuples — not lists). Access with user["name"], test presence with "name" in user, and default safely with user.get("nickname", user["name"]).
Dicts preserve insertion order in modern Python, iterate by key by default, and support items() for (key, value) pairs: for key, value in user.items().
Reach for a dict whenever you would catch yourself writing user_name, user_role, user_email as parallel variables. One dict with one lookup beats three loose variables.

sections.heading: Tuples and sets: when lists are wrong
body: A tuple is an immutable list: point = (3, 4). Use tuples for fixed-shape records (coordinates, rows) and as dict keys. Immutability documents intent: nothing downstream can accidentally mutate a record you were handed.

A set is an unordered collection of unique items with O(1) membership tests: seen = set(); if x in seen. Sets also do algebra — union |, intersection &, difference - — which makes them the right tool for "which tags are new?" questions.

Choosing well: ordered + mutable → list; ordered + immutable + fixed shape → tuple; key-value lookup → dict; uniqueness/membership → set. When unsure, start with a list, then move to the structure that matches how you actually use the data.

lessons.task: Given a hard-coded list of 50 project records (name, owner, status), write code that (1) counts records per status using a dict, (2) finds owners with more than one active project using a set, and (3) prints a report keyed by owner sorted alphabetically. No imports beyond the standard library.

quiz.question: Which data structure should back a lookup of "is this issue id in our processed set?"
choices: list
dict
tuple
set
quiz.explanation: Sets give O(1) membership tests and enforce uniqueness — exactly what a processed/seen set needs. A list would scan every element each check; a dict stores key-value pairs you do not need.

outcomes: Decide whether a problem needs a class or a set of functions, using state, invariants, and call-site clarity as the test.
Write a client class with a constructor, private helpers, a factory, and a useful __repr__.
Replace inheritance with composition so transport, retries, and parsing can be tested and swapped independently.
lessons.mental_model: A class is a small machine with dials set at construction: the dials must stay in valid positions, and the machine should expose buttons, not its wiring.
worked_example: A client class grows to 780 lines covering chat, embeddings, uploads, retries, and CSV export. Every new endpoint copies the same header logic, and mocking a call requires patching three module globals. In a design review, the team keeps ModelClient for configuration and one request() method, moves endpoint-specific payloads into functions, and injects a transport callable. Retries become a wrapper around transport; tests use a fake that returns a 429 once, then a valid body. The class drops to 90 lines, and coverage of the retry path goes from zero to four tests. The decision: a class owns state and one job; everything else is a function or a collaborator.
common_mistakes: Subclassing the client for each provider, then duplicating header and error logic across five fragile children.
Doing network calls in __init__, so constructing the object fails in tests and at service startup.
Making every attribute public and mutable, so any caller can change the base URL mid-request.

key_terms.definition: A condition that must remain true for an object to be valid, such as a base URL with no trailing slash.
Building behaviour by holding a collaborator and delegating to it, instead of inheriting its methods through a class hierarchy.
An alternative constructor declared with @classmethod that builds an instance from configuration, a file, or another object.

checkpoint.question: What test tells you that a group of functions should become a class?
checkpoint.answer: A group of functions should become a class when they share state that must remain valid together and that state requires an invariant to be protected.

checkpoint.question: Why is a network call inside __init__ a problem for tests and for startup?
checkpoint.answer: Network calls in __init__ cause problems because tests cannot construct the object without hitting the real network, and service startup fails if the network is down. Keep __init__ cheap: just store the settings, don't do work.

checkpoint.question: How does injecting a transport change the way you test a 429 retry?
checkpoint.answer: Injecting a transport allows you to pass a fake version that returns a 429 error first, then a success response, enabling you to test retry logic without touching the real network.

checkpoint.question: When is inheritance a better choice than composition, and what must remain true?
checkpoint.answer: Inheritance is better than composition only when the child class is usable anywhere the parent is and adds no surprising behavior—genuine substitution. Otherwise, pass collaborators in as parameters.

checkpoint.question: What belongs in __repr__, and what must never appear there?
checkpoint.answer: __repr__ should show identifying information like the host and request count so logs are readable. Never include headers, tokens, keys, or personal data that could leak secrets.

lessons.goal: Create a Python file and run it from a terminal with an explicit interpreter.
lessons.takeaway: Running a script is like following a recipe: the interpreter reads one step at a time, and the traceback points to the step where the kitchen caught fire.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: The fastest way to stop feeling lost is to run a program you can see, change, and break. This lesson gives you the smallest complete loop: edit a file, run it, read the output, and fix one error.
Running a script is like following a recipe: the interpreter reads one step at a time, and the traceback points to the step where the kitchen caught fire.

sections.heading: A program is a list of instructions
body: Python runs a script from top to bottom. Each line can calculate a value, call a function, or make a decision. print() writes a value
to the terminal so you can see what happened. A variable is just a name attached to a value; it is not a box with a fixed type.

sections.heading: Strings, numbers, and f-strings
body: Text lives inside quotes and numbers do not. The + operator joins strings, but it does not mix strings and numbers automatically. An f-string starts with f and puts expressions inside braces: f"Total: {total:.2f}".
The .2f part asks for two decimal places.

sections.heading: Errors are feedback, not failure
body: A SyntaxError means Python could not understand the file; a NameError means a name was used before it existed; a TypeError means two values could
not be combined. Read the last line of the traceback first, then the line number, then the source line. Change one thing and run again.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Keep runnable scripts in files and commit them; a notebook cell that depends on hidden state is not reproducible.
Run the same interpreter you use in CI. python3 hello.py is more explicit than a double-click.
Never put API keys in a first script. Read secrets from environment variables when you reach the HTTP lesson.

lessons.title: Lists, dictionaries, and loops
lessons.goal: Create lists and dictionaries and access values by position or key.
lessons.takeaway: A list is a queue of parcels; a dictionary is the address label on each parcel. A loop is the courier who visits every parcel once.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: AI APIs return lists of choices and dictionaries of fields. If you can loop over them and pick values safely, you can turn raw responses into useful data instead of copying values by hand.
A list is a queue of parcels; a dictionary is the address label on each parcel. A loop is the courier who visits every parcel once.

sections.heading: Lists keep order
body: A list is written with square brackets: ["read", "write", "delete"]. Indexing starts at zero, and
a slice such as items[1:3] returns a new list. Use a list when order or duplicates matter.

sections.heading: Dictionaries look up by key
body: A dictionary maps keys to values: {"name": "Atlas", "price": 0.5}. Access a known key with data["name"]; use
data.get("price", 0.0) when the field may be absent. Keys must be hashable, so a list cannot be a key.

sections.heading: Loops turn one item into many
body: A for loop visits each item: for model in models: print(model["name"]). A comprehension builds a new collection
in one expression: [model["name"] for model in models]. Both are fine; choose the one a reviewer can read.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Validate collection shape at the boundary and convert it into a typed record before business logic uses it.
Log counts for records read, kept, and skipped; an average over zero records is an outage disguised as a zero.
Keep loops small enough that each one has one reason to change.

lessons.task: Build a catalogue of four models with name, provider, and price, then print the cheapest price (25 minutes). Add one record with a missing price and make the script report how many records were skipped (20 minutes).

A list preserves order and allows duplicates; a dictionary looks up values by key.

lessons.title: Functions, inputs, and return values
lessons.goal: Define a function with parameters and a return value. Turn repeated steps into a named function with a clear input and output. Define a function with parameters and a return value.
lessons.takeaway: A function is a vending machine: you put in clearly labelled inputs, it validates them, and it returns one predictable output. Printing is not the same as returning.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: Functions are how you stop copying code and start making decisions testable. A small function with explicit inputs and a return value can be called by a script, a test, or an API handler without changing its internals.
A function is a vending machine: you put in clearly labelled inputs, it validates them, and it returns one predictable output. Printing is not the same as returning.

sections.heading: A function is a named contract
body: def total_cost(tickets, price): names the function and its inputs. The return statement hands a result back to the
caller. A function that only prints is hard to test; return the value and let the caller decide how to display it.

sections.heading: Parameters are local names
body: Parameters exist only while the function runs. Pass values in rather than reading globals, so the same function works in a script, a test, and
a web request. Default values are useful for safe options, but never use a mutable default such as [] because it is shared between calls.

sections.heading: Fail loudly at the boundary
body: Validate values before doing arithmetic: negative tickets, a non-numeric price, or a missing argument should raise ValueError
or TypeError with a message that names the problem. A wrong answer returned silently is harder to debug than an exception.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Keep calculations pure and push display, logging, and network calls to the edges.
Give every function one job and a name that describes the result, not the implementation.
Write at least one test for the happy path, one boundary, and one invalid input.

lessons.task: Write a function that calculates a total with a discount and rejects negative inputs (20 minutes). Add a second function that formats the result, keeping calculation and display separate (15 minutes).

quiz.question: What does return do that print does not?
choices: Returning hands a value back to the caller; printing only shows it on screen.
Type hints are metadata for tools and readers, not runtime checks.
Raise when the caller violated a contract or the result would be invalid; return None when absence is an expected state.
The default list is created once and shared, so changes leak into later calls.
quiz.explanation: Returning hands a value back to the caller; printing only shows it on screen.

outcomes: Define a function with parameters and a return value.
Validate inputs and raise a clear error when the contract is broken.
Call a function from a script and test it with several inputs.
lessons.mental_model: A function is a vending machine: you put in clearly labelled inputs, it validates them, and it returns one predictable output. Printing is not the same as returning.
worked_example: A support script calculates refunds inline in three places. One copy forgets to validate negative amounts, so a refund of -20 becomes a charge. The team extracts refund_total(amount, fee) with validation and a return value, then replaces all three copies with calls to it. The tests now cover one contract instead of three copies.
common_mistakes: Printing inside a calculation function so callers cannot reuse the result.
Using a mutable default such as items=[] and then appending to it across calls.
Returning None on invalid input, forcing every caller to remember a special case.

key_terms.definition: A named block of code that accepts inputs and can return a result.
A name in a function definition that receives an argument when the function is called.
The result a function hands back to its caller with return.
An exception raised when a value has the right type but an unacceptable value.
A default argument such as [] or {} that is created once and shared across calls.

checkpoint.question: What does return do that print does not?
checkpoint.answer: Returning hands a value back to the caller; printing only shows it on screen.

checkpoint.question: Why is a mutable default argument dangerous?
checkpoint.answer: The default list is created once and shared, so changes leak into later calls.

checkpoint.question: When should a function raise an exception instead of returning None?
checkpoint.answer: Raise when the caller violated a contract or the result would be invalid; return None when absence is an expected state.

checkpoint.question: Why are type hints not enough to validate runtime input?
checkpoint.answer: Type hints are metadata for tools and readers, not runtime checks.

checkpoint.question: What is a pure function, and why is it easier to test?
checkpoint.answer: A pure function depends only on its inputs and returns a value without side effects.

lessons.title: Files, JSON, and the command line
lessons.goal: Read a text file with an explicit encoding. Read a file, parse JSON, and make a small script accept a path from the terminal. Read a text file with an explicit encoding.
lessons.takeaway: A file is a sealed parcel, JSON is the packing list, and your script is the inspector: open it, check the label, and report exactly what is missing.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: Most AI work starts with data on disk and configuration from the environment. Reading a file safely and decoding JSON without crashing are the first steps toward ingestion, evaluation, and reproducible experiments.
A file is a sealed parcel, JSON is the packing list, and your script is the inspector: open it, check the label, and report exactly what is missing.

sections.heading: Paths are objects, not strings
body: pathlib.Path joins paths, checks existence, and reads text without manually concatenating slashes. Always pass encoding="utf-8" so the same file works
on every machine. A relative path depends on the current working directory, which is why command-line tools should show the resolved path in an error.

sections.heading: JSON is text with rules
body: json.loads(text) returns Python dictionaries, lists, strings, numbers, booleans, and None. It raises JSONDecodeError when the text is malformed.
A successful decode does not prove the fields you need exist, so check the top-level type and required keys before using them.

sections.heading: Command-line scripts need a contract
body: sys.argv[1] is the first argument after the script name. If it is missing, print a usage message and exit non-zero. A good
script accepts a path, validates it, reports the number of records it read, and writes output to a predictable place.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Report the resolved path, encoding, and record count when ingestion starts; this makes data incidents reproducible.
Treat files as untrusted input: bound the size you read and validate the shape before loading everything into memory.
Keep sample data small, licensed, and free of personal or secret values.

lessons.task: Create a JSON file with a name and five items, then write a script that prints the count (25 minutes). Add a malformed file and make the script print the filename and a one-line error (20 minutes).

quiz.question: Why is an explicit encoding important even on a machine where the default works?
choices: Syntax errors mean the text is not JSON; schema errors mean the decoded value has the wrong shape or fields.
A short usage message naming the expected argument and exiting non-zero.
Relative paths resolve against the current working directory, which changes between terminals, services, and CI.
The default encoding differs across systems; explicit UTF-8 makes behaviour reproducible.
quiz.explanation: The default encoding differs across systems; explicit UTF-8 makes behaviour reproducible.

outcomes: Read a text file with an explicit encoding.
Decode JSON and validate the shape you expect.
Pass a file path to a script with sys.argv and fail clearly when it is missing.
lessons.mental_model: A file is a sealed parcel, JSON is the packing list, and your script is the inspector: open it, check the label, and report exactly what is missing.
worked_example: A learner downloads an evaluation set and writes data = json.load(open("data.json")). It works on their laptop but fails in CI because the working directory differs, and a malformed file produces a long traceback with no filename. They switch to Path, add encoding, catch JSONDecodeError, and print the resolved path and record count. The next run fails with a useful message in one line.
common_mistakes: Opening a file without an encoding, which works on one laptop and fails on another.
Assuming every decoded JSON object has the fields the script expects.
Hard-coding a personal path such as /Users/me/data.json into a shared script.

key_terms.definition: The standard-library module for working with filesystem paths as objects.
The character mapping used to turn bytes into text; UTF-8 is the safe default for source and data files.
The exception raised when json.loads cannot parse malformed JSON text.
The expected shape and types of a decoded object, checked before business logic uses it.
The list of command-line arguments available to a Python script.

checkpoint.question: Why is an explicit encoding important even on a machine where the default works?
checkpoint.answer: The default encoding differs across systems; explicit UTF-8 makes behaviour reproducible.

checkpoint.question: What is the difference between a JSON syntax error and a schema error?
checkpoint.answer: Syntax errors mean the text is not JSON; schema errors mean the decoded value has the wrong shape or fields.

checkpoint.question: Why does a relative path behave differently in a terminal and in CI?
checkpoint.answer: Relative paths resolve against the current working directory, which changes between terminals, services, and CI.

checkpoint.question: What should a CLI print when the file is missing?
checkpoint.answer: A short usage message naming the expected argument and exiting non-zero.

checkpoint.question: Why should a script report how many records it read?
checkpoint.answer: The count separates an empty valid file from a parser that silently skipped rows.

lessons.title: Python review: data, loops, and tracebacks
lessons.goal: Understand Python's basic data types (strings, numbers, lists, dictionaries)
lessons.takeaway: Working with API data is like unpacking a delivery box. The outer box might be a dictionary with labels (keys) pointing to what's inside. Some things might be single items, others might be lists of items. Your job is to open it up and grab exactly what you need.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: When working with AI APIs, you'll constantly deal with data in the form of lists and dictionaries (JSON). You'll need to loop through results, extract what you need, and handle errors when things go wrong. This lesson teaches just enough Python to get you comfortable with these patterns - no need to become a Python expert, just learn what AI engineers use every day.

Working with API data is like unpacking a delivery box. The outer box might be a dictionary with labels (keys) pointing to what's inside. Some things might be single items, others might be lists of items. Your job is to open it up and grab exactly what you need.

sections.heading: Data Types You'll Use Every Day
body: Think of data types like different kinds of containers. Strings hold text (like messages). Numbers hold values (like costs or counts).

Lists hold ordered collections (like a list of search results). Dictionaries hold key-value pairs (like a person's info - name, email). When you get data from an AI API, it almost always comes as a dictionary with lists inside it.
Learning to navigate these is like learning to read a map.

sections.heading: Loops and Making Decisions
body: Loops let you do the same thing many times without repeating code. If you get 10 results from an API, a loop can process each one. If/else statements let your code make decisions - like 'if the answer is too long, shorten it' or 'if there's an error, try again'.
These are the building blocks of smart, flexible code.

sections.heading: Reading Errors (Your Superpower)
body: Every programmer sees errors constantly - even experts! The difference is knowing how to read them. A Python traceback tells you exactly what went wrong and where.

The most important line is usually at the bottom - it tells you the error type and message. The lines above show the path your code took to get there. Learning to read tracebacks will save you hours of frustration.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Convert and validate external values at one boundary, then pass typed objects inward so every later calculation is arithmetic, not parsing.
Log counts alongside aggregates, including rows read, rows skipped, and rows priced, because an average over zero rows is a silent outage.
Pin the interpreter in CI; a script that only works on your laptop is a liability for the whole team.

lessons.task: Take the aggregation snippet and extend it to report the cheapest model per provider, with a test fixture of five rows (30 minutes). Write a script that deliberately raises KeyError, TypeError, and ValueError, then record the first useful line of each traceback (25 minutes).

quiz.question: Why does appending to a list inside a loop over that same list produce incorrect totals?
choices: A list comprehension builds the whole list in memory, so for a 4 GB file it would consume too much RAM; a generator…
The frame that shows where the exception was raised (the last frame) usually contains the real cause, because it is the…
Appending to a list while looping over it changes the list size during the loop, so some items are skipped or counted…
dict.get('price',0.0) returns 0.0 when the key is missing but does not create a new entry; a membership check would reveal…
quiz.explanation: Appending to a list while looping over it changes the list size during the loop, so some items are skipped or counted twice, giving wrong totals.

outcomes: Understand Python's basic data types (strings, numbers, lists, dictionaries)
Work with lists and dictionaries to handle API responses
Write loops and conditions to process data
Read and understand Python error messages (tracebacks)
Know the difference between running a script vs running as a module
lessons.mental_model: Working with API data is like unpacking a delivery box. The outer box might be a dictionary with labels (keys) pointing to what's inside. Some things might be single items, others might be lists of items. Your job is to open it up and grab exactly what you need.
worked_example: On her first day, Tomas inherits a 60-line script that reports average model prices. It prints GBP 0.00 for every provider. Prices arrive as strings from a CSV, so his patched sum() concatenates them, and his earlier fix divided by the row count with integer division. He rewrites the aggregation as one pass, converts with float(row["price"]) at the boundary, filters rows where context_window is None, and prints a row count beside each average. A three-row fixture with known values guards the fix. The decision: convert types once, at ingestion, never in formatting code.
common_mistakes: Mutating a list while looping over it, so the script skips rows and produces a total nobody can reproduce.
Comparing prices as strings, where "10.0" < "9.5" is true and the cheapest model is reported incorrectly.
Debugging with print statements instead of reading the traceback line the interpreter already named.

key_terms.definition: An ordered collection of items in square brackets [ ]. Like a shopping list - order matters.
A collection of key-value pairs in curly braces { }. Like a contact card - look up by name to find info.
Code that repeats - does something for each item in a list or until a condition is met.
Python's way of showing you where and why an error happened, with the full chain of calls.
Python's way of saying 'nothing here' or 'no value'. Different from zero or empty string!

checkpoint.question: Why does appending to a list inside a loop over that same list produce incorrect totals?
checkpoint.answer: Appending to a list while looping over it changes the list size during the loop, so some items are skipped or counted twice, giving wrong totals.

checkpoint.question: What does dict.get("price", 0.0) hide that an explicit membership check would reveal?
checkpoint.answer: dict.get('price',0.0) returns 0.0 when the key is missing but does not create a new entry; a membership check would reveal that the key was absent and allow you to handle the missing case explicitly.

checkpoint.question: Why is a list comprehension a poor choice for a 4 GB log file?
checkpoint.answer: A list comprehension builds the whole list in memory, so for a 4 GB file it would consume too much RAM; a generator processes one item at a time.

checkpoint.question: Which frame in a traceback usually holds the real cause, and why?
checkpoint.answer: The frame that shows where the exception was raised (the last frame) usually contains the real cause, because it is the line that executed the faulty operation.

checkpoint.question: How does running a file inside a package change sys.path compared with python -m?
checkpoint.answer: Running a file with python -m adds the package’s directory to sys.path, so imports resolve relative to the package; running a script directly does not include that package directory in sys.path.

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.goal: Write a function with an explicit contract: typed parameters, a single return shape, and documented failure behaviour.
lessons.takeaway: A function is a kitchen appliance: one job, a clear input, a predictable output, and a warning label for the ways it can burn you.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: A model client is mostly functions: build a prompt, call an endpoint, parse a response, validate a record, compute a cost. When one function does four of those, a failure in parsing looks like a failure in networking, and tests need a live API to tell the difference. Small, explicit functions make each step observable and let you change one decision without re- running the world.
A function is a kitchen appliance: one job, a clear input, a predictable output, and a warning label for the ways it can burn you.

sections.heading: A function is a contract The signature states what goes in; the return statement
body: A function is a contract The signature states what goes in; the return statement states what comes out; the docstring states what can go wrong. Callers should not need to read the body to use it. Name the unit in the function name: parse_usage(response) returns a Usage or raises ValueError, and it never prints, retries, or writes a file.

When a function needs a paragraph explaining its order of operations, it is probably two functions. Defaults and side effects Default arguments are evaluated once, at definition time, so def add(item, bucket=[]) shares one list across every call. Use None and create the list inside the body.

Keep printing, network calls, and file writes at the edges; a pure function that takes data and returns data can be tested with literals. Inject collaborators such as a fetch callable instead of importing a module-level client, so a test can pass a fake. Composition over cleverness Build behaviour by calling small functions, not by adding flags.

A retry parameter that changes the return type, or a mode string that selects three code paths, is a sign the caller should choose a different function. Keyword-only arguments such as *, timeout_s: float = 10.0 make call sites readable and let you add parameters without breaking positional callers. Return early on errors; keep the happy path unindented.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Log the case identifier on every failure so a partial batch can be rerun without replaying the full set.
Keep network calls in one injectable function; when the provider changes, you edit one place and re-run unit tests.
Set explicit timeouts at the boundary and let them raise a named error rather than returning an empty string that looks like a valid answer.

lessons.task: Refactor a 60-line script into three functions with injected I/O, then add tests for success, empty input, and malformed data (60 minutes). Write a function with a mutable default, demonstrate the bug in four lines, then fix it with a None sentinel (20 minutes).

quiz.question: Why does a list default argument persist between calls, and what replaces it?
choices: A pure function's output depends only on its arguments, and it changes no external state. That lets tests pass simple…
Injecting fetch lets tests pass a fake function that returns a fixed response. Tests can run offline and simulate a timeout…
A list default is created once when the function is defined, so every call shares the same list. Replace it with None and…
A helper should raise when bad input means it cannot produce its promised return value, rather than returning None or an…
quiz.explanation: A list default is created once when the function is defined, so every call shares the same list. Replace it with None and create a new list inside the function.

outcomes: Write a function with an explicit contract: typed parameters, a single return shape, and documented failure behaviour.
Replace mutable default arguments and hidden global state with keyword-only parameters and injected dependencies.
Refactor a long procedure into three composable functions that can each be tested in isolation.
lessons.mental_model: A function is a kitchen appliance: one job, a clear input, a predictable output, and a warning label for the ways it can burn you.
worked_example: An evaluation script has one 140-line run() that loads 500 prompts, calls the model, parses JSON, scores each answer, and writes a CSV. When 12 responses fail schema validation, the whole run exits and no scores are saved. Ana splits it into load_cases, score_case, and write_report, with run() composing them. score_case returns a result dictionary and records an error for a malformed response; run keeps going per case. The rerun completes in 6 minutes, reports the 12 errors instead of losing the batch, and a new unit test covers the malformed case offline. The decision: one failure should cost one case, not the run.
common_mistakes: Using a list default to collect results, then wondering why yesterday's cases appear in today's report.
Letting a helper print progress and return a value, so tests must capture stdout to know whether it worked.
Adding retry=True and quiet=False flags until one function has sixteen combinations nobody tests.

key_terms.definition: A function whose output depends only on its arguments and which changes no external state, so it can be tested with literals.
A parameter default such as a list or dictionary created once when the function is defined and shared by every call.
A parameter placed after the star in the signature, callable only by name, which keeps call sites readable as the API grows.

checkpoint.question: Why does a list default argument persist between calls, and what replaces it?
checkpoint.answer: A list default is created once when the function is defined, so every call shares the same list. Replace it with None and create a new list inside the function.

checkpoint.question: What makes a function pure, and why does purity simplify testing?
checkpoint.answer: A pure function's output depends only on its arguments, and it changes no external state. That lets tests pass simple literal values with no setup.

checkpoint.question: When should a helper raise instead of returning None for bad input?
checkpoint.answer: A helper should raise when bad input means it cannot produce its promised return value, rather than returning None or an empty string that looks like a valid answer. The lesson's example is parse_usage(response), which returns a Usage or raises ValueError.

checkpoint.question: How does injecting fetch change what your tests need to run?
checkpoint.answer: Injecting fetch lets tests pass a fake function that returns a fixed response. Tests can run offline and simulate a timeout without patching module internals.

checkpoint.question: Why is a boolean flag usually a worse API than a second function?
checkpoint.answer: A boolean flag often creates combinations nobody tests and can make one function do several jobs. The caller should choose a different function instead.

lessons.title: Type hints
lessons.goal: Annotate functions and data shapes with builtin generics, unions, TypedDict, and Literal without resorting to Any.
lessons.takeaway: Type hints are a contract sketch: cheap to draw, checked by a machine, and never a substitute for checking the parcel that actually arrived.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: Type hints are executable documentation that a checker verifies. In AI code they are especially valuable because the data is loosely typed JSON: a response may have usage or not, a finish reason is one of four strings, and a missing field becomes None three calls later. Annotations move those failures from production logs into your editor and CI, at the cost of a few minutes per function.
Type hints are a contract sketch: cheap to draw, checked by a machine, and never a substitute for checking the parcel that actually arrived.

sections.heading: Types describe values, not variables An annotation says what a name may hold at
body: Types describe values, not variables An annotation says what a name may hold at that point, and mypy tracks it through assignments and branches. list[dict[str, float]] is a list of dictionaries with string keys and float values; dict[str, list[float]] is a different shape.

Use X | None for values that may be absent and narrow with an early if value is None: return. Avoid Any, which silently disables checking for everything it touches. Model JSON with TypedDict and Literal TypedDict describes a dictionary with fixed keys and per-key types, which matches API payloads better than a wide dict[str, object].

Mark optional keys with NotRequired, or use total=False on a separate class. Literal["stop", "length", "tool_calls"] turns a magic string into a checked set of values. These are static shapes only: they do not validate a response at runtime, so a cast from json.loads is a promise you have not verified.
Gradual typing and the checker loop Start with public functions and the data that crosses a module boundary; private helpers can stay unannotated until they are stable.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Run the type checker in CI with a pinned version; checker upgrades introduce errors, so schedule them like dependency upgrades.
Validate untrusted payloads at runtime with a schema library, then rely on static types inside the process boundary.
Annotate public functions only where the cost is repaid; a private helper with an obvious two-line body does not need ceremony.

lessons.task: Enable mypy strict on an existing package, record the error count, and fix the ten errors at module boundaries (45 minutes). Write a TypedDict for a real API response you have seen, including two optional keys, and a function that returns a safe default (30 minutes).

quiz.question: Why does a clean mypy run not prove that a model response is valid?
choices: list[dict[str, float]] is a list where each item is a dictionary with string keys and float values. dict[str, list[float]]…
An early return such as if value is None: return lets the checker narrow a union (a value that may be one of several types)…
A clean mypy run only checks static shapes. TypedDict and Literal do not validate JSON at runtime, so a response with a…
Use NotRequired when the provider may omit that key. Making it required would misstate the API contract and force every…
quiz.explanation: A clean mypy run only checks static shapes. TypedDict and Literal do not validate JSON at runtime, so a response with a wrong type (for example prompt_tokens as the string "12") can still type-check and fail later.

outcomes: Annotate functions and data shapes with builtin generics, unions, TypedDict, and Literal without resorting to Any.
Run mypy in strict mode on a package and triage errors by boundary, narrowing, and missing annotations.
Decide where runtime validation is still required despite a clean static check.
lessons.mental_model: Type hints are a contract sketch: cheap to draw, checked by a machine, and never a substitute for checking the parcel that actually arrived.
worked_example: During a migration to a second model provider, a client starts failing with TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'NoneType' and 'int' in the cost report. The cause: the new provider omits completion_tokens for cached responses, and the code summed usage.get("completion_tokens") unchecked. The team adds a Usage TypedDict with NotRequired keys, annotates extract_usage(payload: dict[str, object]) -> Usage, and runs mypy strict, which surfaces 23 errors in four modules. They fix the boundary first: parse into Usage with a default of zero and a warning log, then let the rest of the code use plain integers. The decision: absent fields are normalised once, where the payload enters.
common_mistakes: Annotating everything as dict or Any to silence mypy, which leaves the real shape unchecked.
Trusting a TypedDict cast on json.loads output without validating types at the boundary.
Adding hints only to new code so half the package is checked and imports still lie about their contracts.

key_terms.definition: An approach where some functions are fully annotated and checked while unannotated code is treated as compatible, allowing adoption over time.
The process where a type checker uses a runtime check, such as if x is not None, to prove a union has one specific member.
A typing construct describing a dictionary with known string keys and a distinct value type for each key.

checkpoint.question: Why does a clean mypy run not prove that a model response is valid?
checkpoint.answer: A clean mypy run only checks static shapes. TypedDict and Literal do not validate JSON at runtime, so a response with a wrong type (for example prompt_tokens as the string "12") can still type-check and fail later.

checkpoint.question: What is the difference between list[dict[str, float]] and dict[str, list[float]]?
checkpoint.answer: list[dict[str, float]] is a list where each item is a dictionary with string keys and float values. dict[str, list[float]] is a single dictionary whose keys are strings and values are lists of floats.

checkpoint.question: When should an optional payload key be NotRequired rather than required with a default?
checkpoint.answer: Use NotRequired when the provider may omit that key. Making it required would misstate the API contract and force every test or payload to invent a value for it; NotRequired lets the shape match reality.

checkpoint.question: How does an early return help a checker narrow a union?
checkpoint.answer: An early return such as if value is None: return lets the checker narrow a union (a value that may be one of several types) to the remaining type. After that check, mypy knows value is not None and can check later uses safely.

checkpoint.question: Why is Any worse than a missing annotation in strict mode?
checkpoint.answer: Any silently disables checking for everything it touches, so a wrong shape can spread without warnings. In strict mode, a missing annotation is an error you must fix; Any can hide the problem instead.

lessons.title: Classes & OOP
lessons.goal: Decide whether a problem needs a class or a set of functions, using state, invariants, and call-site clarity as the test.
lessons.takeaway: A class is a small machine with dials set at construction: the dials must stay in valid positions, and the machine should expose buttons, not its wiring.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: Your API client will hold configuration and state: a base URL, an auth header, a timeout, a retry budget, and counters for tokens and failures. Those values must stay consistent across calls, and a class is the natural place to enforce that. Classes also go wrong easily, becoming 900-line god objects that mock badly and change for every reason. Knowing when not to use one matters as much as knowing how.
A class is a small machine with dials set at construction: the dials must stay in valid positions, and the machine should expose buttons, not its wiring.

sections.heading: State plus invariants A class earns its place when several functions share state
body: State plus invariants A class earns its place when several functions share state that must remain valid together. A ModelClient owns base_url, timeout_s, and a usage counter; every method can assume the URL has no trailing slash because __init__ normalised it once.

If your class has no state, or the state is a bag of unrelated settings, functions with parameters will be simpler. The test is whether an invariant needs protecting, not whether the domain sounds like a noun. Encapsulation is a convention Python has no private fields, only names with a leading underscore that signal intent.

Use _usage for internals, expose behaviour through methods such as record_usage() and usage_summary(), and keep __init__ cheap: no network calls, no file reads, no sleeps. A __repr__ that shows the model, base URL, and request count makes logs and tracebacks readable.

A classmethod factory such as from_env() centralises configuration parsing without making every test set six environment variables. Composition beats inheritance Subclassing a client for each endpoint or provider creates fragile hierarchies: a change to the base class reaches every child, and mocking a child often means mocking transport too.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Construct clients once per process and reuse the connection pool; a client per request multiplies TLS handshakes and latency.
Keep credentials out of instance attributes that get logged; pass an auth callable or read them at request time.
Emit metrics instead of keeping an unbounded request list, which slowly leaks memory inside a long-running background worker.

lessons.task: Refactor a 200-line procedural client into one stateful class plus pure payload functions, then measure the line counts (45 minutes). Write a fake transport that returns a 429 then a 200, and use it to test a retry wrapper around your client (40 minutes).

quiz.question: What test tells you that a group of functions should become a class?
choices: Injecting a transport allows you to pass a fake version that returns a 429 error first, then a success response, enabling…
A group of functions should become a class when they share state that must remain valid together and that state requires an…
Network calls in __init__ cause problems because tests cannot construct the object without hitting the real network, and…
Inheritance is better than composition only when the child class is usable anywhere the parent is and adds no surprising…
quiz.explanation: A group of functions should become a class when they share state that must remain valid together and that state requires an invariant to be protected.

outcomes: Decide whether a problem needs a class or a set of functions, using state, invariants, and call-site clarity as the test.
Write a client class with a constructor, private helpers, a factory, and a useful __repr__.
Replace inheritance with composition so transport, retries, and parsing can be tested and swapped independently.
lessons.mental_model: A class is a small machine with dials set at construction: the dials must stay in valid positions, and the machine should expose buttons, not its wiring.
worked_example: A client class grows to 780 lines covering chat, embeddings, uploads, retries, and CSV export. Every new endpoint copies the same header logic, and mocking a call requires patching three module globals. In a design review, the team keeps ModelClient for configuration and one request() method, moves endpoint-specific payloads into functions, and injects a transport callable. Retries become a wrapper around transport; tests use a fake that returns a 429 once, then a valid body. The class drops to 90 lines, and coverage of the retry path goes from zero to four tests. The decision: a class owns state and one job; everything else is a function or a collaborator.
common_mistakes: Subclassing the client for each provider, then duplicating header and error logic across five fragile children.
Doing network calls in __init__, so constructing the object fails in tests and at service startup.
Making every attribute public and mutable, so any caller can change the base URL mid-request.

key_terms.definition: A condition that must remain true for an object to be valid, such as a base URL with no trailing slash.
Building behaviour by holding a collaborator and delegating to it, instead of inheriting its methods through a class hierarchy.
An alternative constructor declared with @classmethod that builds an instance from configuration, a file, or another object.

checkpoint.question: What test tells you that a group of functions should become a class?
checkpoint.answer: A group of functions should become a class when they share state that must remain valid together and that state requires an invariant to be protected.

checkpoint.question: Why is a network call inside __init__ a problem for tests and for startup?
checkpoint.answer: Network calls in __init__ cause problems because tests cannot construct the object without hitting the real network, and service startup fails if the network is down. Keep __init__ cheap: just store the settings, don't do work.

checkpoint.question: How does injecting a transport change the way you test a 429 retry?
checkpoint.answer: Injecting a transport allows you to pass a fake version that returns a 429 error first, then a success response, enabling you to test retry logic without touching the real network.

checkpoint.question: When is inheritance a better choice than composition, and what must remain true?
checkpoint.answer: Inheritance is better than composition only when the child class is usable anywhere the parent is and adds no surprising behavior—genuine substitution. Otherwise, pass collaborators in as parameters.

checkpoint.question: What belongs in __repr__, and what must never appear there?
checkpoint.answer: __repr__ should show identifying information like the host and request count so logs are readable. Never include headers, tokens, keys, or personal data that could leak secrets.

lessons.title: Dataclasses
lessons.goal: Define record types with the dataclass decorator, including defaults, field(default_factory=...), and computed properties.
lessons.takeaway: A dataclass is a labelled parts tray: the fields are visible at a glance, each slot gets its own contents, and nothing enters the tray unvalidated.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: AI pipelines are full of small records: a usage report, a scored case, a retrieved chunk, a cost summary. Writing __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ by hand for each is noise that hides bugs. Dataclasses generate those methods from the field list, so the shape of the data is visible in one place. The decisions that remain, defaults, mutability, and invariants, are where the real engineering sits.
A dataclass is a labelled parts tray: the fields are visible at a glance, each slot gets its own contents, and nothing enters the tray unvalidated.

sections.heading: Generated methods, visible shape The dataclass decorator reads the class annotat
body: Generated methods, visible shape The dataclass decorator reads the class annotations and generates __init__, __repr__, and __eq__.

Two instances with the same field values compare equal, which is what you want for records and what you rarely want for clients holding sockets. field(default_factory=list) supplies a new list per instance; a bare class-level list raises at definition because dataclasses reject the shared-default bug outright. asdict() converts nested dataclasses to dictionaries for JSON, at the cost of a deep copy.

Frozen records and invariants dataclass(frozen=True) blocks attribute assignment and makes instances hashable, so a record can key a dictionary or live in a set. Use it for values that represent a fact at a point in time: a usage report does not change, a new report replaces it.

Add __post_init__ to validate combinations the type system cannot express, such as a non-negative token count. Raise ValueError there; a record that exists should already be valid. Dataclass or schema model A dataclass describes data your code already trusts.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Keep dataclasses for internal, trusted values and validate at the edge; the type checker sees shapes, not runtime reality.
Prefer frozen records for anything logged or passed across threads, so a later mutation cannot rewrite history in a trace.
Do not compare records holding floats with equality to decide thresholds; the difference between 0.7999 and 0.8 needs an epsilon.

lessons.task: Convert a hand-written record class to a frozen dataclass with one invariant and a computed property, then diff the line count (30 minutes). Write a two-instance test that proves default_factory prevents shared state, and one that shows a bare default fails at import (20 minutes).

quiz.question: Why does a bare list default fail in a dataclass while the same default is legal in a normal function?
choices: frozen=True blocks attribute assignment after construction and makes instances hashable by field value, so a record can be…
A bare list default fails in a dataclass because dataclasses reject the shared-default bug at definition time: the list…
Value equality helps for records that represent facts, such as a usage report or a CaseResult, where two instances with the…
Post-init checks belong in __post_init__ for invariants the type system cannot express, such as a score being between 0 and…
quiz.explanation: A bare list default fails in a dataclass because dataclasses reject the shared-default bug at definition time: the list would be created once and shared by every instance. A normal function allows a mutable default, but it is also evaluated once and shared across calls, so it can cause the same kind of bug; dataclasses catch it early.

outcomes: Define record types with the dataclass decorator, including defaults, field(default_factory=...), and computed properties.
Choose between mutable and frozen dataclasses based on whether identity or value semantics fit the data.
Explain why a dataclass is not a validation layer and where a schema model must take over.
lessons.mental_model: A dataclass is a labelled parts tray: the fields are visible at a glance, each slot gets its own contents, and nothing enters the tray unvalidated.
worked_example: An evaluation harness stores one CaseResult per prompt and a RunSummary for the batch. The first version uses a plain class with errors = [] as a class attribute, so all 300 results share one list and the summary reports 41 failures instead of 3. The rewrite uses a frozen dataclass for CaseResult and a mutable dataclass with field(default_factory=list) for the summary, plus a post-init check that rejects a score outside 0 to 1. A property computes pass_rate from counts instead of storing it. The decision: records are frozen, aggregates are mutable, and invalid scores fail at construction rather than in a dashboard.
common_mistakes: Using a mutable class attribute for a list of errors, so all instances silently share one bucket.
Marking a record frozen and then needing to update it in a loop, causing an awkward rebuild on every iteration.
Trusting a dataclass to validate API JSON, then discovering that a string token count passed through unchanged.

key_terms.definition: A dataclass whose attributes cannot be assigned after construction, making instances immutable and hashable by field value. post_init hook A method that runs after the generated initialiser, used to validate or derive fields that depend on each other.

checkpoint.question: Why does a bare list default fail in a dataclass while the same default is legal in a normal function?
checkpoint.answer: A bare list default fails in a dataclass because dataclasses reject the shared-default bug at definition time: the list would be created once and shared by every instance. A normal function allows a mutable default, but it is also evaluated once and shared across calls, so it can cause the same kind of bug; dataclasses catch it early.

checkpoint.question: When does value equality help, and when is it misleading for a client object?
checkpoint.answer: Value equality helps for records that represent facts, such as a usage report or a CaseResult, where two instances with the same field values should be treated as the same. It is misleading for client objects that hold unique resources like sockets, where identity matters more than matching field values.

checkpoint.question: What does frozen=True guarantee, and what does it not prevent?
checkpoint.answer: frozen=True blocks attribute assignment after construction and makes instances hashable by field value, so a record can be used as a dictionary key or in a set. It does not make nested mutable objects deeply immutable; for example, a list field can still be mutated.

checkpoint.question: Which checks belong in the post-init hook rather than in a caller?
checkpoint.answer: Post-init checks belong in __post_init__ for invariants the type system cannot express, such as a score being between 0 and 1 or a non-negative token count. These checks make the record valid at construction, so callers do not have to enforce them later.

checkpoint.question: Why is a dataclass a poor choice for parsing an untrusted API response?
checkpoint.answer: A dataclass does not coerce types (like turning the string "12" into 12), reject unknown fields, or explain validation errors to an API caller. Use a schema model such as Pydantic at the trust boundary where untrusted JSON arrives, then convert to a dataclass for internal use.

lessons.title: Pydantic
lessons.goal: Define a Pydantic model with field constraints, strict types, and cross-field validation for an external payload.
lessons.takeaway: A schema is a customs checkpoint: nothing enters the application until its paperwork is checked, and rejected items are logged rather than quietly smuggled through.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: Models receive JSON from providers, LLM output, and databases, and every field can be missing, misnamed, or the wrong type. Pydantic checks that data at runtime, at the point it enters your program, so the rest of the code works with typed objects and one clear failure contract. Without that boundary, a string where an integer belongs surfaces three functions later as a confusing TypeError.
A schema is a customs checkpoint: nothing enters the application until its paperwork is checked, and rejected items are logged rather than quietly smuggled through.

sections.heading: Parse at the boundary A dataclass describes shape; Pydantic also enforces it whi
body: Parse at the boundary A dataclass describes shape; Pydantic also enforces it while constructing the object. Declare a BaseModel for each external payload, such as catalogue rows or tool arguments, and call model_validate or model_validate_json as soon as bytes arrive.

Inside the function you then hold a typed instance whose attributes are guaranteed, so downstream code needs no defensive checks. Validation is a runtime contract, not a type hint: mypy never sees the JSON that arrives at 03:00. Constraints and coercion Field carries the rules: min_length, max_length, gt, ge, le, pattern, and default.
Pydantic's default lax mode coerces '128000' to 128000 and 'true' to True, which helps with sloppy CSV exports but hides breakage; use StrictInt or strict=True where a numeric string must fail.

Setting extra='forbid' rejects unknown keys and catches provider drift such as context_windows. model_validate_json parses once from bytes, avoiding a json.loads call that loses the original error positions. Errors are structured data A failed parse raises one ValidationError containing every problem, each with loc, msg, type, and input.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Version schemas and keep the previous reader working during a rollout; adding optional fields is safer than renaming one.
Emit reject counts per provider and per field, and alert before a quiet schema change becomes a routing incident.
Store quarantined payloads with sensitive text redacted and a retention limit, so failures can be replayed without keeping customer data forever.

lessons.task: Model a real API response with three constrained fields and a cross-field rule, then validate a valid and an invalid fixture (40 minutes). Add per-record error reporting to a loop that imports a JSON file, and print a total accepted and rejected count (35 minutes).

quiz.question: Why does a dataclass alone fail to protect a function that parses provider JSON?
choices: Coercion helps with messy input, such as a sloppy CSV export where the string '128000' should become the number 128000. It…
A cross-field validator runs after the individual fields have passed. If a field fails validation first, there is no valid…
The loc tuple is the machine-readable path to the failing field, including nested model prefixes, like ('pricing',…
A dataclass only describes the shape of the data; it does not enforce it. Pydantic also enforces the shape while…
quiz.explanation: A dataclass only describes the shape of the data; it does not enforce it. Pydantic also enforces the shape while constructing the object, so a string where an integer belongs fails right at the boundary instead of surfacing three functions later as a confusing TypeError.

outcomes: Define a Pydantic model with field constraints, strict types, and cross-field validation for an external payload.
Validate JSON into typed objects with model_validate_json and reject unknown fields before they reach your code.
Read ValidationError locations to quarantine bad records while keeping the valid ones.
lessons.mental_model: A schema is a customs checkpoint: nothing enters the application until its paperwork is checked, and rejected items are logged rather than quietly smuggled through.
worked_example: Tomás runs ingestion for a model-routing startup that resells nine providers. Every night he pulls a 2,400-row catalogue where prices are quoted per million tokens. A provider once renamed context_window to context_windows, and his loader silently wrote rows with a zero context limit; routing sent 11% of long prompts to a model that truncated them. He now validates each row into an Offer model with extra='forbid', context_window: int = Field(gt=0, le=2_000_000), and a validator that rejects output prices below input prices. On the first run 61 of 2,400 rows fail, including the renamed field. The decision is to quarantine rejects with provider and row number, alert above a 0.5% reject rate, and continue with 2,339 valid offers.
common_mistakes: Validating only after writing to the database, so bad rows are already visible to dashboards and other services.
Catching ValidationError and returning a default object, which turns a contract violation into silent wrong data.
Hand-reading nested dictionaries with .get chains while assuming the type hints describe what actually arrived.

key_terms.definition: The Pydantic class that declares fields and validates input at construction; every external payload model inherits from it.
The single exception raised when one or more fields fail validation; it carries a structured list of locations and messages.
The automatic conversion of compatible input, such as the string '42' to the integer 42, before validation rules are applied.

checkpoint.question: Why does a dataclass alone fail to protect a function that parses provider JSON?
checkpoint.answer: A dataclass only describes the shape of the data; it does not enforce it. Pydantic also enforces the shape while constructing the object, so a string where an integer belongs fails right at the boundary instead of surfacing three functions later as a confusing TypeError.

checkpoint.question: When is coercion helpful, and when does it hide a defect you need to see?
checkpoint.answer: Coercion helps with messy input, such as a sloppy CSV export where the string '128000' should become the number 128000. It hides a defect when a numeric string must fail, such as a price arriving as 'cheap' or a context window as '128k', so use StrictInt or strict=True on those fields.

checkpoint.question: What information does the loc tuple add that the error message does not?
checkpoint.answer: The loc tuple is the machine-readable path to the failing field, including nested model prefixes, like ('pricing', 'input_usd'). The msg tells you what went wrong but not which field in a nested payload, so loc is what lets you pinpoint and log the exact field.

checkpoint.question: Why can a cross-field validator be skipped even when one of its fields is present?
checkpoint.answer: A cross-field validator runs after the individual fields have passed. If a field fails validation first, there is no valid object to check, so the cross-field validator never runs; fix the field-level errors before debugging business rules.

checkpoint.question: How would you reject one bad record without abandoning a 2,400-row import?
