checkpoint.answer: Wrap each record in try/except ValidationError, log the record index, the error loc, and the error type, then continue with the next row. That way one bad record is quarantined and the rest of the 2,400-row import still completes.

lessons.title: Async Python
lessons.goal: Distinguish concurrency from parallelism and decide when an AI workload needs asyncio rather than threads or processes.
lessons.takeaway: Async is one fast waiter serving many tables: he takes orders while food cooks, but stops serving entirely if he starts cooking a dish himself.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: Model calls spend almost all their time waiting on a network, so a service that handles them one at a time wastes capacity. Async Python lets one thread keep hundreds of requests in flight, but only while every operation yields. Understanding the loop explains both the throughput gain and the outages caused by one synchronous library call.
Async is one fast waiter serving many tables: he takes orders while food cooks, but stops serving entirely if he starts cooking a dish himself.

sections.heading: One thread, many waiting requests The event loop is a single-threaded scheduler
body: One thread, many waiting requests The event loop is a single-threaded scheduler holding a queue of ready callbacks. When a coroutine awaits network I/O, it registers a callback and yields, and the loop runs another request until the socket is ready. Concurrency comes from overlapping waits, not from doing two things at once.

Two hundred pending model calls can share one thread because each is idle most of its lifetime. CPU-bound work has no await point, so it occupies the thread completely and queues everything behind it.

The blocking trap Any synchronous call inside a coroutine blocks the loop: requests.get, time.sleep, a large pandas operation, or a tokenizer that releases the GIL only intermittently. One blocked loop means every request misses its deadline, which looks like a provider outage.

Use async-native clients such as httpx.AsyncClient, and move unavoidable blocking work to a worker thread with asyncio.to_thread or a process pool. Enable asyncio debug mode in staging, where slow callbacks are logged with their stack. Bounded fan-out and backpressure Fan-out needs a ceiling.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Set a global concurrency cap per provider and a queue deadline; unbounded fan-out converts a slow dependency into an outage.
Expose in-flight tasks, queue wait, and event-loop lag as metrics; lag above 100 ms means something is blocking.
Use one client per process with explicit connection limits, and close it during shutdown so sockets and tasks drain.

lessons.task: Benchmark 100 calls with a synchronous client and an async client bounded at 8, then record elapsed time and errors (40 minutes). Add event-loop lag monitoring to a spare service and reproduce a stall with one time.sleep(2) call (30 minutes).

quiz.question: Why does a single blocking requests.get degrade every request, not just the one that called it?
choices: All 200 calls fired at once overwhelmed the provider: requests were rejected with 429 and the connection pool closed, so…
A thread pool is better when the blocking library cannot be rewritten or calls into C extensions that hold the GIL anyway —…
While a coroutine awaits a socket read, the event loop registers interest in that file descriptor and runs other ready…
requests.get is synchronous: it blocks the calling thread until the response arrives. Inside a coroutine on a single…
quiz.explanation: requests.get is synchronous: it blocks the calling thread until the response arrives. Inside a coroutine on a single event-loop thread, every other pending task stops being served for the whole 190 ms, so one slow call stalls all requests in flight.

outcomes: Distinguish concurrency from parallelism and decide when an AI workload needs asyncio rather than threads or processes.
Explain how the event loop schedules coroutines and why one blocking call stalls every pending request.
Choose between asyncio.gather, TaskGroup, and a bounded semaphore for fan-out model calls.
lessons.mental_model: Async is one fast waiter serving many tables: he takes orders while food cooks, but stops serving entirely if he starts cooking a dish himself.
worked_example: Tomas benchmarks enrichment of 200 support tickets at a nine-person search startup. The synchronous client takes 41 seconds because each 190 ms model call waits for the last. His first async version fires all 200 with gather, then fails after 60 seconds with 429 responses and a closed connection pool. He limits concurrency to 16 with a semaphore, reuses one httpx.AsyncClient, and sets a 20-second timeout per call. The batch finishes in 3.1 seconds with zero retries. The decision: keep concurrency at 16, because 32 saved only 200 ms while doubling rate-limit errors. He records the result beside the provider's documented limit of 20 requests per second.
common_mistakes: Calling requests.get or time.sleep inside a coroutine, which freezes every other task on the loop.
Using asyncio.gather on an unbounded list, then blaming the provider when 200 parallel calls return 429.
Running CPU-heavy parsing or local embedding on the event loop instead of a worker thread or process.

key_terms.definition: A single-threaded scheduler that runs ready callbacks and resumes coroutines when their awaited I/O completes.
A limit that slows producers when downstream capacity is full, preventing queues, connection pools, or providers from being overwhelmed.
A function defined with async def that can pause at await and resume later with a result or exception.

checkpoint.question: Why does a single blocking requests.get degrade every request, not just the one that called it?
checkpoint.answer: requests.get is synchronous: it blocks the calling thread until the response arrives. Inside a coroutine on a single event-loop thread, every other pending task stops being served for the whole 190 ms, so one slow call stalls all requests in flight.

checkpoint.question: What does the event loop do while a coroutine awaits a socket read?
checkpoint.answer: While a coroutine awaits a socket read, the event loop registers interest in that file descriptor and runs other ready coroutines. When the OS signals the socket is readable, the loop resumes the suspended coroutine with the data.

checkpoint.question: When is a thread pool a better answer than rewriting a library as async?
checkpoint.answer: A thread pool is better when the blocking library cannot be rewritten or calls into C extensions that hold the GIL anyway — you offload the blocking call to a worker thread and keep the loop responsive. Rewriting as async is worthwhile when the library is I/O-bound, maintained, and a true async version exists.

checkpoint.question: Why did 200 concurrent calls perform worse than 16 in the example?
checkpoint.answer: All 200 calls fired at once overwhelmed the provider: requests were rejected with 429 and the connection pool closed, so retries and queuing dominated while concurrency beyond the server limit bought nothing. Sixteen workers matched the provider’s published 20 requests per second, finishing in 3.1 seconds with zero retries.

checkpoint.question: What does TaskGroup do to sibling tasks when one raises an exception?
checkpoint.answer: If one task in a TaskGroup raises, the group cancels all sibling tasks and waits for them to finish unwinding, then propagates an ExceptionGroup (or the original error in a plain context). No sibling is left running in the background after the failure.

lessons.title: async / await
lessons.goal: Write async functions, await coroutines, and explain why calling one without awaiting returns a coroutine object.
lessons.takeaway: await is a hand-off, not an ordinary call: your task pauses, the loop runs someone else, and you resume when the result is ready.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: Most async bugs are syntax-shaped: a missing await, a coroutine created and never scheduled, or a cancellation swallowed by a bare except. These mistakes pass review because the code looks concurrent. Precise knowledge of await, task lifetime, and cancellation turns asyncio from a source of mystery failures into predictable control flow.
await is a hand-off, not an ordinary call: your task pauses, the loop runs someone else, and you resume when the result is ready.

sections.heading: await is a suspension point Calling an async function creates a coroutine object
body: await is a suspension point Calling an async function creates a coroutine object; nothing runs until it is awaited or scheduled as a task. At await, the current task suspends and the event loop runs other work until the awaitable completes.

This is why two sequential awaits still take the sum of both latencies: the second call is created only after the first returns. Use asyncio.gather or a TaskGroup when calls are independent, and check for RuntimeWarning: coroutine was never awaited in tests.

Tasks own lifetimes A Task is a scheduled coroutine with its own lifecycle. asyncio.TaskGroup creates children inside a scope that waits for all of them; if one fails, the others are cancelled and the error surfaces as an ExceptionGroup at scope exit.

Cancellation arrives as CancelledError at the next await point and must be allowed to propagate after cleanup. A bare except Exception swallows it, so the task appears to finish normally while the caller believes the work stopped.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Translate TimeoutError to 504 and cancellation to no response; a client that disconnected should never receive a stale payload.
Keep a registry of background tasks and await or cancel every one at shutdown; fire-and-forget work loses exceptions silently.
Log task name, trace ID, and elapsed time at each await boundary so a stuck coroutine can be located without a profiler.

lessons.task: Write a failing test that calls an async function without await, observe the warning, then fix it and keep the test (30 minutes). Convert two sequential awaits into a TaskGroup, then measure the latency difference over 20 runs (40 minutes).

quiz.question: What happens when you call an async function without awaiting it?
choices: Calling an async function creates a coroutine object; nothing runs until it is awaited or scheduled as a task. If you call…
CancelledError means the task is being cancelled, often because the client disconnected or a timeout fired. If you catch…
TaskGroup is structured: if one child fails, the other children are cancelled and the error surfaces as an ExceptionGroup…
Sequential awaits do not overlap because the next call or awaitable is created/started only after the previous await…
quiz.explanation: Calling an async function creates a coroutine object; nothing runs until it is awaited or scheduled as a task. If you call it and discard it, you may only see RuntimeWarning: coroutine was never awaited at garbage collection, and you can accidentally serialize the coroutine object instead of its result.

outcomes: Write async functions, await coroutines, and explain why calling one without awaiting returns a coroutine object.
Propagate exceptions and cancellation correctly across tasks, timeouts, and TaskGroup boundaries.
Use async context managers and async iterators to manage clients, sessions, and streamed responses.
lessons.mental_model: await is a hand-off, not an ordinary call: your task pauses, the loop runs someone else, and you resume when the result is ready.
worked_example: Rin ships a usage endpoint that returns a tokens field containing <coroutine object get_usage at 0x...>. The handler calls usage = get_usage(user_id) and never awaits it, so the coroutine object is serialised and a RuntimeWarning is the only clue. While fixing it, she finds a second problem: when the client disconnects, the handler returns but the model task keeps running and bills for a response nobody receives. She awaits the call, wraps two lookups in asyncio.TaskGroup, adds asyncio.timeout(8), and lets CancelledError propagate after closing the stream. The endpoint now returns real numbers, and traces show cancelled tasks ending within 50 ms. The decision: no bare except Exception around awaits, because it hides cancellation as well as errors.
common_mistakes: Forgetting await, then serialising a coroutine object into a response body or a database column.
Catching Exception around an await and logging cancellation as a normal error, leaving work running in the background.
Creating background tasks with create_task and dropping the returned reference, so the task can be garbage-collected mid-flight.

key_terms.definition: An object usable with await, typically a coroutine, Task, or Future, that eventually produces a value or raises an exception.
A request to stop a task, delivered as CancelledError at its next await point and expected to propagate after cleanup.
A pattern where child tasks live inside a scope that cannot exit until every child finishes, fails, or is cancelled.

checkpoint.question: What happens when you call an async function without awaiting it?
checkpoint.answer: Calling an async function creates a coroutine object; nothing runs until it is awaited or scheduled as a task. If you call it and discard it, you may only see RuntimeWarning: coroutine was never awaited at garbage collection, and you can accidentally serialize the coroutine object instead of its result.

checkpoint.question: Why does awaiting two calls sequentially fail to overlap their latency?
checkpoint.answer: Sequential awaits do not overlap because the next call or awaitable is created/started only after the previous await returns. The total latency is the sum: two 5-second calls awaited one after another take about 10 seconds. Use asyncio.gather or a TaskGroup when the calls are independent.

checkpoint.question: How does TaskGroup error handling differ from gather with return_exceptions=True?
checkpoint.answer: TaskGroup is structured: if one child fails, the other children are cancelled and the error surfaces as an ExceptionGroup when the scope exits, so no child outlives the block. gather with return_exceptions=True does not fail-fast-cancel siblings; it lets tasks finish and returns each result or exception in the result list.

checkpoint.question: Why must CancelledError usually be re-raised rather than converted to a 500?
checkpoint.answer: CancelledError means the task is being cancelled, often because the client disconnected or a timeout fired. If you catch it, do cleanup and re-raise it so the caller knows the work stopped; converting it to a 500 can send a stale payload to a client that already left and can hide the cancellation.

checkpoint.question: When is asyncio.shield justified, and what risk does it introduce?
checkpoint.answer: asyncio.shield is justified only when an awaitable must keep running even if its parent task is cancelled. The risk is an orphaned task that keeps running after the request stops, may waste resources, and may lose its exceptions unless it is tracked, awaited, or cancelled at shutdown.

outcomes: Model a problem with variables, expressions and well-named functions
Choose control flow and data structures that match the task
Trace and explain a program line by line before running it

modules.title: Python Foundations
modules.description: Python language fundamentals for engineering applications

lessons.title: Python Basics
lessons.goal: Run Python programs two ways — the interactive interpreter and script files — and write a small program that reads input, computes a result, and prints it.
lessons.takeaway: Python favours readable, explicit code: simple statements, truthy conditions and f-strings cover most everyday scripting.

sections.heading: Two ways to run Python
body: The interpreter (python3) is a live REPL: type an expression, see the value instantly. Perfect for probing syntax and trying one-liners. Scripts are files ending in .py that run top-to-bottom — the unit of work you keep in version control.

Indentation is syntax, not style: Python groups the body of an if/for/def by leading spaces. Four spaces is the convention; mixing tabs and spaces is the fastest way to an error that makes no sense at first glance.
Comments with # explain why code does what it does, not what it obviously does. A comment that restates the code is noise; a comment that records a constraint or a failed approach is gold.

sections.heading: Input, processing, output
body: Almost every beginner program is a pipeline: read something (input(), CLI args, a file), transform it, emit something (print(), a file, a return value). The pipeline framing keeps big programs understandable.

input() returns a string — always. "42" is text, not the number 42. Convert deliberately: int("42") raises ValueError on bad input, which is exactly the moment you want the program to fail loudly and tell you the problem.
print() formats with f-strings: f"{price:.2f}" renders 3.5 as 3.50. Formatting at the boundary (the print) beats scattering round() calls through your logic.

sections.heading: Naming, errors, and the traceback
body: Names are lowercase_with_underscores. Constants in caps (TAX_RATE). Avoid single letters except loop indices. A good name is the cheapest documentation a language will ever give you.

A traceback is not an enemy; it is the program telling you exactly where and why it died. Read it bottom-up: the last line names the error type and message; the frames above it walk back to your code.

Common first-week errors you will meet: NameError (used before defined), SyntaxError (typo in the code), TypeError (wrong kind of thing), ValueError (right kind, bad value), and IndentationError (the whitespace betrayed you).

lessons.task: Write a script area_converter.py that asks for a room name and its width and length in metres (as text), computes the floor area, and prints "<name>: <area> m^2". Handle non-numeric input by printing a friendly message and exiting with code 1. Test it with three rooms, including one invalid entry.

quiz.question: What does input("Age: ") + 1 do?
choices: Returns the next integer
Concatenates text like "31" + 1
A TypeError
Prints Age: 1
quiz.explanation: input() returns str; str + int is a TypeError. Convert first with int(), and handle ValueError for non-numeric input.

outcomes: Write a function with an explicit contract: typed parameters, a single return shape, and documented failure behaviour.
Replace mutable default arguments and hidden global state with keyword-only parameters and injected dependencies.
Refactor a long procedure into three composable functions that can each be tested in isolation.
lessons.mental_model: A function is a kitchen appliance: one job, a clear input, a predictable output, and a warning label for the ways it can burn you.
worked_example: An evaluation script has one 140-line run() that loads 500 prompts, calls the model, parses JSON, scores each answer, and writes a CSV. When 12 responses fail schema validation, the whole run exits and no scores are saved. Ana splits it into load_cases, score_case, and write_report, with run() composing them. score_case returns a result dictionary and records an error for a malformed response; run keeps going per case. The rerun completes in 6 minutes, reports the 12 errors instead of losing the batch, and a new unit test covers the malformed case offline. The decision: one failure should cost one case, not the run.
common_mistakes: Using a list default to collect results, then wondering why yesterday's cases appear in today's report.
Letting a helper print progress and return a value, so tests must capture stdout to know whether it worked.
Adding retry=True and quiet=False flags until one function has sixteen combinations nobody tests.

key_terms.definition: A function whose output depends only on its arguments and which changes no external state, so it can be tested with literals.
A parameter default such as a list or dictionary created once when the function is defined and shared by every call.
A parameter placed after the star in the signature, callable only by name, which keeps call sites readable as the API grows.

checkpoint.question: Why does a list default argument persist between calls, and what replaces it?
checkpoint.answer: A list default is created once when the function is defined, so every call shares the same list. Replace it with None and create a new list inside the function.

checkpoint.question: What makes a function pure, and why does purity simplify testing?
checkpoint.answer: A pure function's output depends only on its arguments, and it changes no external state. That lets tests pass simple literal values with no setup.

checkpoint.question: When should a helper raise instead of returning None for bad input?
checkpoint.answer: A helper should raise when bad input means it cannot produce its promised return value, rather than returning None or an empty string that looks like a valid answer. The lesson's example is parse_usage(response), which returns a Usage or raises ValueError.

checkpoint.question: How does injecting fetch change what your tests need to run?
checkpoint.answer: Injecting fetch lets tests pass a fake function that returns a fixed response. Tests can run offline and simulate a timeout without patching module internals.

checkpoint.question: Why is a boolean flag usually a worse API than a second function?
checkpoint.answer: A boolean flag often creates combinations nobody tests and can make one function do several jobs. The caller should choose a different function instead.

lessons.title: Lists and Dictionaries
lessons.goal: Model collections of items with lists and dictionaries, iterate them without indexing errors, and pick the right container for the job.
lessons.takeaway: Lists keep order and dictionaries keep lookup fast; reach for the one whose access pattern matches the question.

sections.heading: Lists: ordered, mutable, indexable
body: items = [3, 1, 4] keeps order and lets you read, replace or remove by position. items[0] is the head; items[-1] is the tail; items[1:3] is a slice (start inclusive, stop exclusive) that produces a new list.

Lists are mutable: append, extend, insert, pop, remove, sort. sort() rearranges in place; sorted(items) returns a new list. Copying naively with b = a aliases the same list — use b = a.copy() or b = list(a) when you need independence.
Common idioms: sum(items), len(items), max/min, any/all, and the membership test x in items. Looping with enumerate(items) gives both index and value — no range(len(...)) needed.

sections.heading: Dictionaries: keys to values
body: points = {"alice": 3, "bob": 7} maps string keys to values. Read with points["alice"] (KeyError if absent) or points.get("carol", 0) (default when absent). Check membership with "alice" in points — not in points.values().

Dicts preserve insertion order (since Python 3.7) and iterate the keys by default; points.items() yields (key, value) pairs; points.values() yields values. Use update() to merge and pop(key, default) to remove with a default.
Grouping with dicts is idiomatic: bucket = {}; for item in items: bucket.setdefault(item.kind, []).append(item). setdefault creates the list the first time a new kind appears.

sections.heading: Choosing between them
body: Ask one question: do I look things up by position/order (list) or by label (dict)? Ordered rolls of participants → list. Score by name → dict. Unique tags → set. Fixed shape → tuple (or a small class when meaning grows).

Lists cost O(n) for membership; dicts cost O(1). A list of ten thousand records scanned per lookup is slow at scale; one dict lookup is instant. Measured intuition like this is half of data-structure choice.

List comprehensions compress loop-and-build patterns: [p * 2 for p in prices if p > 0] builds a filtered, transformed list in one expression. Use them for clarity; if the logic inside grows a second sentence, write the loop.

lessons.task: Given a hard-coded list of order dicts {"item": str, "qty": int, "price": float}, produce (1) total revenue per item as a dict, (2) the three best-selling items by total quantity as a sorted list, (3) a flat list of unit revenues (qty * price) with any non-positive price filtered out, using a comprehension.

quiz.question: What does items[1:3] produce for items = [10, 20, 30, 40]?
quiz.explanation: Slicing is start-inclusive, stop-exclusive: indices 1 and 2, giving [20, 30]. items[1:4] would include 40.

outcomes: Define a Pydantic model with field constraints, strict types, and cross-field validation for an external payload.
Validate JSON into typed objects with model_validate_json and reject unknown fields before they reach your code.
Read ValidationError locations to quarantine bad records while keeping the valid ones.
lessons.mental_model: A schema is a customs checkpoint: nothing enters the application until its paperwork is checked, and rejected items are logged rather than quietly smuggled through.
worked_example: Tomás runs ingestion for a model-routing startup that resells nine providers. Every night he pulls a 2,400-row catalogue where prices are quoted per million tokens. A provider once renamed context_window to context_windows, and his loader silently wrote rows with a zero context limit; routing sent 11% of long prompts to a model that truncated them. He now validates each row into an Offer model with extra='forbid', context_window: int = Field(gt=0, le=2_000_000), and a validator that rejects output prices below input prices. On the first run 61 of 2,400 rows fail, including the renamed field. The decision is to quarantine rejects with provider and row number, alert above a 0.5% reject rate, and continue with 2,339 valid offers.
common_mistakes: Validating only after writing to the database, so bad rows are already visible to dashboards and other services.
Catching ValidationError and returning a default object, which turns a contract violation into silent wrong data.
Hand-reading nested dictionaries with .get chains while assuming the type hints describe what actually arrived.

key_terms.definition: The Pydantic class that declares fields and validates input at construction; every external payload model inherits from it.
The single exception raised when one or more fields fail validation; it carries a structured list of locations and messages.
The automatic conversion of compatible input, such as the string '42' to the integer 42, before validation rules are applied.

checkpoint.question: Why does a dataclass alone fail to protect a function that parses provider JSON?
checkpoint.answer: A dataclass only describes the shape of the data; it does not enforce it. Pydantic also enforces the shape while constructing the object, so a string where an integer belongs fails right at the boundary instead of surfacing three functions later as a confusing TypeError.

checkpoint.question: When is coercion helpful, and when does it hide a defect you need to see?
checkpoint.answer: Coercion helps with messy input, such as a sloppy CSV export where the string '128000' should become the number 128000. It hides a defect when a numeric string must fail, such as a price arriving as 'cheap' or a context window as '128k', so use StrictInt or strict=True on those fields.

checkpoint.question: What information does the loc tuple add that the error message does not?
checkpoint.answer: The loc tuple is the machine-readable path to the failing field, including nested model prefixes, like ('pricing', 'input_usd'). The msg tells you what went wrong but not which field in a nested payload, so loc is what lets you pinpoint and log the exact field.

checkpoint.question: Why can a cross-field validator be skipped even when one of its fields is present?
checkpoint.answer: A cross-field validator runs after the individual fields have passed. If a field fails validation first, there is no valid object to check, so the cross-field validator never runs; fix the field-level errors before debugging business rules.

checkpoint.question: How would you reject one bad record without abandoning a 2,400-row import?
checkpoint.answer: Wrap each record in try/except ValidationError, log the record index, the error loc, and the error type, then continue with the next row. That way one bad record is quarantined and the rest of the 2,400-row import still completes.

lessons.title: Modules and Packages
lessons.goal: Import standard library modules confidently, split a program across files, and understand what __name__ == "__main__" does.
lessons.takeaway: Modules and packages turn a script into a system: import what you need, keep a clear public surface and avoid circular imports.

sections.heading: The standard library is huge
body: Batteries included: math (sqrt, floor, ceil), statistics (mean, median), random (choice, randint, shuffle, seed), json (load, dump), pathlib (cross-platform paths), datetime, collections (Counter, deque, defaultdict), itertools, re, and dozens more.

import json then json.loads(text), or from json import loads then loads(text). The first keeps provenance visible (json.loads is obviously JSON); the second saves typing when a module is used heavily.
The docs at docs.python.org are the canonical reference. Reading one page of real documentation beats any tutorial for building durable skill.

sections.heading: Your own modules and __main__
body: Any .py file is a module. A folder with an __init__.py is a package. Splitting helpers into geometry.py and importing it from main.py is how scripts graduate into maintainable projects.

Every module has a built-in name __name__. It is "__main__" when the file is executed directly, and the module name when imported. The guard if __name__ == "__main__": main() lets the same file be both importable library and runnable script without side effects on import.
Import order convention: stdlib, third-party, your package — alphabetically inside each group, one group per block. Linters (ruff, flake8) enforce it so diffs stay clean.

sections.heading: Dependencies and environments
body: Third-party packages (requests, numpy, flask) are installed into environments, not globally into the OS interpreter. venv creates an isolated environment per project: python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate && pip install requests.
requirements.txt (or pyproject.toml) records exact dependencies so the project builds identically on your machine and CI. Commit it always; commit .venv never.
Locking matters because "it works on my machine" is usually "my machine has different package versions". Deterministic environments are how teams stop arguing about ghosts.

lessons.task: Create a package shop/ with __init__.py, pricing.py (compute_total(items) where items are price, qty tuples) and cli.py with a main() that prints a receipt for a fixed basket. Guard cli.py with __name__ == "__main__". Add a README-free test: run python -m shop.cli and python -c "from shop.pricing import compute_total; print(compute_total([(2.5, 3)]))".

quiz.question: Why does a file use if __name__ == "__main__"?
choices: To enable hot reload
To avoid running main() on import
To satisfy the linter
To make imports faster
quiz.explanation: When imported, __name__ is the module name, not "__main__"; the guard keeps import side-effect free while still allowing direct execution.

outcomes: Create a src layout with a package, an entry point, and a tests directory that imports the package without path hacks.
Draw the dependency direction between schemas, I/O, domain logic, and the command-line entry point.
Explain why python -m package avoids the import failures caused by running a file inside the package.
lessons.mental_model: A package is a building with labelled rooms: the corridor is short, the doors face one direction, and you never climb through a window to reach the database.
worked_example: At a four-person team building a model-catalogue client, loader.py starts importing catalog.py to reuse a price formatter, while catalog.py already imports loader.py to read files. Tests pass on one laptop because the modules were imported in a lucky order, then fail in CI with ImportError: partially initialized module. In the review, the team moves the formatter into formatting.py, points both modules at it, and adds __main__.py. They also replace sys.path.append("..") in the tests with an editable install. The CI run drops from four minutes to ninety seconds because tests no longer resolve three copies of the package. The decision: no module may import a module that imports it, and shared helpers get their own home.
common_mistakes: Adding sys.path.append in tests instead of installing the package, so CI and containers keep failing.
Putting HTTP calls, file reads, and argument parsing in __init__.py, where every import pays for them.
Creating one utils.py that everything imports, which becomes a second, unnamed package with no owner.

key_terms.definition: The single function or module Python runs to start the program, kept separate from the library code it calls.
A failure where two modules import each other, usually revealing that responsibilities or dependency direction are wrong.

checkpoint.question: Why does the src layout make a passing test more trustworthy than a test run from the repository root?
checkpoint.answer: It stops Python from accidentally importing loose files in the folder you run from. A test can pass only by importing the installed package, so it matches CI and containers.

checkpoint.question: What symptom in CI usually points to a circular import rather than a missing dependency?
checkpoint.answer: CI may fail with ImportError: partially initialized module, while local tests pass because modules were imported in a lucky order. That points to two modules importing each other.

checkpoint.question: Which code belongs in __main__.py, and which belongs in a callable main()?
checkpoint.answer: __main__.py should contain the small launcher and guard that let python -m model_catalog work. The callable main() should contain the real startup work, such as loading data and printing, so tests can import it without running that work.

checkpoint.question: How would you break a cycle where two modules genuinely need the same helper?
checkpoint.answer: Move the shared helper into its own module, such as formatting.py, and have both modules import that. If needed, pass the helper in as an injected function instead.

checkpoint.question: Why should importing a module never read data/models.json or open a network connection?
checkpoint.answer: Importing should have no side effects, so tests stay fast and do not need data or network access. File reads and API calls belong in main(), where tests can choose not to run them.

lessons.title: Error Handling
lessons.goal: Handle expected failures with try/except, choose the exception type deliberately, and decide between crashing loudly and recovering gracefully.
lessons.takeaway: Errors are information, not shame: catch the specific exception you can recover from and let the rest surface with context.

sections.heading: try, except, else, finally
body: try: runs the risky block; except SomeError: handles the known failure; else: runs when no exception occurred (ideal for the success path); finally: always runs — use it for cleanup like closing files.

Catch the narrowest exception that names what can actually go wrong. except Exception: is a net that swallows bugs you did not foresee; except ValueError: is a contract that names the exact failure you planned for.

except Exception as e: lets you read the message; raise ValueError("bad total") from e re-raises with context preserved for the caller. Never catch and silently pass — silent failure is the hardest bug class to find.

sections.heading: The exceptions you will meet constantly
body: ValueError — right type, bad value: int("abc"), float("nan") edge cases. KeyError — dict key missing: use .get() or accept the error deliberately. IndexError — list index out of range: check bounds or let it crash with context.
FileNotFoundError — file missing: check the path first, or catch and print a helpful message. TypeError — wrong kind of argument. ZeroDivisionError — exactly what it says; check the denominator.
Catching TypeError/KeyError blindly is a code smell: it usually means the program entered an impossible state, and continuing produces silently wrong results. Crash beats corrupt.

sections.heading: Fail loud, recover deliberate
body: The design question is never "how do I avoid crashing?" It is "who is responsible for handling this?" — the function that detects the problem (validate and raise) or the caller that has context to recover (log, retry, default).

For user-facing input (CLI, forms), recover gracefully with a clear message and ask again. For internal invariants, crash immediately: an violated precondition (e.g., negative quantity) means the program is already broken, and continuing corrupts data.
Error messages are for the human: say what happened, what input caused it, and what to do next. "invalid literal for int() with base 10: '12,5'" is fine; "error" is not.

lessons.task: Write a word frequency counter over a user-supplied file that (1) exits with a clear message if the file is missing, (2) skips blank lines, (3) reports a summary of the 5 most common words as "word: count", and (4) raises ValueError with a helpful message if the file contains no words. Provide three sample inputs: normal text, empty file, missing file.

quiz.question: Which exception should you catch around int("abc")?
choices: TypeError
KeyError
ValueError
Exception
quiz.explanation: int("abc") has the right type (string) but an invalid value, which raises ValueError. Catching it names the exact failure you anticipated.

outcomes: Distinguish transient failures from permanent ones and choose retry, fallback, or fail-fast for each.
Build an exception hierarchy and re-raise with context so tracebacks preserve the original cause.
Route exhausted work to a dead-letter path and alert on skip rates instead of swallowing errors.
lessons.mental_model: Errors are mail: sort each item into retry, return to sender, or escalate; a bin marked miscellaneous is how deliveries disappear.
worked_example: Nadia owns a nightly pipeline that embeds 9,000 support tickets for a search index. A ticket with a null body raised KeyError inside a loop wrapped in except Exception: continue, so the run reported success while 1,340 tickets were silently absent. A week later retrieval accuracy fell from 84% to 61%, with no explanation. She replaces the blanket handler with an IngestError hierarchy. Missing fields raise PermanentIngestError and go to quarantine; embedding timeouts raise TransientIngestError and are retried three times with jitter. The job now ends with a count: 8,972 indexed, 28 quarantined, a 0.31% skip rate. The decision is to page on-call only above 1% and to replay quarantine after every schema fix.
common_mistakes: Catching Exception at the top of a loop and continuing, so a schema bug looks like a successful run.
Retrying every failure, including 401 and 422, which burns quota and delays the real error.
Logging only str(exc) without the traceback, record identifier, or provider, leaving nothing to debug.

key_terms.definition: Linking a new exception to the original with raise ... from exc, so the traceback shows the cause and the translation boundary.
A caller-supplied identifier that lets a server recognise a repeated write and return the first result instead of creating a duplicate.
A holding area for messages that exhausted retries, kept with their error details so they can be inspected and replayed.

checkpoint.question: Why is KeyError usually a bug rather than a condition to handle at a loop boundary?
checkpoint.answer: KeyError usually means your code asked for a field or key that is not there, such as a record with no body field. That is a programming bug, not a normal production condition, so it should crash in development instead of being swallowed at a loop boundary.

checkpoint.question: Which HTTP status codes should never be retried, and what does each retry cost?
checkpoint.answer: Never retry 400, 401, 403, or 422. They will fail identically on the second attempt, waste quota, and delay surfacing the real error.

checkpoint.question: How does raise NewError(...) from exc change what an on-call engineer sees?
checkpoint.answer: raise NewError(...) from exc preserves the original exception as __cause__, so the traceback shows both the translation boundary and the underlying cause. An on-call engineer sees the full story instead of only the new error.

checkpoint.question: What makes a write safe to retry, and what happens without that property?
checkpoint.answer: A write is safe to retry only when it has an idempotency key, which lets the server recognize a repeated write and return the first result instead of creating a duplicate. Without it, a retried POST can create two orders.

checkpoint.question: Why can nested retry policies turn three attempts into sixteen requests?
checkpoint.answer: If an outer job and an inner client both retry, the attempts multiply; the lesson’s example is that four attempts can become sixteen. Put the retry policy in one layer and pass the remaining deadline down.

lessons.title: Python project structure
lessons.goal: Create a src layout with a package, an entry point, and a tests directory that imports the package without path hacks.
lessons.takeaway: A package is a building with labelled rooms: the corridor is short, the doors face one direction, and you never climb through a window to reach the database.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: AI clients grow from one script into a package with schemas, an HTTP layer, retries, and tests. Without a layout, imports work only from the directory you happen to be in, and the first CI run or container build fails. A deliberate structure keeps the dependency graph acyclic, makes the public surface obvious, and lets you move a module without editing every caller.

sections.heading: src layout, not script soup Place the importable package under src/, for example
body: src layout, not script soup Place the importable package under src/, for example src/model_catalog/, and keep tests, data, and configuration beside it at the repository root.

The extra directory prevents Python from importing the working directory by accident, so a test can only pass by importing the installed package. pyproject.toml declares the package name, version, and dependencies; one editable install then serves your shell, editor, and CI.

Boundaries follow change Group code by the reason it changes, not by technical type. schemas.py holds data shapes, loader.py owns file and network I/O, catalog.py holds pure business rules, and main.py wires them together. Dependencies point one way: main imports catalog, catalog imports schemas, and schemas import nothing from the project.

When loader needs catalog you have a cycle, and the fix is usually a new module or an injected function. Entry points and import-time calm Expose one main() and guard it with if __name__ == "__main__":.

lessons.takeaway: Errors are mail: sort each item into retry, return to sender, or escalate; a bin marked miscellaneous is how deliveries disappear.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: Production code fails in expected ways: a provider returns 503, a file is missing, one record has no body field. A broad except Exception turns those into silence, and silence becomes wrong data. Good handling means deciding which failures are retryable, which are fatal, and which must be reported. The goal is not fewer exceptions; it is that every failure has an owner, a visible signal, and a defined outcome.
Errors are mail: sort each item into retry, return to sender, or escalate; a bin marked miscellaneous is how deliveries disappear.

sections.heading: Catch what you can act on An exception is a typed signal, so catch the narrowest
body: Catch what you can act on An exception is a typed signal, so catch the narrowest type you can handle: FileNotFoundError to fall back to defaults, httpx.TimeoutException to retry, ValidationError to quarantine one record. Let programming errors such as KeyError and AttributeError crash in development, because they indicate a bug rather than a condition.

At a layer boundary, translate library exceptions into your own types with raise DomainError('...') from exc, which preserves __cause__ and keeps callers independent of the library. Retry only what can succeed twice Retry timeouts, 429, and 502/503/504 with exponential backoff and full jitter, cap attempts at three to five, and hold a total deadline.

A 400, 401, 403, or 422 will fail identically on the second attempt and wastes quota. Writes need an idempotency key before retries are safe, or a retried POST can create two orders. If an outer job and an inner client both retry, four attempts become sixteen; place the policy in one layer and pass the remaining deadline down.

Keep a dead-letter queue for records that exhausted retries, with the payload and error type, so recovery is a replay rather than a mystery.
