Missing fields raise PermanentIngestError and go to quarantine; embedding timeouts raise TransientIngestError and are retried three times with jitter. The job now ends with a count: 8,972 indexed, 28 quarantined, a 0.31% skip rate. The decision is to page on-call only above 1% and to replay quarantine after every schema fix.
common_mistakes: Catching Exception at the top of a loop and continuing, so a schema bug looks like a successful run.
Retrying every failure, including 401 and 422, which burns quota and delays the real error.
Logging only str(exc) without the traceback, record identifier, or provider, leaving nothing to debug.

key_terms.definition: Linking a new exception to the original with raise ... from exc, so the traceback shows the cause and the translation boundary.
A caller-supplied identifier that lets a server recognise a repeated write and return the first result instead of creating a duplicate.
A holding area for messages that exhausted retries, kept with their error details so they can be inspected and replayed.

checkpoint.question: Why is KeyError usually a bug rather than a condition to handle at a loop boundary?
checkpoint.answer: KeyError usually means your code asked for a field or key that is not there, such as a record with no body field. That is a programming bug, not a normal production condition, so it should crash in development instead of being swallowed at a loop boundary.

checkpoint.question: Which HTTP status codes should never be retried, and what does each retry cost?
checkpoint.answer: Never retry 400, 401, 403, or 422. They will fail identically on the second attempt, waste quota, and delay surfacing the real error.

checkpoint.question: How does raise NewError(...) from exc change what an on-call engineer sees?
checkpoint.answer: raise NewError(...) from exc preserves the original exception as __cause__, so the traceback shows both the translation boundary and the underlying cause. An on-call engineer sees the full story instead of only the new error.

checkpoint.question: What makes a write safe to retry, and what happens without that property?
checkpoint.answer: A write is safe to retry only when it has an idempotency key, which lets the server recognize a repeated write and return the first result instead of creating a duplicate. Without it, a retried POST can create two orders.

checkpoint.question: Why can nested retry policies turn three attempts into sixteen requests?
checkpoint.answer: If an outer job and an inner client both retry, the attempts multiply; the lesson’s example is that four attempts can become sixteen. Put the retry policy in one layer and pass the remaining deadline down.

lessons.title: JSON
lessons.goal: Map Python values to JSON types and name the four values that need an explicit encoder.
lessons.takeaway: JSON is a shipping container: standard outside, but you must pack and unpack it yourself because your workshop holds tools the container cannot carry.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: Every model API, tool call, config file, and evaluation report speaks JSON, but Python's json module makes losses easy: tuples become arrays, datetimes fail, NaN is written as invalid JSON, and floats lose decimal digits. Each of those becomes a 500 in another language or a schema rejection downstream. Treating encoding and decoding as explicit boundaries, with tests, prevents most integration surprises.
JSON is a shipping container: standard outside, but you must pack and unpack it yourself because your workshop holds tools the container cannot carry.

sections.heading: A narrower type system JSON has objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and
body: A narrower type system JSON has objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null. Python adds tuples, sets, bytes, datetime, Decimal, and non-string dictionary keys, none of which encode without help; json.dumps raises TypeError for most of them and silently turns a tuple into a list.

Numbers carry no integer or float distinction, so a 64-bit identifier can lose precision in a JavaScript client. Duplicate object keys are legal in the grammar but the result is undefined, and NaN and Infinity are Python extensions that strict parsers reject.

Encoding is a decision, not a default json.dumps is intentionally conservative: it escapes non-ASCII unless ensure_ascii=False, keeps insertion order, and emits NaN unless allow_nan=False. Supply a default function for Decimal, datetime, UUID, and sets, converting datetimes to UTC ISO 8601 and Decimal to a string when money is involved.

Use sort_keys for reviewable diffs, indent for humans, and compact separators for wire payloads. Decode with parse_float=Decimal when precision matters and parse_constant to reject non-finite values at the door.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Validate decoded payloads with a schema, cap request and file size, and reject unknown fields at the boundary.
Version stored JSON documents and keep the old readers during a migration; additive fields are safer than renames.
Use JSONL for append-only events and evaluation runs so a truncated final line costs one record, not the file.

lessons.task: Take one payload from your project, encode and decode it, and record every type that changed (30 minutes). Add a strict JSON contract test to CI that rejects NaN and validates the decoded object against a schema (45 minutes).

quiz.question: Which Python types in your payloads have no direct JSON equivalent, and what do you emit for each?
choices: allow_nan=False makes json.dumps raise ValueError at the moment an NaN or Infinity would be written, instead of emitting…
Tuples encode as arrays (silently losing the tuple type), sets have no encoder (TypeError), datetimes and UUIDs fail…
JSON Lines is one JSON value per line, so it supports append-only writes, streaming line-by-line processing without loading…
JSON numbers carry no integer/float distinction, so a 64-bit identifier falls outside the exactly-representable range of…
quiz.explanation: Tuples encode as arrays (silently losing the tuple type), sets have no encoder (TypeError), datetimes and UUIDs fail without a default function, and Decimal needs an explicit decision. Non-string dictionary keys and bytes also have no natural JSON equivalent and raise TypeError.

outcomes: Map Python values to JSON types and name the four values that need an explicit encoder.
Encode reports that reject NaN and read numbers back without losing decimal precision.
Choose between json.load, JSONL, and streaming for small, append-only, and large payloads.
lessons.mental_model: JSON is a shipping container: standard outside, but you must pack and unpack it yourself because your workshop holds tools the container cannot carry.
worked_example: Ines ships evaluation scores from a Python runner to a TypeScript dashboard. One Friday, 2 of 180 runs produced score: NaN because a metric divided by an empty test set, and json.dump wrote bare NaN. Python reloaded the file happily, but JSON.parse rejected the response and the dashboard showed an empty chart for the whole week. Her fix is three decisions: dump with allow_nan=False so the runner fails at the boundary, represent money and scores as strings, and add a contract test that reloads every report with a strict parser and validates it against the dashboard's schema. A score of 0.9166666666666666 became '0.917', and the alert now names the run id that produced invalid JSON.
common_mistakes: Writing Python's NaN or Infinity into a response and assuming every client parses it as JSON.
Using json.dumps inside an f-string to build nested JSON, which double-encodes strings and breaks consumers.
Loading an unbounded upload with json.load before checking its size, letting one request exhaust memory.

key_terms.definition: A format of one JSON value per line, allowing append-only writes and streaming reads without loading the entire file.
Converting an in-memory object into bytes or text that another process or language can parse.
A floating-point value meaning not-a-number; Python emits it unquoted, but strict JSON parsers reject it.

checkpoint.question: Which Python types in your payloads have no direct JSON equivalent, and what do you emit for each?
checkpoint.answer: Tuples encode as arrays (silently losing the tuple type), sets have no encoder (TypeError), datetimes and UUIDs fail without a default function, and Decimal needs an explicit decision. Non-string dictionary keys and bytes also have no natural JSON equivalent and raise TypeError.

checkpoint.question: Why can a JSON number be unsafe for a 64-bit identifier read by JavaScript?
checkpoint.answer: JSON numbers carry no integer/float distinction, so a 64-bit identifier falls outside the exactly-representable range of IEEE 754 doubles once it exceeds 2^53. A JavaScript client that parses the literal can get a different number than the server stored.

checkpoint.question: What does allow_nan=False change, and where does the failure appear?
checkpoint.answer: allow_nan=False makes json.dumps raise ValueError at the moment an NaN or Infinity would be written, instead of emitting Python-extension literals that strict parsers (like JavaScript’s JSON.parse) reject. The failure appears at dump time, at the boundary, not in the consumer later.

checkpoint.question: When is JSONL a better choice than a single array document?
checkpoint.answer: JSON Lines is one JSON value per line, so it supports append-only writes, streaming line-by-line processing without loading the whole file, and partial recovery after a crash. It is the usual choice for evaluation runs, logs, and fine-tuning data; a single array document suits small, whole-at-once payloads.

checkpoint.question: How does parse_float=Decimal differ from float in a round trip?
checkpoint.answer: parse_float=Decimal decodes every JSON number as an exact Decimal with the digits written in the file, so a round trip preserves the value. Plain float decoding introduces binary floating-point error immediately, making exact comparisons and money handling unreliable.

lessons.title: HTTP requests
lessons.goal: Build a request with the correct method, headers, JSON body, and status handling for an AI API.
lessons.takeaway: Treat a remote API like a parcel courier: agree packaging and addresses, set a delivery deadline, and track the parcel instead of assuming it arrived.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: Almost every AI feature is a network client: model providers, vector databases, embedding services, and internal APIs. Those calls are slower and less reliable than local functions, and a missing timeout can hold a worker for minutes. The difference between a demo and a service is usually a few decisions about deadlines, retries, connection reuse, and malformed responses.
Treat a remote API like a parcel courier: agree packaging and addresses, set a delivery deadline, and track the parcel instead of assuming it arrived.

sections.heading: A request is a typed message A request carries a method, URL, headers, and an op
body: A request is a typed message A request carries a method, URL, headers, and an optional body; a response carries a status, headers, and a body. Use POST for model calls, GET for idempotent reads, and never put an API key in the query string, where proxies and logs record it.

A 2xx means the transport succeeded, not that the payload is usable: check Content-Type, decode JSON, then validate against a schema. A 401 or 403 is a configuration failure, 422 is a request bug, and 5xx is the provider's problem.

Deadlines and retries httpx.Timeout separates connect, read, write, and pool waits; a 3-second connect with a 20-second read handles slow generation without hanging on a dead host. Set a total deadline at the caller and shrink it for each retry.

Retry only 429, 502, 503, 504, and timeouts, honour Retry-After when present, and add jitter so a fleet does not synchronise. Cap attempts at three or four and surface the final error with the provider request id. Never retry a non-idempotent write without an idempotency key.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Set the total deadline below the caller's timeout, propagate a request id, and cancel downstream work when the caller disconnects.
Log status, latency, retry count, and provider request id per call; alert on 5xx rate and p95, not just exceptions.
Pin the provider API version and validate responses, because a successful 200 with a new field can still break parsing.

lessons.task: Build a client for a public API with explicit timeouts and retries, then test 200, 429, and 503 against a mock server (50 minutes). Measure p95 latency for 100 requests with and without a reused client, and write down the difference (30 minutes).

quiz.question: Why does a 200 response not prove that a model call succeeded for your application?
choices: A 200 means the transport succeeded, not that the payload is usable. You still must check Content-Type, decode the JSON,…
The client should retry only transient status codes such as 429, 502, 503, and 504, and it should honor Retry-After when…
Reusing one client skips repeated DNS, TCP, and TLS setup. Set pool limits, such as 50 total connections and 20 keep-alive…
Automatic redirects can send an authenticated request to a different host. A 302 could forward your bearer token, so…
quiz.explanation: A 200 means the transport succeeded, not that the payload is usable. You still must check Content-Type, decode the JSON, and validate its shape against a schema before your application trusts it.

outcomes: Build a request with the correct method, headers, JSON body, and status handling for an AI API.
Set connect and read timeouts, then retry only 429, 5xx, and timeouts within a total deadline.
Reuse a connection pool and validate the decoded response before it enters application code.
lessons.mental_model: Treat a remote API like a parcel courier: agree packaging and addresses, set a delivery deadline, and track the parcel instead of assuming it arrived.
worked_example: Yusuf runs a translation service that calls a model gateway at 40 requests per second at peak. Each worker used requests.post(url, json=payload) with no timeout and a fresh session, so one stalled response held a worker for six minutes. During a provider incident, retries amplified traffic and p95 reached nine seconds. He moves to one shared httpx.Client per process with a 3-second connect timeout, a 20-second read timeout, and a 50-connection limit. Retries cover 429 and 5xx only: four attempts, 0.5-second base backoff with jitter, honouring Retry-After. p95 falls to 1.8 seconds and the error rate to 0.4%. The decision is recorded with a 25-second total deadline so callers fail before their own 30- second limit.
common_mistakes: Calling a provider without a timeout, so one stalled socket can occupy a worker until the client restarts.
Retrying every non-2xx response, including 401 and 422, adds load and hides the real error.
Creating a new client or session per request and paying DNS, TCP, and TLS overhead on every call.

key_terms.definition: The property that repeating a request produces the same result as sending it once, which makes retries safe.
A set of reusable sockets kept open by a client so successive requests skip DNS, TCP, and TLS setup.
A response header giving the number of seconds or a date after which the client may retry.

checkpoint.question: Why does a 200 response not prove that a model call succeeded for your application?
checkpoint.answer: A 200 means the transport succeeded, not that the payload is usable. You still must check Content-Type, decode the JSON, and validate its shape against a schema before your application trusts it.

checkpoint.question: Which failures should be retried at the client, and which belong to the job wrapper?
checkpoint.answer: The client should retry only transient status codes such as 429, 502, 503, and 504, and it should honor Retry-After when present. Transport timeouts belong to one job-level wrapper so retries do not multiply.

checkpoint.question: What does connection reuse save, and what limits should cap the pool?
checkpoint.answer: Reusing one client skips repeated DNS, TCP, and TLS setup. Set pool limits, such as 50 total connections and 20 keep-alive connections, to bound concurrency and match worker concurrency.

checkpoint.question: Why must an authenticated request disable automatic redirects, and what could leak?
checkpoint.answer: Automatic redirects can send an authenticated request to a different host. A 302 could forward your bearer token, so disable redirects for authenticated calls.

checkpoint.question: How does Retry-After change the backoff calculation, and what if it is a date?
checkpoint.answer: Retry-After tells you when to try again instead of using your normal backoff. It can be a number of seconds or an HTTP date, and production code must parse both forms.

lessons.title: Environment variables
lessons.goal: Move endpoints, credentials, and feature flags out of code and into environment variables with clear precedence.
lessons.takeaway: Configuration is the address label on a container: the contents stay identical, but the label decides which door it enters.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: The same application must run in development, staging, and production without code edits, and the differences are mostly endpoints and credentials. Hard-coded values turn a deployment into a merge request, while a silent default can send test traffic to production. Environment variables solve the first problem; validation at startup and a secret strategy solve the second.
Configuration is the address label on a container: the contents stay identical, but the label decides which door it enters.

sections.heading: Configuration lives outside the code The same image should run in dev, staging
body: Configuration lives outside the code The same image should run in dev, staging, and production; only the environment changes. Environment variables are the common interface because shells, systemd, Docker, and every cloud runtime can set them. A .env file is a local convenience that Pydantic Settings or python-dotenv loads, not a deployment mechanism.

Precedence matters: real environment variables should override the file, so a container setting is never silently replaced by a stale local file. Never commit .env, and keep .env.example as documentation.

Validate at startup, not at first use os.environ['API_KEY'] raises KeyError at the moment of access, which may be inside a request handler hours after deploy. Load every setting once into a typed object, check required fields, regexes for environment names, and numeric bounds for timeouts and pool sizes.

On failure, report all problems and exit non-zero before the server binds a port. Defaults are acceptable for safe values such as a 10-second timeout; they are dangerous for secrets, database URLs, and endpoints, where a wrong default sends traffic somewhere real.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Scope credentials per environment and per service, and keep production values out of developer laptops and CI logs.
Have a tested rotation procedure for every secret, including planned overlap windows so deploys do not fail mid-rotation.
Log the resolved environment name and non-secret settings at startup, then verify the deployment targets the expected one.

lessons.task: Move every hard-coded endpoint and timeout in your project into a typed Settings class with validation (45 minutes). Write a startup test that runs with an empty environment and asserts a non-zero exit naming each missing field (30 minutes).

quiz.question: Why is a .env file unsuitable as the production configuration mechanism?
choices: SecretStr masks the value in repr, logs, and tracebacks (they show asterisks), which keeps keys out of diagnostics and…
A .env file is a local convenience loaded by Pydantic Settings or python-dotenv, not a deployment mechanism — it depends on…
If a required API base URL is missing and you fall back to a default, the service silently targets some real system…
Safe defaults are fine for non-secret, forgiving values such as a 10-second timeout. Required values, secrets, database…
quiz.explanation: A .env file is a local convenience loaded by Pydantic Settings or python-dotenv, not a deployment mechanism — it depends on a file path and a working directory, is easy to commit by accident, and drifts between machines. Production configuration belongs in the platform or secret store, with environment variables as the common interface.

outcomes: Move endpoints, credentials, and feature flags out of code and into environment variables with clear precedence.
Load settings into a typed object that fails fast with every invalid field named.
Store secrets so they never appear in Git, images, logs, or tracebacks.
lessons.mental_model: Configuration is the address label on a container: the contents stay identical, but the label decides which door it enters.
worked_example: Owen joins a media company for six weeks to add a search reindexer. His script reads API_BASE with a default of the public production URL, and the staging shell does not override it. A dry run with --limit 50 works, so on his second day the full run re-embeds 14,000 documents against the production index, costs USD 610, and leaves 90 minutes of inconsistent search results. The postmortem finds three causes: a default for a required endpoint, no APP_ENV check, and a .env file copied from another engineer. The team now requires APP_ENV in dev, staging, or prod, keeps credentials only in the platform secret store, commits .env.example without values, and requires --confirm-prod for destructive jobs.
common_mistakes: Giving a required production endpoint or API key a default, so an unset variable silently targets the wrong system.
Committing .env because it is convenient, then rotating keys after the file reaches Git history and a clone.
Reading os.environ deep inside functions, which hides required settings until a rare code path executes.

key_terms.definition: The practice of storing configuration in the environment, separately from code, so one build runs in every environment.

A Pydantic type that masks its value in repr and logs; the real value requires an explicit accessor call. dotenv file A local key-value file, usually .env, loaded into the process environment for development and never committed.

checkpoint.question: Why is a .env file unsuitable as the production configuration mechanism?
checkpoint.answer: A .env file is a local convenience loaded by Pydantic Settings or python-dotenv, not a deployment mechanism — it depends on a file path and a working directory, is easy to commit by accident, and drifts between machines. Production configuration belongs in the platform or secret store, with environment variables as the common interface.

checkpoint.question: What is the failure mode of defaulting a required API base URL?
checkpoint.answer: If a required API base URL is missing and you fall back to a default, the service silently targets some real system (staging or production) instead of failing fast. The lesson’s example: an unset staging shell defaulted to the public production URL and re-embedded 14,000 production documents.

checkpoint.question: Which settings deserve defaults, and which must fail closed when absent?
checkpoint.answer: Safe defaults are fine for non-secret, forgiving values such as a 10-second timeout. Required values, secrets, database URLs, and endpoints must fail closed when absent — a wrong default there sends traffic somewhere real, whereas a wrong timeout is caught immediately.

checkpoint.question: How does SecretStr reduce exposure, and when does the value still become visible?
checkpoint.answer: SecretStr masks the value in repr, logs, and tracebacks (they show asterisks), which keeps keys out of diagnostics and errors. It still becomes fully visible wherever you call get_secret_value() — typically when constructing the client — and anywhere the process environment itself is printed or dumped.

checkpoint.question: Why should configuration be validated before the service binds its port?
checkpoint.answer: Settings load once into a typed object at startup, validation runs before the server binds a port, and on failure the process prints every invalid field and exits non-zero. A bad deployment fails deploy time instead of the first customer request, and the error list names all problems at once.

lessons.title: Virtual environments
lessons.goal: Create a project virtual environment with a pinned Python version and use it without relying on activation.
lessons.takeaway: A virtual environment is a project's own toolbox: same workshop, separate tools, so borrowing a wrench cannot break the other bench.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: Python installs packages into whichever interpreter is active, so a global upgrade for one tutorial can break three services that expected an older Pydantic. Virtual environments give each project its own site-packages directory, and a lockfile makes that directory reproducible on another machine. This is unglamorous work, but most works-on-my-machine incidents start with an ambiguous interpreter and end with a dependency conflict nobody can reproduce.
A virtual environment is a project's own toolbox: same workshop, separate tools, so borrowing a wrench cannot break the other bench.

sections.heading: Isolation is a directory on sys
body: Isolation is a directory on sys.path A virtual environment is a folder containing a symlink to a base interpreter, its own pyvenv.cfg, and a site-packages directory that appears early on sys.path. Activation only edits PATH and VIRTUAL_ENV for the current shell; it does not change the code.

Calling .venv/bin/python -m pip or .venv/bin/python -m pytest is deterministic, while a bare python in a cron job or IDE may resolve elsewhere. Check sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix before blaming the package. Create, pin, and rebuild Create one environment per repository with python3.11 -m venv .venv, upgrade pip once, and add .venv/ to .gitignore.

Record the interpreter version in .python-version and declare dependencies in pyproject.toml; a lockfile pins exact versions and hashes for every platform you support. In CI and Docker, build a fresh environment from the lock rather than copying a developer folder, because a venv contains absolute paths and native wheels tied to the machine that built it.

A venv isolates but does not pin Two projects can each have a venv and still drift if both install pydantic>=2 on different days. Lockfiles, constraints, and hashed installs turn that drift into a reviewable diff. Use pip check or uv pip check to catch conflicting requirements, and run the test suite inside the same environment that deployment uses.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Build images and CI jobs from the committed lockfile with a frozen install, and fail the build on any resolution change.
Pin the Python minor version in the image and in .python-version so local, CI, and production builds agree.
Run pip check and the test suite inside the built artefact before deploying, not only in a developer environment.

lessons.task: Create a fresh .venv for your project, record sys.executable, and rebuild it from the lockfile in a second directory (35 minutes). Add a CI job that installs frozen dependencies and runs tests, then confirm it fails when the lockfile is stale (45 minutes).

quiz.question: What does activation actually change, and why is it not required to run a project?
choices: pyvenv.cfg records the home Python installation the venv was created from (home path, include-system-site-packages flag,…
Two projects can share a .venv shape but still drift because a fresh install resolves the newest allowed versions at…
A .venv records absolute paths in pyvenv.cfg and scripts, and contains platform- and even Python-patch-version-specific…
Activation puts the project’s .venv/bin directory first on PATH and sets VIRTUAL_ENV, so bare `python` and `pip` resolve to…
quiz.explanation: Activation puts the project’s .venv/bin directory first on PATH and sets VIRTUAL_ENV, so bare `python` and `pip` resolve to that interpreter. It is not required to run anything — you can always invoke .venv/bin/python directly, and tools like uv do that without activating.

outcomes: Create a project virtual environment with a pinned Python version and use it without relying on activation.
Rebuild the environment from a lockfile in CI and containers, and prove the result matches.
Diagnose import shadowing and version drift using sys.prefix, pip check, and explicit interpreter paths.
lessons.mental_model: A virtual environment is a project's own toolbox: same workshop, separate tools, so borrowing a wrench cannot break the other bench.
worked_example: A six-person team maintains four services in one monorepo. Service A pins pydantic 1.10 for an old FastAPI version; Service B needs pydantic 2.9. A developer upgrades pydantic globally to follow a tutorial, and within a day three services fail at import because BaseSettings moved to pydantic-settings. The team recreates each service's .venv from its own lockfile, adds .python-version files pinning 3.11, and changes CI to install with uv sync --frozen into a fresh environment. The immediate cost is two days of cleanup; the lasting change is that dependency updates now arrive as reviewed lockfile diffs with a green test run.
common_mistakes: Installing packages globally with pip install because activation happened to be active in one terminal.
Committing .venv to Git, which ships absolute paths and platform-specific binaries that fail elsewhere.
Assuming a virtual environment pins versions, when a fresh install can resolve newer releases than yesterday.

key_terms.definition: A directory holding a Python interpreter link and an isolated site-packages tree used by one project.
A shell script that puts a virtual environment's bin directory first on PATH for the current session.
A generated file recording exact dependency versions and hashes so installs are reproducible across machines.

checkpoint.question: What does activation actually change, and why is it not required to run a project?
checkpoint.answer: Activation puts the project’s .venv/bin directory first on PATH and sets VIRTUAL_ENV, so bare `python` and `pip` resolve to that interpreter. It is not required to run anything — you can always invoke .venv/bin/python directly, and tools like uv do that without activating.

checkpoint.question: How can two projects both use a venv and still drift apart in dependency versions?
checkpoint.answer: Two projects can share a .venv shape but still drift because a fresh install resolves the newest allowed versions at install time; different creation dates or unpinned ranges produce different trees. The shared cause is resolving loosely instead of installing from each project’s own lockfile.

checkpoint.question: Why is copying a .venv between machines or into an image a bad idea?
checkpoint.answer: A .venv records absolute paths in pyvenv.cfg and scripts, and contains platform- and even Python-patch-version-specific binaries and links. Copied elsewhere or into an image, it breaks in confusing ways and ships a resolved set of packages instead of the declared, reviewable one.

checkpoint.question: What does pyvenv.cfg record, and which part of it breaks on a different machine?
checkpoint.answer: pyvenv.cfg records the home Python installation the venv was created from (home path, include-system-site-packages flag, and the base prefix). The `home` path is machine-specific, so pointing another machine at it fails or silently uses the wrong base interpreter.

checkpoint.question: When would --system-site-packages be justified, and what risk does it add?
checkpoint.answer: --system-site-packages is justified when a base image provides large pre-installed scientific packages you do not want duplicated. It adds the risk that system packages leak into the project and cause version conflicts that are invisible to a fresh-lockfile install.

lessons.title: Dependencies
lessons.goal: Separate direct, transitive, and development dependencies, and explain why only direct ones belong in pyproject.toml.
lessons.takeaway: A dependency file is a contract; the lockfile is the signed copy. Declare what you need, freeze exactly what you got, and renegotiate deliberately.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: An AI service inherits hundreds of transitive packages from an SDK, an HTTP client, and a test stack. An unpinned install can change behaviour between Tuesday and Friday without a line of your code changing. Dependencies are also an attack surface: a compromised release runs with your credentials. Treating them as reviewed, locked inputs keeps builds reproducible and incidents explainable.
A dependency file is a contract; the lockfile is the signed copy. Declare what you need, freeze exactly what you got, and renegotiate deliberately.

sections.heading: Direct, transitive, and locked A direct dependency is a package your code import
body: Direct, transitive, and locked A direct dependency is a package your code imports or a tool your build invokes. A transitive dependency is anything those packages require, often dozens deep. pyproject.toml declares intent with version ranges; a lockfile records the exact resolved version and hash of every package in the graph.

AI SDKs are unusually heavy: one client can pull httpx, pydantic, tokenizers, and a telemetry stack. Most of your runtime is then unreviewed. Constraints and resolution Python version constraints follow PEP 440, not npm's caret syntax.

A lower bound such as httpx>=0.27 states a minimum but permits any future major release; a compatible-release specifier like ~=0.27.3 permits patch updates only. The resolver must choose one version per package that satisfies every constraint simultaneously. Conflicts usually come from two direct dependencies with incompatible upper bounds.

Read the resolution error, then loosen one direct constraint or upgrade the package that pins the shared dependency. Supply chain and blast radius Every package you add runs with your credentials in CI and production, so dependency choice is a security decision.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Build images with uv sync --frozen or pip install --require-hashes, and fail the build when pyproject.toml and the lockfile disagree.
Run pip-audit and a licence check on every pull request; block critical vulnerabilities and unapproved licences before any merge.
Keep a dependency budget: require a one-line justification for each new runtime package and review the transitive count every quarter.

lessons.task: Audit one project: list direct dependencies, count transitive packages, and delete two that nothing imports (30 minutes). Introduce a lockfile, add a frozen install to CI, and prove that a clean checkout reproduces the same package versions (45 minutes).

quiz.question: Why is a lower bound such as httpx>=0.24 insufficient for a reproducible build?
choices: The resolver builds a graph of all version constraints from every package in play and selects, for each shared transitive…
A lower bound only states the minimum the resolver may choose; it is free to pick any newer release, so CI and production…
Development plugins (pytest-asyncio, coverage, linters) run at development and CI time, not in the request path; they add…
pyproject.toml declares intent: the direct dependencies and the ranges you are willing to accept. uv.lock records the…
quiz.explanation: A lower bound only states the minimum the resolver may choose; it is free to pick any newer release, so CI and production can install different code weeks apart. Reproducibility requires an exact, frozen set of versions — a lockfile — not an open-ended range.

outcomes: Separate direct, transitive, and development dependencies, and explain why only direct ones belong in pyproject.toml.
Generate and verify a lockfile so installs resolve identically on a laptop, in CI, and in a container.
Audit a dependency set for version conflicts, abandoned packages, and supply-chain risk before merging.
lessons.mental_model: A dependency file is a contract; the lockfile is the signed copy. Declare what you need, freeze exactly what you got, and renegotiate deliberately.
worked_example: Mei maintains a document-extraction service at a 30-person insurer. A Monday build fails because requirements.txt lists httpx>=0.24, so pip installed 0.28, while the vendor SDK still calls a removed argument. Production had installed three weeks earlier and was unaffected, which means staging and production were running different code. Mei generates uv.lock, pins httpx>=0.27,<0.29, and splits runtime and development groups so pytest plugins no longer ship in the image. The resolver also flags conflicting pydantic ranges from two SDKs. She chooses one compatible range, adds uv lock --check and pip-audit to CI, and schedules the httpx upgrade as a tested change rather than letting the next deploy decide.
common_mistakes: Committing requirements.txt without a lockfile, so transitive versions change silently between CI runs and production deploys.
Pinning every transitive package by hand, then spending days untangling a graph the resolver could maintain.
Adding a package because a tutorial used it, without checking maintenance, licence, or whether the standard library suffices.

key_terms.definition: A package your code imports or a tool your project invokes, declared explicitly in pyproject.toml with a version constraint.
A generated record of the exact resolved version and hash of every package, including transitive ones, for reproducible installs.
The process of choosing one version per package that satisfies every constraint in the graph, or failing with a conflict.

checkpoint.question: Why is a lower bound such as httpx>=0.24 insufficient for a reproducible build?
checkpoint.answer: A lower bound only states the minimum the resolver may choose; it is free to pick any newer release, so CI and production can install different code weeks apart. Reproducibility requires an exact, frozen set of versions — a lockfile — not an open-ended range.

checkpoint.question: What is the difference between what pyproject.toml declares and what uv.lock records?
checkpoint.answer: pyproject.toml declares intent: the direct dependencies and the ranges you are willing to accept. uv.lock records the resolved reality: every direct and transitive package at an exact version, plus hashes, so any machine reproduces the same tree.

checkpoint.question: How does a resolver decide which version of a shared transitive package to install?
checkpoint.answer: The resolver builds a graph of all version constraints from every package in play and selects, for each shared transitive package, a single version that satisfies every constraint simultaneously, backtracking when a choice fails. When constraints conflict it reports the conflict instead of silently mixing versions.

checkpoint.question: Why should test plugins live in a development group rather than runtime dependencies?
checkpoint.answer: Development plugins (pytest-asyncio, coverage, linters) run at development and CI time, not in the request path; they add supply-chain surface and install weight for no runtime benefit. A development dependency group keeps production installs minimal and focused on runtime needs.

checkpoint.question: What supply-chain attack does an exact-version pin with a hash defend against?
checkpoint.answer: A pin plus hash defends against a compromised or replaced upstream distribution: even if an attacker publishes the same version number again, the digest will not match the recorded hash and the install fails instead of running substituted code.

lessons.title: Testing with pytest
lessons.goal: Structure unit, integration, and contract tests so a failing build identifies the broken boundary.
lessons.takeaway: Tests are a contract with your future self: pin the behaviour you depend on, fake what you do not control, and keep the boundary honest.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: A model response is variable, slow, and sometimes invalid, so tests that call a live provider are flaky and expensive. The reliable strategy is to test your code's decisions at the edges: request construction, schema validation, retries, and error mapping. A fast suite plus a few recorded contract tests catches regressions before users do, without turning CI into a billing event.
Tests are a contract with your future self: pin the behaviour you depend on, fake what you do not control, and keep the boundary honest.

sections.heading: Test the seams, not the model Unit tests cover pure transforms: prompt assembly
body: Test the seams, not the model Unit tests cover pure transforms: prompt assembly, response parsing, retry classification, and cost calculation. Integration tests run your client against a fake transport and assert request headers, body, status handling, and timeouts. Contract tests hit a sandbox provider occasionally to detect schema drift.

Never put live model quality in the default suite; that belongs to evaluation. Test your decisions, not the model's mood today. Fixtures and parametrisation A fixture prepares a client, temp directory, or environment variable and is injected by name; yield fixtures close resources after the test.

Prefer function scope unless setup is genuinely expensive, because shared mutable state creates order- dependent failures. Parametrise tables of inputs and expected outcomes so each case reports separately: a 400, a 429, a 500, a timeout, and malformed JSON. Give cases readable ids.

Mock at the transport Patch HTTP at the transport layer with httpx.MockTransport or respx, not your own functions. The real client then builds URLs, serialises JSON, applies auth headers, follows its retry loop, and parses the response, so a broken request is caught. Patching your own method proves only that the mock was called.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Require the fast suite on every pull request and publish its duration; a suite over 90 seconds gets skipped under deadline pressure.
Run a small contract suite nightly against a sandbox key, and alert when the provider changes a response shape.
Track flaky tests explicitly and quarantine them with an owner; rerunning until green erodes trust in the gate.

lessons.task: Take one untested function in your module project and write five tests covering success, invalid input, and two error paths (45 minutes). Replace a live HTTP call with MockTransport, add a retry test, and measure the suite's before-and-after duration (40 minutes).

The real client still builds URLs, sends headers, serialises JSON, retries, and parses responses, so broken requests are…
A parametrised test reports each input case separately, often with readable ids. A loop inside one test reports only one…
Unit tests cover pure transforms such as prompt assembly, response parsing, retry classification, and cost calculation.…
quiz.explanation: The real client still builds URLs, sends headers, serialises JSON, retries, and parses responses, so broken requests are caught. Patching your own method only proves the mock was called.

outcomes: Structure unit, integration, and contract tests so a failing build identifies the broken boundary.
Use fixtures, parametrisation, and mocking to test HTTP, timeouts, and malformed model output without network calls.
Make tests deterministic and fast enough to run as a required gate on every pull request.

worked_example: Nadia owns the Python client for a translation API used by 40 internal services. The suite takes six minutes because 28 tests call the live endpoint, and two fail most Fridays when the provider is slow. She replaces those calls with transport- level fakes: a 200 response, a 429 then 200 sequence, a 500 with a malformed body, and a read timeout. Parametrised cases assert that only 429 and 5xx are retried, that backoff caps at eight seconds, and that a 400 surfaces as InvalidRequest without a retry. The suite drops to 340 tests in 4.2 seconds and immediately exposes a bug: retries were also firing on 401. Running one test body against a table of inputs and expected results, reporting each case as a separate test.
A small suite that verifies your client still matches a provider's real request and response shapes, run less often.

checkpoint.answer: The real client still builds URLs, sends headers, serialises JSON, retries, and parses responses, so broken requests are caught. Patching your own method only proves the mock was called.

checkpoint.answer: Unit tests cover pure transforms such as prompt assembly, response parsing, retry classification, and cost calculation. Nightly contract tests check your client still matches the provider's real request and response shapes.

modules.title: Software Engineering Foundations
modules.description: Version control, testing, and project structure

lessons.title: Git Basics
lessons.goal: Track work in git: init, add, commit, branch, and understand what each one does to the history of a project.
lessons.takeaway: Git records snapshots, not files: commit small, coherent changes with messages that explain why.

sections.heading: A snapshot history, not a file backup
body: Git records snapshots of your tree over time. Each commit is a full snapshot plus metadata (who, when, message) and pointers to parent commits. Navigating that history is the whole game: checkout, log, diff, blame.

git init starts tracking in a directory; git add stages changes; git commit -m "message" snapshots the staged changes. The staging area is a deliberate design choice: you decide what belongs in each snapshot — three files fixed a bug, two are unrelated experimentation that stays unstaged.
Configuration is identity: git config user.name and git config user.email label every commit you make. Expect the question "who wrote this?" answered by the git log.

sections.heading: Reading history: log, diff, show
body: git log --oneline --graph shows the commit graph. git diff HEAD shows uncommitted changes against the last commit; git diff HEAD~1 HEAD shows what changed in the last commit. git show <sha> inspects one commit in full.

Messages matter because history is read more than it is written: imperative mood ("Add retry logic", not "added retry" or "fixes"), one line under 72 chars, body if the why is not obvious. Future-you is the audience.
Blame (git blame file) annotates every line with who touched it and when — not to assign fault but to find the person who knows why. Ask them before you rewrite.

sections.heading: Branches are cheap
body: A branch is a movable pointer to a commit. git switch -c feature/login creates and moves to a new one; git switch main goes back; git merge feature/login incorporates it. Branching is free, so branch per piece of work.

Merging integrates; conflicts occur when the same lines changed in both branches. Git marks conflicts in the file with <<<<<<< ======= >>>>>>> markers — you choose, then git add and commit. Conflicts are routine, resolve calmly.
Uncommitted work does not block switching branches — git stash parks it temporarily (stash list, stash pop). Clean tree before big operations you fear losing.

lessons.task: In a scratch directory: create a project with two commits on main, branch to feature/uppercase, make a change, commit, switch back to main and observe the difference in files. Merge back and resolve any induced conflict by editing the marked file, staging it, and committing. Write down the commands you ran.

quiz.question: What does git commit -m "msg" actually record?
choices: A backup of the working directory
A snapshot of the staged index plus parent pointers
A list of changed files only
A copy in the remote repository
quiz.explanation: A commit is a full snapshot of what was staged (the index), with metadata and parent references. Working-directory changes that were not staged are not in the commit.

outcomes: Initialise a repository and make a first commit.
Write a commit message that explains why a change exists.
Keep secrets and generated files out of version control.
lessons.mental_model: A commit is a labelled photograph of your project, not a video of everything you did. The message is the note on the back explaining why you took it.
worked_example: A learner commits a .env file with an API key, then deletes it in the next commit. The key still exists in the first commit and in every clone. They rotate the key, add .env to .gitignore, commit .env.example with empty values, and write a short note in the README. The fix is rotation and prevention, not a prettier diff.
common_mistakes: Committing .env or a virtual environment because the repository is private.
Mixing unrelated changes in one commit so a rollback removes more than intended.
Force-pushing a shared branch and overwriting someone else's commits.

key_terms.definition: A directory whose changes Git tracks as a history of commits.
A snapshot of staged changes plus a message, author, and parent commit.
A named copy of a repository hosted elsewhere, usually on GitHub.
A file listing paths Git should not track.
A request to review and merge changes from one branch into another.

checkpoint.question: What is the difference between the working tree, the staging area, and a commit?
checkpoint.answer: The working tree is the files you edit; staging selects what goes into the next commit; a commit is the recorded snapshot.

checkpoint.question: Why should a commit message describe why, not just what?
checkpoint.answer: The why lets a future reader decide whether the change still applies.

checkpoint.question: What belongs in .gitignore for a Python AI project?
checkpoint.answer: At minimum .env, .venv/, __pycache__/, and large generated artefacts.

checkpoint.question: Why does deleting a secret in a later commit fail to remove it from history?
checkpoint.answer: The old commit still contains the value and clones retain it; rotate the credential.

checkpoint.question: When is a force push acceptable?
checkpoint.answer: Only on a branch you alone own, after coordinating, and never to erase evidence on a shared branch.

lessons.title: Repository Workflow
lessons.goal: Follow the daily engineering loop — issue, branch, commit, pull request, review, merge — and write a PR a reviewer can act on.
lessons.takeaway: A branch isolates work, a pull request reviews it and a clean history makes both easy to follow.

sections.heading: The working rhythm
body: Real teams run a loop: pick an issue → cut a branch (feature/short-description) → make small commits → push to origin → open a pull request → review → merge → delete the branch. Rinse, repeat.
Small commits with clear messages beat monumental ones: they review better, revert cleaner, and bisect easier. One logical change per commit is the discipline.
Pull --rebase before you start work on an existing branch, and again before you merge: it folds in upstream changes and keeps history linear instead of a braid of merge commits.

sections.heading: The pull request is the unit of collaboration
body: A PR is a conversation, not a submission. Title it imperatively ("Add request-id header"). Body: what changed, why, how to test it. Link the issue (#123). Paste evidence (logs, screenshots, before/after) when behaviour changed.
Reviewers look for: does it do what it says, is it tested, is it safe to merge. Write code that is easy to say yes to: small diffs, tests included, no unrelated refactors riding along.
Respond to review comments as commits responding to each thread, not as a rebuttal essay — though reasoned pushback is expected when the reviewer missed context.

sections.heading: Protected branches and CI
body: main is protected: no direct pushes, force-push disabled, merge requires green CI. Every merge to main must come through a reviewed, green PR. This single rule is why main stays shippable.
CI runs on every push: tests, lint, type checks. Red CI blocks merge — fix it before anything else, because the next engineer inherits the red too.
Tagging releases (v1.1.0) marks immutable points in history. Release notes in the repo tell operators what changed without reading 300 commits.

lessons.task: Draft a pull request description (markdown, not posted anywhere) for a fix you actually made this week: title, summary of the change, why, how to test, and a checklist. Then write the review comment you would leave on someone else's PR of the same change.

quiz.question: Before opening a PR from a long-lived branch, which is the better hygiene?
choices: Force-push main to match your branch
git pull --rebase origin main into your branch
git stash everything
git merge main into main
quiz.explanation: Rebasing your branch onto the latest main keeps your diff focused and prevents avoidable conflicts surfacing during review.

outcomes: Create focused commits and branches that make a change easy to review, revert, and trace to an issue.
Resolve divergence with rebase or merge deliberately, and recover lost work with reflog and bisect.
Configure GitHub protection, review, and CI rules that keep main deployable and secrets out of history.
lessons.mental_model: A branch is a hypothesis, a commit is a decision, and main is the current best explanation; review is how the team agrees to believe it.
worked_example: Owen leads a four-engineer team maintaining a legal-research assistant. After a release, accuracy on the 180-case evaluation set drops from 91% to 84%, but no test fails. The branch contains 37 commits: a prompt rewrite, a dependency bump, and a chunk-size change. Owen runs git bisect with the evaluation script as the test command; six iterations identify the prompt commit that removed the instruction to cite sources. The team reverts it on main, tags v2.4.1, and reopens the change as a small pull request with an evaluation report attached. The decision: prompt changes now require an eval run in CI and a reviewer from the retrieval group. Owen adds the prompt log command to the runbook.
common_mistakes: Committing .env files, database dumps, or model weights because the repository is private, then discovering forks and caches keep them.
Mixing a prompt change, a dependency bump, and a refactor in one 900-line pull request, making rollback and review guesswork.
Force-pushing a shared branch to tidy history and overwriting colleagues' commits during the rewrite.

key_terms.definition: A merge that moves the branch pointer forward without a merge commit because the target has no new commits.
A local log of where HEAD and branch tips pointed, used to recover commits after a reset or rebase.
A binary search through commits, driven by a test command, that identifies the change that introduced a regression.

checkpoint.question: What information belongs in a commit body that a diff cannot show?
checkpoint.answer: The commit body should record why the change was made, the trade-offs, the supporting evidence, and the issue link—details a diff cannot show.

checkpoint.question: When is rebasing inappropriate, and what should you do instead?
checkpoint.answer: Do not rebase a branch that others have already pulled, because rebasing creates new commit hashes. Use merge for shared branches instead.

checkpoint.question: How does git bisect turn a quality regression into a specific commit?
checkpoint.answer: Git bisect uses a test command to binary-search through commits, halving the range each time until it identifies the commit that introduced the regression.

checkpoint.question: Why does deleting a secret from the latest commit fail to make it safe?
checkpoint.answer: Deleting it from the latest commit does not remove copies already cloned, cached, or forked. Rewriting history does not unshare the secret, so rotate the key.

checkpoint.question: Which branch protection rules keep main deployable without blocking small fixes?
checkpoint.answer: Require pull requests, one approval, passing CI, and linear history; block force pushes and branch deletion. Small fixes still go through a quick pull request.

lessons.title: Testing fundamentals
lessons.goal: Write tests that fail when the code breaks, understand what a test is proving, and know the three layers of testing.
lessons.takeaway: A good test is small, deterministic and named after the behaviour it protects; run it before you trust a refactor.

sections.heading: Why tests are non-negotiable
body: Untested code works until someone changes it — then nobody knows what still works. Tests are the executable specification: they tell the next engineer what behaviour is expected and catch regressions the moment they appear.

The red/green loop: write a failing test first (red), make the smallest change that passes (green), refactor safely with the test as your safety net. Even without strict TDD discipline, every bug fix should come with a test that would have caught it.
Flaky tests (pass sometimes, fail sometimes) erode trust worse than no tests — people stop reading them. Fix or delete flaky tests immediately; never ship with them.

sections.heading: The test pyramid: unit, integration, end-to-end
body: Unit tests exercise one function with controlled inputs — milliseconds each, hundreds of them. Integration tests exercise components together (route + database + serializer) — seconds, dozens of them. End-to-end tests drive the real system (browser, real DB) — minutes, a few of them.
Mostly unit tests, some integration, few e2e is the pyramid — and it is why "add more tests" almost always means "write unit tests for the broken unit".
Test behaviour, not implementation: prefer testing what comes out over how it was computed, unless the how is the whole point (e.g., choosing the right index).

sections.heading: Anatomy of a good test
body: Arrange–act–assert: set up inputs, call the unit, assert the observable outcome. One logical assertion per test; if two behaviours matter, write two tests.

assert_equal(actual, expected) style APIs produce readable failures; when a test fails, its message should tell you what broke, not just that something did. Name tests after the behaviour: test_expired_token_is_rejected, not test_1.
Determinism: no real clocks, no real network, no random seeds unpinned. Freeze time, stub HTTP, seed RNG — a test that fails only on Tuesdays in CI is worse than no test.

lessons.task: Write three pytest tests for a function discount(price, pct) with rules: pct in [0, 100] (else ValueError), result is never negative, and discount of 0 returns the price unchanged. Include one test that would have caught a real bug you have made before.

quiz.question: Which is the first question to ask when writing a test?
choices: What coverage number will this reach?
What behaviour should this prove?
How fast must it run?
Which mocking library?
quiz.explanation: A test exists to prove a behaviour. Coverage numbers and mocking are means to that end, not the end itself.

Use fixtures, parametrisation, and mocking to test HTTP, timeouts, and malformed model output without network calls.
Make tests deterministic and fast enough to run as a required gate on every pull request.

lessons.title: Project Structure
lessons.goal: Lay out a small project so it scales past the first hundred lines: src layout, entry points, configuration, and documentation.
lessons.takeaway: A predictable directory layout, a README and explicit configuration let teammates contribute without archaeology.

sections.heading: Layout conventions that work
body: src/<package>/ for importable code, tests/ for tests, pyproject.toml (or setup.cfg) for metadata and dependencies, README.md for humans. The flat layout breaks past a few modules; the src layout never surprises import paths.
Keep entry points thin: cli.py parses arguments and calls a main() in a module; it imports logic rather than embedding it. This makes the logic importable and testable without the shell.
Name by domain meaning: billing/, not helpers/utils/stuff/misc/. When everything fits in a module, the module name IS the map.

sections.heading: Configuration and secrets outside the tree
body: Config (ports, feature flags, timeouts) belongs in environment variables or a config file not committed with secrets. Code reads env vars at startup, with sensible defaults for local dev.

Secrets never enter git: no keys in code, no keys in config files, no keys in commit messages. Use .env locally (gitignored), and the platform secret manager in production. If a secret ever lands in a commit, rotate it — do not scrub history and pretend.
Fail fast on missing config: crash at startup with "GEMINI_API_KEY is required" rather than a confusing NoneType error at hour 3 of production.

sections.heading: README and docs are the front door
body: README answers: what is this, who is it for, how do I run it, how do I contribute. That is 80% of what a README needs. Screenshots for UI, quickstart commands for CLIs.
Architecture diagrams age well when small: one box-and-arrow image of the main flows beats ten pages of prose. Update it when the system changes, not when you remember to.
CHANGELOG.md (or release notes) answers "what changed since I last pulled?" — it is the difference between an upgrade you trust and an upgrade you fear.

lessons.task: Sketch the layout of a CLI todo app (name its files): src package, entry point, tests, config approach, README outline, and .gitignore entries. Then implement the skeleton (directories + files with docstrings, no logic) and verify pytest collects the (empty) test files without error.

quiz.question: Where should the CLI argument parsing live in a well-structured project?
choices: Inside every business-logic module
In a thin entry-point module that calls into importable logic
In a Makefile
In the tests
quiz.explanation: A thin entry point keeps business logic importable and testable without invoking the shell or parsing argv.

outcomes: Create a src layout with a package, an entry point, and a tests directory that imports the package without path hacks.
Draw the dependency direction between schemas, I/O, domain logic, and the command-line entry point.
Explain why python -m package avoids the import failures caused by running a file inside the package.
lessons.mental_model: A package is a building with labelled rooms: the corridor is short, the doors face one direction, and you never climb through a window to reach the database.
worked_example: At a four-person team building a model-catalogue client, loader.py starts importing catalog.py to reuse a price formatter, while catalog.py already imports loader.py to read files. Tests pass on one laptop because the modules were imported in a lucky order, then fail in CI with ImportError: partially initialized module. In the review, the team moves the formatter into formatting.py, points both modules at it, and adds __main__.py. They also replace sys.path.append("..") in the tests with an editable install. The CI run drops from four minutes to ninety seconds because tests no longer resolve three copies of the package. The decision: no module may import a module that imports it, and shared helpers get their own home.
common_mistakes: Adding sys.path.append in tests instead of installing the package, so CI and containers keep failing.
Putting HTTP calls, file reads, and argument parsing in __init__.py, where every import pays for them.
Creating one utils.py that everything imports, which becomes a second, unnamed package with no owner.

key_terms.definition: The single function or module Python runs to start the program, kept separate from the library code it calls.
A failure where two modules import each other, usually revealing that responsibilities or dependency direction are wrong.

checkpoint.question: Why does the src layout make a passing test more trustworthy than a test run from the repository root?
checkpoint.answer: It stops Python from accidentally importing loose files in the folder you run from. A test can pass only by importing the installed package, so it matches CI and containers.

checkpoint.question: What symptom in CI usually points to a circular import rather than a missing dependency?
checkpoint.answer: CI may fail with ImportError: partially initialized module, while local tests pass because modules were imported in a lucky order. That points to two modules importing each other.

checkpoint.question: Which code belongs in __main__.py, and which belongs in a callable main()?
checkpoint.answer: __main__.py should contain the small launcher and guard that let python -m model_catalog work. The callable main() should contain the real startup work, such as loading data and printing, so tests can import it without running that work.

checkpoint.question: How would you break a cycle where two modules genuinely need the same helper?
checkpoint.answer: Move the shared helper into its own module, such as formatting.py, and have both modules import that. If needed, pass the helper in as an injected function instead.

checkpoint.question: Why should importing a module never read data/models.json or open a network connection?
checkpoint.answer: Importing should have no side effects, so tests stay fast and do not need data or network access. File reads and API calls belong in main(), where tests can choose not to run them.

This first lesson shows you the map of the journey ahead, sets you up with the right tools, and teaches you how to learn effectively - so you can go from complete beginner to building real AI products with confidence.

sections.heading: What is AI Engineering?
body: Think of building with AI like building a house. A foundation model (like GPT, Claude, or LLaMA) is like a very talented builder - incredibly skilled at many things, but not reliable on its own for your specific needs.

AI engineering is about everything around that builder: the blueprint (your app design), the plumbing and electricity (APIs and connections), the safety checks (testing and guardrails), the permits and maintenance (deployment and monitoring), and making sure it all works together reliably for real users.
You're not just asking an AI to write something - you're building a complete system that uses AI to solve real problems.

sections.heading: How to Learn: Build > Watch
body: The most common mistake is watching videos and reading without coding. Your brain learns by doing.

For every lesson: (1) Understand the 'why' - read why it matters, (2) Learn the concept - go through each idea one by one and explain it out loud in your own words, (3) Follow the worked example - type it yourself, don't copy-paste blindly, (4) Do the hands-on tasks - this is the most important part, (5) Check yourself with the questions.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Real AI products need to be reliable - if they break when 100 people use them, that's bad. You'll learn to build for reliability from the start.

Measure things - don't just say 'it works', say 'it answers in 2 seconds for $0.001 per request'

lessons.goal: Explain what an AI engineer does vs data scientist vs ML engineer
lessons.takeaway: If AI models are like powerful engines, AI engineers are the ones who design the whole vehicle - steering wheel, seats, safety features, fuel system - so anyone can drive it safely to their destination.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: Before diving into code, it's important to understand the role you're training for. Many people think AI engineering is just using ChatGPT or building chatbots, but it's much more. Knowing what AI engineers actually do will help you focus on the right skills and understand why this course is structured the way it is.

If AI models are like powerful engines, AI engineers are the ones who design the whole vehicle - steering wheel, seats, safety features, fuel system - so anyone can drive it safely to their destination.

sections.heading: AI Engineer vs Other Roles
body: A Data Scientist mostly analyzes data and finds insights. An ML Engineer focuses on training and optimizing machine learning models. An AI Engineer takes existing models (like GPT) and builds products with them - connecting them to apps, adding features, making them reliable and useful.
Think of it as: ML engineers build the engines, AI engineers build the cars people actually drive.

sections.heading: From Model to Product
body: Having access to an AI model is just the beginning. To make a real product, you need to handle user input, call the model correctly, process its response, handle errors, add safety checks, store data, authenticate users, and more. AI engineering is 80% building the 'plumbing' around the model and 20% working with the model itself.
That's why this course spends a lot of time on APIs, databases, and backend development.

sections.heading: The Build-Measure-Improve Loop
body: AI engineering is iterative. You build a simple version, test it with real use cases, see what breaks or could be better, then improve it. You don't need perfection on day one.
You need to ship something small, learn from it, and make it better. This is how real products are built.

sections.heading: Production notes

Make the evaluation set a release gate and version it alongside prompts and model identifiers.
Design an explicit escalation and fallback path for low confidence, provider failure, and policy-sensitive requests.

worked_example: Marcus leads three engineers at a logistics startup handling 8,000 support tickets a month. A vendor demo appears to resolve 90% of questions, but on 300 sampled tickets the team finds 18 intents and a tricky refund policy. A keyword baseline routes 46% correctly; a model with six worked examples, a JSON schema, and policy retrieval reaches 82%. Marcus decides against an autonomous agent and ships a fixed triage workflow with a confidence threshold and a human queue for uncertain cases. The measured cost is about USD 0.003 per ticket and p95 latency is 2.1 seconds. The decision is documented with the failed alternatives so the team can revisit it when volume doubles.
common_mistakes: Comparing providers on price per million tokens without measuring token counts for your own prompts and outputs.
Calling a prototype accurate because a handful of impressive demos worked, then skipping a representative evaluation set.
Removing the human escalation path before proving that the model handles low-confidence and adversarial cases.

checkpoint.question: Why can a fixed workflow be a better engineering choice than an agent?
checkpoint.answer: A fixed workflow can be faster, cheaper, and more reliable for narrowly defined tasks because it uses simple rules or classifiers instead of a complex agent, reducing errors, latency, and cost.

checkpoint.question: What does the five-part loop produce after each iteration?
checkpoint.answer: After each iteration the loop produces a clear indication of which part of the system needs change—prompt, data source, schema, or operations—so you can decide the next experiment based on the biggest measured risk.

checkpoint.question: How would you explain the hosted-API versus open-weight trade-off to a finance stakeholder?
checkpoint.answer: Explain that a hosted API is a managed service you pay per use, while an open‑weight model means you own the model and must host, maintain, and scale it yourself, affecting cost, control, and latency.

checkpoint.question: Why is cost per successful request more useful than cost per token?
checkpoint.answer: Because it shows how much money is spent for each correct answer, not just how many tokens the model processes, helping decide if the service is worth it.

lessons.goal: Draw the six layers of an AI application and state the responsibility of each.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: Understanding the pieces before building makes everything less confusing. You'll see how user interface, backend, AI model, data, and monitoring all work together.

An AI app is like a restaurant: UI = dining room (customers see this), Backend = kitchen (does the work), AI Model = special chef, Database = pantry/storage, Deployment/Operations = keeping doors open 24/7.

sections.heading: The Five Layers of an AI App
body: Every modern AI app has layers: (1) User Interface - what people see and click, (2) Backend/API - the brain that coordinates everything, (3) AI Model - the intelligence
that generates responses, (4) Data Layer - stores user data, past conversations, etc., (5) Infrastructure/Operations - keeps it running, secure, and fast.

sections.heading: How a Request Flows
body: When a user asks a question: it goes from UI → Backend (which adds context, checks permissions) → AI Model (generates answer)
→ Backend (processes answer, saves it) → UI (shows to user). Understanding this flow helps you debug when things go wrong.

sections.heading: Building This Course's App
body: Throughout this course, you'll build all these layers for your own AI app. You'll start
simple and add pieces each module until you have a complete, production-ready system.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Allocate a latency budget across authentication, retrieval, model time, validation, and streaming, then enforce deadlines at each hop.
Make retried writes idempotent and cancel downstream work when the client disconnects.
Redact secrets and sensitive personal data from traces while retaining enough structure to debug the request path.

lessons.task: Trace one request in a production AI product and draw its six layers, marking at least three unknowns (40 minutes). Run the sample handler with fake retrieve and generate functions, then add tests for invalid JSON, zero citations, and timeout (60 minutes).

The backend layer owns authentication, authorisation, limits, and persistence. Orchestration should not implement…
Streaming complicates persistence because tokens arrive before the full response, so the backend must assemble and validate…
quiz.explanation: The backend layer owns authentication, authorisation, limits, and persistence. Orchestration should not implement authentication because it is responsible for assembling context and controlling the model loop; keeping authentication in the backend gives security one explicit boundary and contract.

worked_example: A customer asks a retail assistant, 'Where is order 4821, and can I still change the address?' The browser sends the message to a FastAPI service, which authenticates the session and loads six recent turns. The orchestrator retrieves two shipping-policy chunks and calls the order service, which responds in 340 ms with status packed and address_editable false. The model must return an answer plus source IDs; validation confirms both citations exist. The order service then exceeds its 800 ms deadline on a second attempt, so the assistant reports the known policy, says the live status is temporarily unavailable, and offers a callback. The trace records 3.2 seconds total, 1,180 input tokens, 96 output tokens, and the degraded path; no order status is invented.
common_mistakes: Treating the model as a database and asking it for facts that live in an order or account system.
Putting all conversation state into one ever-growing prompt instead of loading and trimming the relevant history.
Adding a fallback message without a timeout or test, so requests hang until the user gives up.

checkpoint.question: Which layer owns authentication, and why should orchestration not implement it?
checkpoint.answer: The backend layer owns authentication, authorisation, limits, and persistence. Orchestration should not implement authentication because it is responsible for assembling context and controlling the model loop; keeping authentication in the backend gives security one explicit boundary and contract.

checkpoint.question: What should happen when retrieval succeeds but the model returns invalid JSON?
checkpoint.answer: Validate the model output against a schema. If the model returns invalid JSON, schema validation fails, so reject the output and return a safe fallback such as “I cannot verify that answer right now,” while recording the validation failure in the trace.

checkpoint.question: Why must a cited source ID be checked against retrieved chunks?
checkpoint.answer: A cited source ID must be checked against the retrieved chunks so the model cannot invent sources. Only chunk IDs that point to actually retrieved chunks are valid; if none match, the answer is rejected.

checkpoint.question: Where does streaming complicate persistence and cancellation?
checkpoint.answer: Streaming complicates persistence because tokens arrive before the full response, so the backend must assemble and validate the complete answer before persisting the turn. It complicates cancellation because if the client disconnects, the server must cancel downstream work rather than continue paying for an answer nobody receives.

checkpoint.question: Give an example of a degradation that is better than a generic error.
checkpoint.answer: When the order service times out, the assistant can report the known policy, say the live status is temporarily unavailable, and offer a callback. That is better than a generic error because it still gives the user useful, verified information.

lessons.title: AI Engineering Stack
lessons.goal: Map infrastructure, data, model access, orchestration, product, and operations to concrete tools.
lessons.takeaway: Build the smallest stack you can operate, then add a component only when a measured bottleneck or risk cannot be handled by the layer you already have.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: Stack choices compound: a queue added too early creates operational work, while a missing data store or observability layer blocks production. Vendors also change pricing, schemas, and availability. An AI engineer needs a defensible selection process rather than a list of fashionable tools.
Build the smallest stack you can operate, then add a component only when a measured bottleneck or risk cannot be handled by the layer you already have.

sections.heading: Boring infrastructure and data Start with a container runtime, a relational data
body: Boring infrastructure and data Start with a container runtime, a relational database, object storage, and a cache or queue only when a workload requires one. PostgreSQL with pgvector can hold millions of chunks and, more importantly, keeps metadata filtering, permissions, and transactions beside your application data.

A dedicated vector database earns its place when scale, indexing features, or isolation justify another service to operate. The same logic applies to Kubernetes: three engineers serving 12,000 documents a month rarely need it.

Model access through a stable boundary A gateway gives the application one interface for providers while centralising keys, quotas, retries, fallbacks, caching, and usage accounting. It also lets you switch models without editing every service.

Keep the gateway thin: validate the request, enforce a timeout, route to a provider, normalise the response, and record cost. If the gateway becomes a second application with its own agent framework and business rules, it has stopped reducing complexity.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Apply per-tenant quotas, budget alarms, and rate limits at the gateway; unbounded model access is an availability and finance risk.
Pin model and dependency versions, but rehearse upgrades against the evaluation set because hosted models can change behaviour.
Test backup restoration and provider failover, not just their configuration; a documented fallback that has never run is an assumption.
