lessons.mental_model: Build the smallest stack you can operate, then add a component only when a measured bottleneck or risk cannot be handled by the layer you already have.
worked_example: A three-engineer team is building an invoice assistant for 12,000 invoices a month on AWS. Their envelope is 99.5% availability, p95 under five seconds, and USD 0.02 per document. They choose FastAPI on ECS Fargate, RDS PostgreSQL with pgvector, S3 for originals, and SQS plus a worker for OCR because parsing can take 40 seconds. A managed model sits behind an internal gateway with per-tenant quotas and a fallback provider. They postpone Kubernetes, a dedicated vector database, and multi-region deployment, and record the triggers that would reopen each decision. The first month costs roughly USD 900 in infrastructure and model usage, well below the cost of operating a larger platform.
common_mistakes: Adding a dedicated vector database and Kubernetes before there is enough traffic or a feature that requires them.
Hard-coding one provider's request schema throughout the application, then discovering that a fallback needs a second schema.
Logging full prompts and responses that contain customer data, secrets, or personal information.

checkpoint.question: What belongs in a model gateway, and what should stay in application services?
checkpoint.answer: The gateway should handle provider access: keys, quotas, retries, fallbacks, caching, timeouts, routing, normalising responses, and cost records. Business rules and agent logic stay in application services.

checkpoint.question: Why is team operating capacity a technical constraint rather than an organisational detail?
checkpoint.answer: Every service you add must be run, monitored, and fixed by your team. If the team cannot operate it, the architecture is not technically suitable, even if it looks impressive.

checkpoint.question: Which metrics would trigger a review of a managed-model decision?
checkpoint.answer: Review if cost per document, p95 latency, quality scores, or availability move outside your requirements envelope, or if the provider changes pricing, schemas, or availability.

checkpoint.question: How does an ADR differ from a runbook?
checkpoint.answer: An ADR records why a choice was made, what alternatives existed, its consequences, and when to revisit it. A runbook gives steps for operating or fixing something.

lessons.title: Course Roadmap
lessons.goal: Sequence the modules and explain which prerequisites each later module assumes.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: A broad curriculum fails when it becomes an unordered playlist. Dependencies matter: agents assume HTTP, tool calling, and state, while production work assumes a working application to observe. A plan protects the scarce resource, your attention, and turns each module into evidence rather than another unfinished tutorial.
A curriculum is a dependency graph, not a playlist: do not play a module until the modules it imports are working.

sections.heading: The dependency spine Modules 1 and 2 build Python and backend foundations, becau
body: The dependency spine Modules 1 and 2 build Python and backend foundations, because every later feature needs a request, validation, storage, and tests. Modules 3 and 4 add model behaviour, prompting, structured output, streaming, and reliability.

Module 5 adds retrieval; Modules 6 to 8 add agents, orchestration, and MCP; Modules 9 to 11 cover production, deployment, and system design; Module 12 integrates them. Skipping the backend or production modules does not save time, because their gaps reappear as incident work during the capstone.

One product through-line Choose a capstone domain by Module 2 and keep using the same repository. Each module then adds a capability to one product: extraction to the intake path, RAG to the knowledge path, tools to actions, MCP to integration, evaluation to the release gate, and deployment to the delivery path.

Reuse is not laziness; it exposes the integration problems that isolated demos hide. Write down the scope boundary so the capstone stays achievable alongside the lessons. Cadence, gates, and evidence A workable pace is five to seven hours a week for roughly twenty weeks, with at least half the time spent building.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Treat the capstone as a product with a real user, environment, budget, and on-call path; a local demo is not the finish line.
Keep evaluation, cost, and latency targets visible from the first version so architecture decisions are anchored to service objectives.
Preserve decision records and incident notes; they demonstrate engineering maturity and make future changes safer.

worked_example: Aisha is a data analyst with six hours a week and an 18-week target: a permit-document assistant for 250 colleagues. She maps Module 1 to a Python ingestion script, Module 2 to a FastAPI service, Module 5 to RAG over 4,000 pages, Module 6 to a read-only lookup tool, Module 9 to an evaluation and tracing gate, and Module 12 to a staging deployment. At week 12 she finds that retrieval answers 88% of 150 test questions correctly, but a multi-agent rewrite adds latency without improving accuracy. The decision is to keep the fixed workflow, spend the saved week on permission filtering, and document the rejected alternative. Her buffer week absorbs a provider outage instead of becoming catch-up debt.

checkpoint.answer: Module 2 (Backend Engineering) is where the first network-facing service gets built (a FastAPI API with validation and storage). It assumes Module 1: typed Python, virtual environments, locked dependencies, and a tested understanding of HTTP calls.

checkpoint.question: How does one capstone domain reduce integration risk across thirteen modules?
checkpoint.answer: Keeping one capstone domain means every module adds a reusable capability to the same product and repository instead of producing throwaway demos. Integration problems surface early, where they are cheap, and the capstone is assembled continuously rather than started from scratch at the end.

checkpoint.question: What evidence should let you mark a module complete?
checkpoint.answer: A working artefact (service, evaluation report, diagram, or decision record), corrected self-check answers, at least one real evaluation or test result, and a short decision record. Gate on demonstrated capability — if you cannot explain and reproduce the artefact, repeat the task rather than mark the module done.

checkpoint.question: Why are buffer weeks part of a realistic schedule?
checkpoint.answer: Five to seven hours a week for roughly twenty weeks never survives contact with real life unchanged. Two buffer weeks absorb provider outages, travel, and surprise integration work, so normal variance does not turn into permanent catch-up debt or a reason to abandon the plan.

lessons.title: Git and GitHub from zero
lessons.goal: Initialise a repository and make a first commit. Save snapshots of your work, write a useful commit message, and keep secrets out of history. Initialise a repository and make a first commit.
lessons.takeaway: A commit is a labelled photograph of your project, not a video of everything you did. The message is the note on the back explaining why you took it.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: AI projects change quickly: prompts, evaluation sets, and dependencies all move. Git gives you a reviewable history and a safe way to recover when an experiment breaks. GitHub adds a remote copy and a place to run automated checks.
A commit is a labelled photograph of your project, not a video of everything you did. The message is the note on the back explaining why you took it.

sections.heading: A repository is a history of decisions
body: git init creates a local repository. git status shows what changed, git add stages a file, and git commit records a snapshot
with a message. A commit is not a backup of your whole computer; it is a reviewable diff plus the reason for it.

sections.heading: Commit messages are for future readers
body: Start with a short imperative subject such as "Add JSON reader" and keep it under about 72 characters. Use the body to explain why the change
was needed, what trade-off you made, and how you verified it. "Update stuff" forces the next reader to reverse-engineer your intent.

sections.heading: Never commit secrets or generated files
body: A .gitignore lists files Git should not track: .env, .venv/, __pycache__/, and large model weights. Deleting a secret in
a later commit does not remove it from history; rotate the credential and rewrite history only with a deliberate plan.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Protect the main branch with review and automated checks once you collaborate.
Commit small changes with a reason and a verification note; future you is the main reader.
Run a secret scan before pushing and rotate any credential that was ever committed.

lessons.task: Create a repository, add a .gitignore, and commit your first script (20 minutes). Write a commit body that records the problem, the change, and how you checked it (15 minutes).

quiz.question: What is the difference between the working tree, the staging area, and a commit?
choices: The old commit still contains the value and clones retain it; rotate the credential.
The why lets a future reader decide whether the change still applies.
The working tree is the files you edit; staging selects what goes into the next commit; a commit is the recorded snapshot.
At minimum .env, .venv/, __pycache__/, and large generated artefacts.
quiz.explanation: The working tree is the files you edit; staging selects what goes into the next commit; a commit is the recorded snapshot.

outcomes: Initialise a repository and make a first commit.
Write a commit message that explains why a change exists.
Keep secrets and generated files out of version control.
lessons.mental_model: A commit is a labelled photograph of your project, not a video of everything you did. The message is the note on the back explaining why you took it.
worked_example: A learner commits a .env file with an API key, then deletes it in the next commit. The key still exists in the first commit and in every clone. They rotate the key, add .env to .gitignore, commit .env.example with empty values, and write a short note in the README. The fix is rotation and prevention, not a prettier diff.
common_mistakes: Committing .env or a virtual environment because the repository is private.
Mixing unrelated changes in one commit so a rollback removes more than intended.
Force-pushing a shared branch and overwriting someone else's commits.

key_terms.definition: A directory whose changes Git tracks as a history of commits.
A snapshot of staged changes plus a message, author, and parent commit.
A named copy of a repository hosted elsewhere, usually on GitHub.
A file listing paths Git should not track.
A request to review and merge changes from one branch into another.

checkpoint.question: What is the difference between the working tree, the staging area, and a commit?
checkpoint.answer: The working tree is the files you edit; staging selects what goes into the next commit; a commit is the recorded snapshot.

checkpoint.question: Why should a commit message describe why, not just what?
checkpoint.answer: The why lets a future reader decide whether the change still applies.

checkpoint.question: What belongs in .gitignore for a Python AI project?
checkpoint.answer: At minimum .env, .venv/, __pycache__/, and large generated artefacts.

checkpoint.question: Why does deleting a secret in a later commit fail to remove it from history?
checkpoint.answer: The old commit still contains the value and clones retain it; rotate the credential.

checkpoint.question: When is a force push acceptable?
checkpoint.answer: Only on a branch you alone own, after coordinating, and never to erase evidence on a shared branch.

lessons.title: Git & GitHub essentials
lessons.goal: Create focused commits and branches that make a change easy to review, revert, and trace to an issue.
lessons.takeaway: A branch is a hypothesis, a commit is a decision, and main is the current best explanation; review is how the team agrees to believe it.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: AI projects change prompts, model versions, and evaluation data alongside code, so history is often the only record of why a result changed. A clean commit graph lets you bisect a quality regression, revert a bad prompt safely, and review a provider migration. Git skills also prevent the two expensive mistakes: committing a key and rewriting shared history.
A branch is a hypothesis, a commit is a decision, and main is the current best explanation; review is how the team agrees to believe it.

sections.heading: Commits are snapshots with intent A commit records a complete tree plus a messag
body: Commits are snapshots with intent A commit records a complete tree plus a message explaining why the tree changed. Keep commits atomic: one behaviour, one prompt, or one dependency bump, never formatting mixed with logic. Write an imperative subject under 72 characters and use the body for evidence, trade-offs, and the issue link.

Small commits make review faster and revert safer, because you can undo one decision without unpicking a week of unrelated work. Divergence: rebase or merge Rebase replays your commits onto a new base, producing a linear history that is easy to read and bisect; it creates new hashes, so never rebase a branch others have pulled.

Merge preserves real history and is the safer choice for shared branches. Resolve conflicts deliberately and run tests after each resolution, and use force-with-lease rather than a bare force push. Tags mark releases, because a branch head keeps moving while a tag does not.

Review and repository protection A pull request is a conversation about a diff, so keep it under roughly 400 changed lines and include reproduction steps, risk, and rollback. Protect main with required reviews, passing checks, linear history, and blocked force pushes.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Protect main: require a pull request, one approval, passing CI, and linear history; block force pushes and branch deletion.
Tag every deploy with an annotated version and record the commit SHA in release notes so incidents map back to code.
Enable secret scanning and dependency alerts, and give the repository a CODEOWNERS file that names the required reviewers.

lessons.task: Rewrite the last five commits on a practice branch into atomic commits with bodies, then compare the log with the original (35 minutes). Reproduce a regression in a sample repository and locate it with git bisect using a test command (40 minutes).

quiz.question: What information belongs in a commit body that a diff cannot show?
choices: The commit body should record why the change was made, the trade-offs, the supporting evidence, and the issue link—details…
Deleting it from the latest commit does not remove copies already cloned, cached, or forked. Rewriting history does not…
Do not rebase a branch that others have already pulled, because rebasing creates new commit hashes. Use merge for shared…
Git bisect uses a test command to binary-search through commits, halving the range each time until it identifies the commit…
quiz.explanation: The commit body should record why the change was made, the trade-offs, the supporting evidence, and the issue link—details a diff cannot show.

outcomes: Create focused commits and branches that make a change easy to review, revert, and trace to an issue.
Resolve divergence with rebase or merge deliberately, and recover lost work with reflog and bisect.
Configure GitHub protection, review, and CI rules that keep main deployable and secrets out of history.
lessons.mental_model: A branch is a hypothesis, a commit is a decision, and main is the current best explanation; review is how the team agrees to believe it.
worked_example: Owen leads a four-engineer team maintaining a legal-research assistant. After a release, accuracy on the 180-case evaluation set drops from 91% to 84%, but no test fails. The branch contains 37 commits: a prompt rewrite, a dependency bump, and a chunk-size change. Owen runs git bisect with the evaluation script as the test command; six iterations identify the prompt commit that removed the instruction to cite sources. The team reverts it on main, tags v2.4.1, and reopens the change as a small pull request with an evaluation report attached. The decision: prompt changes now require an eval run in CI and a reviewer from the retrieval group. Owen adds the prompt log command to the runbook.
common_mistakes: Committing .env files, database dumps, or model weights because the repository is private, then discovering forks and caches keep them.
Mixing a prompt change, a dependency bump, and a refactor in one 900-line pull request, making rollback and review guesswork.
Force-pushing a shared branch to tidy history and overwriting colleagues' commits during the rewrite.

key_terms.definition: A merge that moves the branch pointer forward without a merge commit because the target has no new commits.
A local log of where HEAD and branch tips pointed, used to recover commits after a reset or rebase.
A binary search through commits, driven by a test command, that identifies the change that introduced a regression.

checkpoint.question: What information belongs in a commit body that a diff cannot show?
checkpoint.answer: The commit body should record why the change was made, the trade-offs, the supporting evidence, and the issue link—details a diff cannot show.

checkpoint.question: When is rebasing inappropriate, and what should you do instead?
checkpoint.answer: Do not rebase a branch that others have already pulled, because rebasing creates new commit hashes. Use merge for shared branches instead.

checkpoint.question: How does git bisect turn a quality regression into a specific commit?
checkpoint.answer: Git bisect uses a test command to binary-search through commits, halving the range each time until it identifies the commit that introduced the regression.

checkpoint.question: Why does deleting a secret from the latest commit fail to make it safe?
checkpoint.answer: Deleting it from the latest commit does not remove copies already cloned, cached, or forked. Rewriting history does not unshare the secret, so rotate the key.

checkpoint.question: Which branch protection rules keep main deployable without blocking small fixes?
checkpoint.answer: Require pull requests, one approval, passing CI, and linear history; block force pushes and branch deletion. Small fixes still go through a quick pull request.

outcomes: Work confidently with branches, commits, merges and pull requests
Write focused, repeatable tests for behaviour that matters
Organise a project so another engineer can pick it up quickly

modules.title: Development Tools and Workflow

lessons.title: CI/CD Basics
lessons.goal: Explain what continuous integration and continuous delivery actually do on every push, and trace a failing pipeline to its step.
lessons.takeaway: CI is a habit made automatic: every push runs the same checks so surprises are caught before review.

sections.heading: What CI actually checks
body: Continuous integration means every push is built, linted, type-checked and tested automatically on a clean machine. The goal is not ceremony — it is that no commit lands on main without a robot vouching for it.

A typical pipeline: checkout the commit, install dependencies (deterministically, from a lockfile), compile/lint/type-check, run the test suite, build artifacts, report status back to the PR. Each stage fails fast and loudly.
CI that takes an hour is fiction — nobody waits for it. Keep the core suite under ~10 minutes by splitting slow integration/e2e tests into separate jobs that run in parallel or nightly.

sections.heading: CD: shipping what passed
body: Continuous delivery packages every green commit into a deployable artifact; continuous deployment additionally promotes it automatically. Most teams do CD to staging and gated CD to production.

Deterministic builds matter: same inputs → same artifact. Pin base images, pin dependency versions, stamp artifacts with the commit SHA, and store them in a registry. "It deployed from my laptop" is not a release.
The pipeline is code — review it like code. A bad YAML edit that disables tests is a security incident, not a style nit.

sections.heading: Reading a failing pipeline
body: Click the red X on the PR. Find the first red job. Read its log from the failure upwards — the first error is usually the real one; later errors are cascade noise.
Classic failures: dependency resolution changed (lockfile drifted), flaky test, missing secret/permission, timeout, lint regression. Each has a signature in the log; learn to spot them fast.
Re-running the job fixes flaky infrastructure, not flaky tests. If re-run passes, note which test flapped and quarantine or fix it — do not shrug.

lessons.task: Find the workflow file in this very repository (.github/workflows/ci.yml). Write a short description of each job: what it builds/tests/verifies, and why each one exists. Flag any job you do not understand and look up its purpose — CI configs are documentation you can execute.

quiz.question: What does a green CI check on a PR actually certify?
choices: The code is correct and bug-free
The automated gates the project defined passed on that commit
The reviewer approved it
The deploy to production succeeded
quiz.explanation: CI certifies exactly the gates defined in the workflow — tests, lint, builds — nothing more. It says nothing about human review or production health.

outcomes: Compare at-most-once, at-least-once, and exactly-once claims with the behaviour they actually deliver.
Configure acknowledgement, prefetch, visibility timeout, and dead-letter routing for a consumer.
Design partitioning, backpressure, and ordering rules for a queue that must scale.
lessons.mental_model: A queue is a conveyor belt with a receipt: the belt moves work, but someone must confirm each item and set aside the ones that jam.
worked_example: A media pipeline ingests 240,000 images a day and fans them into thumbnail, moderation, and metadata queues. Thumbnail workers used a 30-second visibility timeout while p99 rendering took 48 seconds, so 6% of images were rendered twice and billed twice. The team raises the timeout to 120 seconds, adds a heartbeat that extends it during long renders, and sets prefetch to 5 per worker. One image that crashes the decoder is retried three times, then routed to a dead-letter queue with its S3 key and error. Throughput rises from 180 to 260 images per minute because workers no longer duplicate the slowest work.
common_mistakes: Acknowledging a message before the work succeeds, so a crash loses the job with no record anywhere.
Using one global ordering key for every event, which forces a single consumer and removes all parallelism.
Leaving a poison message in the queue, where it is redelivered forever and blocks everything behind it.

key_terms.definition: The window after delivery during which a message is hidden from other consumers; expiry causes redelivery.
A separate queue receiving messages that failed too often, so they can be inspected without blocking traffic.
The gap between the newest message produced and the newest one processed, measured in messages or seconds.

checkpoint.question: What is the goal of Queues?
checkpoint.answer: Compare at-most-once, at-least-once, and exactly-once claims with the behaviour they actually deliver.

checkpoint.question: Why does queues matter in practice?
checkpoint.answer: A queue is a conveyor belt with a receipt: the belt moves work, but someone must confirm each item and set aside the ones that jam.

lessons.title: Debugging
lessons.goal: Debug systematically: reproduce, isolate, hypothesize, verify — instead of changing code randomly until the error stops.
lessons.takeaway: Debugging is a loop: reproduce, form a hypothesis, test it, then keep the smallest change that fixes the cause.

sections.heading: The method before the tools
body: Reproduce first: make the bug happen on demand, ideally in the smallest input. If you cannot make it happen reliably, you do not yet know you have found it. Shrink the repro until it is embarrassingly small.
Read the error message fully, then the traceback bottom-up. Most beginners stop at the first line — the actual failing line and error type tell you what went wrong and where.
Hypothesize one cause at a time and test it. "I changed three things and it works now" tells you nothing — you cannot fix, only revert blindly next time.

sections.heading: Print debugging, done right
body: Printing values is a legitimate first tool. Do it with labels: print("totals:", totals, "items=", len(items)) so the log is greppable and tells a story. Print at boundaries, not on every line.
Bisect: when a bug appeared, ask "which commit introduced it?" via git bisect to binary-search the history. It reliably finds the culprit in minutes instead of days.
Compare good vs bad: run the working case and the broken case side by side and diff the values. The first divergence is usually where the bug lives.

sections.heading: Debuggers and structured logs
body: A real debugger (pdb/ipdb, IDE breakpoints) pauses execution and inspects state: step over/into, watch expressions, change values mid-flight. Learn five commands — n, s, c, p expr, l — and you are 80% productive.
Logging with levels (debug/info/warning/error) and structured fields (json) beats print for anything that ships. The failing request will tell you the exact inputs if you log them with a request-id.

When stuck for more than ~20 minutes on "why is this happening?", change strategy: rubber-duck the problem out loud, or ask someone with no context — your attempt to explain exposes the wrong assumption reliably.

lessons.task: Take any bug you fixed recently. Write down: the exact repro, the first wrong value you observed, the hypothesis you tested first (and whether it was right), and the smallest change that fixed it. Then do the same for a bug someone else wrote in this repo history (use git log to find a fix commit and trace its test).

quiz.question: Your function returns the wrong value. What is the first debugging step?
choices: Add more prints everywhere
Rewrite the function
Reproduce the wrong output with the smallest failing input and identify the first incorrect intermediate value
Revert the last commit
quiz.explanation: You cannot fix what you cannot reproduce, and you cannot find a cause without locating the first divergence from expected behaviour.

outcomes: Understand Python's basic data types (strings, numbers, lists, dictionaries)
Work with lists and dictionaries to handle API responses
Write loops and conditions to process data
Read and understand Python error messages (tracebacks)
Know the difference between running a script vs running as a module
lessons.mental_model: Working with API data is like unpacking a delivery box. The outer box might be a dictionary with labels (keys) pointing to what's inside. Some things might be single items, others might be lists of items. Your job is to open it up and grab exactly what you need.
worked_example: On her first day, Tomas inherits a 60-line script that reports average model prices. It prints GBP 0.00 for every provider. Prices arrive as strings from a CSV, so his patched sum() concatenates them, and his earlier fix divided by the row count with integer division. He rewrites the aggregation as one pass, converts with float(row["price"]) at the boundary, filters rows where context_window is None, and prints a row count beside each average. A three-row fixture with known values guards the fix. The decision: convert types once, at ingestion, never in formatting code.
common_mistakes: Mutating a list while looping over it, so the script skips rows and produces a total nobody can reproduce.
Comparing prices as strings, where "10.0" < "9.5" is true and the cheapest model is reported incorrectly.
Debugging with print statements instead of reading the traceback line the interpreter already named.

key_terms.definition: An ordered collection of items in square brackets [ ]. Like a shopping list - order matters.
A collection of key-value pairs in curly braces { }. Like a contact card - look up by name to find info.
Code that repeats - does something for each item in a list or until a condition is met.
Python's way of showing you where and why an error happened, with the full chain of calls.
Python's way of saying 'nothing here' or 'no value'. Different from zero or empty string!

checkpoint.question: Why does appending to a list inside a loop over that same list produce incorrect totals?
checkpoint.answer: Appending to a list while looping over it changes the list size during the loop, so some items are skipped or counted twice, giving wrong totals.

checkpoint.question: What does dict.get("price", 0.0) hide that an explicit membership check would reveal?
checkpoint.answer: dict.get('price',0.0) returns 0.0 when the key is missing but does not create a new entry; a membership check would reveal that the key was absent and allow you to handle the missing case explicitly.

checkpoint.question: Why is a list comprehension a poor choice for a 4 GB log file?
checkpoint.answer: A list comprehension builds the whole list in memory, so for a 4 GB file it would consume too much RAM; a generator processes one item at a time.

checkpoint.question: Which frame in a traceback usually holds the real cause, and why?
checkpoint.answer: The frame that shows where the exception was raised (the last frame) usually contains the real cause, because it is the line that executed the faulty operation.

checkpoint.question: How does running a file inside a package change sys.path compared with python -m?
checkpoint.answer: Running a file with python -m adds the package’s directory to sys.path, so imports resolve relative to the package; running a script directly does not include that package directory in sys.path.

lessons.title: Tool Integration
lessons.goal: Automate the repetitive parts of engineering work — editor, linter, formatter, test runner, pre-commit hooks — so the tools serve the work.
lessons.takeaway: Tooling pays off only when it is shared: configure formatters, linters and tasks in the repository, not in one person’s editor.

sections.heading: Editor as a force multiplier
body: One editor, configured deeply: syntax highlighting, format-on-save, lint-on-type, go-to-definition, rename-symbol. Keybindings over menus. The 30 seconds you spend configuring a tool saves hours across the year.

Know three shortcuts cold: search project files, find symbol, find references. Everything else is optional. Learn your editor's escape hatch for "my editor is misbehaving" — restart with safe mode rarely loses work.
Dotfiles in a repo (git mirror of ~/.config) make a new machine productive in one command — a hallmark of senior engineers.

sections.heading: Lint, format, and type checks
body: Lint (ruff, flake8) catches suspicious code: unused imports, bare excepts, undefined names. Format (black, ruff-format) removes style arguments forever by deciding them mechanically. Type checks (mypy, pyright) prove calling conventions before runtime.
Configure them in the repo (pyproject.toml) so the project, not your machine, owns the rules. CI enforces them; editors show them; both are cheaper than review comments about style.
Pre-commit hooks (pre-commit framework) run format/lint on staged files before every commit — the fastest feedback loop you can buy, seconds instead of a CI round trip.

sections.heading: Scripts and task runners
body: Stop typing long commands: Makefile, just, npm scripts, or a tasks.py — give the common workflows names (test, lint, migrate, run). New contributors should not need to memorise incantations.

Make scripts report loudly: "✓ 412 passed" is better than silence; "✗ 2 failed: test_total, test_split" tells you where to look. Exit codes propagate — scripts that hide failures are worse than no script.
Automate the boring: changelog generation, dependency bumping (renovate/dependabot), license checks, bundle analysis. Every manual step is a future mistake.

lessons.task: Add a Makefile with targets test, lint and run to a scratch project with one passing test and one deliberate lint violation. Run make test and make lint and record the outputs. Then add a pre-commit hook that blocks commits containing trailing whitespace and test it with a deliberately dirty file.

quiz.question: What is the strongest argument for configuring lint/format in the repository rather than per developer?
choices: Faster editor startup
Every contributor and CI enforces identical rules, so style never enters review
It saves disk space
It makes the editor quieter
quiz.explanation: Repo-owned config makes the rules part of the project: humans and machines apply the same gate, ending style debates and drift.

outcomes: Create a project virtual environment with a pinned Python version and use it without relying on activation.
Rebuild the environment from a lockfile in CI and containers, and prove the result matches.
Diagnose import shadowing and version drift using sys.prefix, pip check, and explicit interpreter paths.
lessons.mental_model: A virtual environment is a project's own toolbox: same workshop, separate tools, so borrowing a wrench cannot break the other bench.
worked_example: A six-person team maintains four services in one monorepo. Service A pins pydantic 1.10 for an old FastAPI version; Service B needs pydantic 2.9. A developer upgrades pydantic globally to follow a tutorial, and within a day three services fail at import because BaseSettings moved to pydantic-settings. The team recreates each service's .venv from its own lockfile, adds .python-version files pinning 3.11, and changes CI to install with uv sync --frozen into a fresh environment. The immediate cost is two days of cleanup; the lasting change is that dependency updates now arrive as reviewed lockfile diffs with a green test run.
common_mistakes: Installing packages globally with pip install because activation happened to be active in one terminal.
Committing .venv to Git, which ships absolute paths and platform-specific binaries that fail elsewhere.
Assuming a virtual environment pins versions, when a fresh install can resolve newer releases than yesterday.

key_terms.definition: A directory holding a Python interpreter link and an isolated site-packages tree used by one project.
A shell script that puts a virtual environment's bin directory first on PATH for the current session.
A generated file recording exact dependency versions and hashes so installs are reproducible across machines.

checkpoint.question: What does activation actually change, and why is it not required to run a project?
checkpoint.answer: Activation puts the project’s .venv/bin directory first on PATH and sets VIRTUAL_ENV, so bare `python` and `pip` resolve to that interpreter. It is not required to run anything — you can always invoke .venv/bin/python directly, and tools like uv do that without activating.

checkpoint.question: How can two projects both use a venv and still drift apart in dependency versions?
checkpoint.answer: Two projects can share a .venv shape but still drift because a fresh install resolves the newest allowed versions at install time; different creation dates or unpinned ranges produce different trees. The shared cause is resolving loosely instead of installing from each project’s own lockfile.

checkpoint.question: Why is copying a .venv between machines or into an image a bad idea?
checkpoint.answer: A .venv records absolute paths in pyvenv.cfg and scripts, and contains platform- and even Python-patch-version-specific binaries and links. Copied elsewhere or into an image, it breaks in confusing ways and ships a resolved set of packages instead of the declared, reviewable one.

checkpoint.question: What does pyvenv.cfg record, and which part of it breaks on a different machine?
checkpoint.answer: pyvenv.cfg records the home Python installation the venv was created from (home path, include-system-site-packages flag, and the base prefix). The `home` path is machine-specific, so pointing another machine at it fails or silently uses the wrong base interpreter.

checkpoint.question: When would --system-site-packages be justified, and what risk does it add?
checkpoint.answer: --system-site-packages is justified when a base image provides large pre-installed scientific packages you do not want duplicated. It adds the risk that system packages leak into the project and cause version conflicts that are invisible to a fresh-lockfile install.

lessons.title: Redis
lessons.goal: Choose a Redis data structure and key naming scheme for a concrete access pattern.
lessons.takeaway: Redis is the whiteboard beside the filing cabinet: fast, shared, and wiped without warning, so anything that must survive belongs in the cabinet.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: Redis answers in under a millisecond because everything lives in memory, and that is exactly why it must be treated as expendable. Teams lose sessions, rate limits, and locks when an instance restarts without persistence, or when a missing TTL fills memory and the eviction policy deletes keys nobody expected. Using it well means knowing which command is atomic and what happens when a key is absent.
Redis is the whiteboard beside the filing cabinet: fast, shared, and wiped without warning, so anything that must survive belongs in the cabinet.

sections.heading: Keys, structures, and TTL Everything is a key mapped to a typed value: string fo
body: Keys, structures, and TTL Everything is a key mapped to a typed value: string for counters and cached blobs, hash for objects whose fields change individually, sorted set for leaderboards and time-ordered work, stream for an append-only log with consumer groups. Namespace keys as service:entity:id:version, because SCAN output is unreadable otherwise.

Set a TTL on every key that is not a lock, and prefer SET key value EX 300 NX over separate SET and EXPIRE calls. Atomicity is per command One Redis command is atomic; two commands from your client are not, because another connection can interleave between them. INCR is a safe counter and SET NX EX is a safe lock acquisition.

For multi-step logic use a Lua script or MULTI/EXEC, which runs without interruption. A read-modify-write in Python is a race: two workers both read 9 and both write 10, and your rate limit silently allows double the traffic. Test the race with concurrent clients.

Memory, eviction, and durability Redis executes commands on one thread, so an O(N) command such as KEYS * or a 100,000-member SMEMBERS blocks every other client. Set maxmemory and choose an eviction policy deliberately: allkeys-lru for a pure cache, noeviction for queues and locks where silent loss breaks correctness.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Run a replica with sentinel or managed failover, set client timeouts, and treat a connection error as a cache miss.
Separate cache and queue workloads onto different instances or logical databases, so eviction cannot delete jobs that no worker acknowledged.
Track used_memory, evicted_keys, connected_clients, and latency percentiles; a rising eviction rate predicts user-visible misses within minutes.

lessons.task: Model five Redis keys with structure, TTL, and miss behaviour, then create them with redis-cli and inspect MEMORY USAGE (40 minutes). Rewrite a two-call counter as a Lua script, then fire 200 concurrent requests and show the count never exceeds the limit (45 minutes).

quiz.question: Why is reading a counter and writing it back in Python unsafe under concurrency?
choices: Choose a Redis data structure and key naming scheme for a concrete access pattern.
Make compound operations atomic with single commands, transactions, or Lua scripts.
Set TTLs and an eviction policy so memory stays bounded and misses degrade predictably.
A per-key expiry in seconds or milliseconds after which Redis deletes the key and later reads report a miss.
quiz.explanation: Choose a Redis data structure and key naming scheme for a concrete access pattern.

outcomes: Choose a Redis data structure and key naming scheme for a concrete access pattern.
Make compound operations atomic with single commands, transactions, or Lua scripts.
Set TTLs and an eviction policy so memory stays bounded and misses degrade predictably.
lessons.mental_model: Redis is the whiteboard beside the filing cabinet: fast, shared, and wiped without warning, so anything that must survive belongs in the cabinet.
worked_example: An API gateway limits 4,000 tenants to 60 requests per minute. The first version calls INCR then EXPIRE as two commands; when a worker dies between them the key never expires and the tenant stays blocked. During an incident an engineer runs KEYS ratelimit:* and stalls all traffic for 900 ms. The team moves to one Lua script that increments and sets the window expiry only when the counter is 1, keeps a 90-second TTL, and scans with SCAN in batches of 200. Memory falls from 3.1 GB to 640 MB after tenant configs gain a 120-second TTL, and p99 latency holds at 0.4 ms.
common_mistakes: Treating Redis as the system of record for orders or profiles, then losing rows on a restart.
Running KEYS *, SMEMBERS on huge sets, or another blocking command on the main connection during traffic.
Setting a cache key without a TTL and relying on manual deletion that nobody ever performs.

key_terms.definition: A per-key expiry in seconds or milliseconds after which Redis deletes the key and later reads report a miss.
The rule Redis applies at maxmemory, such as allkeys-lru, volatile-ttl, or noeviction, which rejects writes.
A script executed atomically inside Redis, combining reads and writes that must not interleave with other clients.

checkpoint.question: What is the goal of Redis?
checkpoint.answer: Choose a Redis data structure and key naming scheme for a concrete access pattern.

checkpoint.question: Why does redis matter in practice?
checkpoint.answer: Redis is the whiteboard beside the filing cabinet: fast, shared, and wiped without warning, so anything that must survive belongs in the cabinet.

lessons.title: Caching
lessons.goal: Calculate whether a cache pays for itself using hit rate, latency, and tolerated staleness.
lessons.takeaway: A cache is a photocopy left on the counter: fast to grab, occasionally out of date, and useless if nobody agrees which copy is current.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: A cache is a copy that can be wrong, and every cache adds failure modes: stale reads, a thundering herd when a popular key expires, and a memory bill for data nobody reads twice. It earns its place only when the same read repeats, the origin is slower or costlier than the cache, and the product tolerates the staleness you choose.
A cache is a photocopy left on the counter: fast to grab, occasionally out of date, and useless if nobody agrees which copy is current.

sections.heading: Cache-aside and its arithmetic In cache-aside the application reads the cache, f
body: Cache-aside and its arithmetic In cache-aside the application reads the cache, falls back to the database on a miss, then writes the value with a TTL. Break-even depends on the hit rate: at 40 ms per query behind a 2 ms cache, 50% hits cut average latency from 40 to 21 ms. At 5% hits you added a dependency and kept almost all the load.

Measure the ratio before and after rather than assuming repetition, and check distinct key count as well as request rate. Stampedes and negative caching When a hot key expires, every concurrent request misses and queries the database together; 2,000 requests per second become 2,000 queries.

Add TTL jitter of ten to twenty percent and a short lock so one worker recomputes while others serve stale data or wait 100 ms. Cache negative results for a brief TTL, because a request for a missing id otherwise hits the database on every retry. Jitter must vary per write, not per process, or a whole fleet still expires in lockstep.

Invalidation is the hard part Delete-on-write keeps the cache closer to truth but races with an in-flight read that stores an old value after the delete. Version the key by config_version or updated_at so a stale entry becomes unreachable instead of merely wrong. Never cache a permission decision without the permission set in the key.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Treat the cache as optional: on timeout or connection failure, fall through to the origin and count a cache_error metric.
Keep TTLs in configuration and review them with the data owner; a 24-hour TTL on permissions is a security decision.
Warm critical keys after deploy and watch the first ten minutes, when hit ratio and origin load move fastest.

lessons.task: Instrument one endpoint and record hit ratio, p50, p95, and origin query count before and after caching (50 minutes). Add TTL jitter and a single-flight lock, then fire 500 concurrent requests at an expired key and count origin queries (45 minutes).

quiz.question: How do you compute whether a cache will reduce average latency at a given hit ratio?
choices: When the same missing id is looked up repeatedly. Without negative caching, every retry for a nonexistent id hits the…
Delete-on-write can race with an in-flight read: the reader misses, fetches the old value, and stores it back into the…
A stampede happens when a hot key expires and every concurrent request misses at once, so 2,000 requests per second become…
Multiply the hit rate by the cache latency and the miss rate by the origin latency, then add the two. At 50% hits with a 40…
quiz.explanation: Multiply the hit rate by the cache latency and the miss rate by the origin latency, then add the two. At 50% hits with a 40 ms origin query and a 2 ms cache read, average latency is 0.5 × 2 + 0.5 × 40 = 21 ms, down from 40 ms. At a 5% hit rate you have added a dependency while keeping almost all the origin load.

outcomes: Calculate whether a cache pays for itself using hit rate, latency, and tolerated staleness.
Implement cache-aside with TTL jitter, negative caching, and single-flight protection.
Invalidate safely on write and measure hit ratio, entry age, and origin load.
lessons.mental_model: A cache is a photocopy left on the counter: fast to grab, occasionally out of date, and useless if nobody agrees which copy is current.
worked_example: A tenant-config endpoint serves 1,800 requests per second from Postgres at 62 ms p95. The team caches 4,100 tenant documents for 300 seconds. Their first version expires every key together every five minutes, so the database sees 4,000 queries in 800 ms and connection waits spike. They add 15% TTL jitter, a 2-second single-flight lock, and a config_version in the key that is bumped on write. Hit ratio settles at 98.7%, p95 falls to 3 ms, and database CPU drops from 71% to 9%. They never cache the permissions table, which changes on every login.
common_mistakes: Caching a query before checking its hit rate, then maintaining invalidation code for data read once a day.
Caching per-user responses under a key that omits the tenant, leaking one customer's data to another.
Deleting the key inside a slow transaction, so readers repopulate it with pre-commit data.

key_terms.definition: The share of reads served from the cache, computed as hits divided by hits plus misses over a window.
A burst of concurrent misses on the same expired key, all recomputing and loading the origin at once.
Storing a short-lived record that something does not exist, so repeated lookups for missing ids skip the database.

checkpoint.question: How do you compute whether a cache will reduce average latency at a given hit ratio?
checkpoint.answer: Multiply the hit rate by the cache latency and the miss rate by the origin latency, then add the two. At 50% hits with a 40 ms origin query and a 2 ms cache read, average latency is 0.5 × 2 + 0.5 × 40 = 21 ms, down from 40 ms. At a 5% hit rate you have added a dependency while keeping almost all the origin load.

checkpoint.question: What causes a stampede, and which two controls reduce it without changing the data model?
checkpoint.answer: A stampede happens when a hot key expires and every concurrent request misses at once, so 2,000 requests per second become 2,000 queries against the database. The two controls are TTL jitter of ten to twenty percent (varied per write, not per process, so a whole fleet does not expire in lockstep) and a short single-flight lock so one worker recomputes while others wait or serve stale data.

checkpoint.question: Why is deleting a key on write not sufficient on its own to prevent stale reads?
checkpoint.answer: Delete-on-write can race with an in-flight read: the reader misses, fetches the old value, and stores it back into the cache after your delete completes. Version the key by config_version or updated_at so a stale entry becomes unreachable instead of merely wrong, and old entries age out without a delete storm.

checkpoint.question: When is caching a negative result better than caching nothing at all?
checkpoint.answer: When the same missing id is looked up repeatedly. Without negative caching, every retry for a nonexistent id hits the database; storing a short-lived record that the item does not exist lets those repeated lookups skip the origin.

checkpoint.question: What makes a per-tenant cache key safe, and what happens when the tenant id is omitted?
checkpoint.answer: The key must include the tenant id, and the user or permission scope where data is not public — never cache a permission decision without the permission set in the key. If the tenant id is omitted, one customer's cached data can be served to another tenant, leaking data across tenants.

lessons.title: Background Jobs
lessons.goal: Decide which work belongs in the request and which becomes a background job.
lessons.takeaway: A background job is a receipt, not a promise: the user gets an identifier now, and the system must later say exactly what happened to it.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: A request should fail fast and predictably. Work that takes 40 seconds, calls three flaky services, or can be retried belongs behind a job boundary, where the client gets a 202 and a status URL. Moving work without adding idempotency and visibility only relocates the failure: the table fills with duplicates and nobody knows which of 12,000 jobs actually finished.
A background job is a receipt, not a promise: the user gets an identifier now, and the system must later say exactly what happened to it.

sections.heading: Draw the request boundary Keep in the request only what the user needs immediate
body: Draw the request boundary Keep in the request only what the user needs immediately: validate input, authorise, write the intent, and return an identifier. Send anything slow, external, retryable, or fan-out to a worker. A 40-second PDF render, a 900-row import, an email, and an embedding batch all qualify.

The request should finish in tens of milliseconds even when the job takes minutes, and the response must say where to check progress, including a status field for failed work. Idempotency is the contract At-least-once delivery means every job must tolerate a second run.

Use a natural key such as (tenant_id, document_id, kind) behind a unique constraint, and store state as queued, running, succeeded, or failed. A duplicate insert then becomes a no-op instead of a second invoice.

A heartbeat or locked_at timestamp lets a supervisor reclaim work whose worker died, and a max_attempts counter stops an infinite retry loop that burns capacity all night. Retries need a policy Retry only transient failures: timeouts, 429, and 5xx. A validation error or a 404 will fail identically forever, so mark it failed with a reason immediately.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Expose job counts by state, age of the oldest queued job, and retry rate; alert when depth grows for ten minutes.
Drain workers on shutdown: stop claiming, finish the current job, and let the lease expire for the rest.
Keep job payloads small and reference stored data by id, so a schema change cannot break work already queued.

lessons.task: Convert one synchronous endpoint into a 202 plus job-status flow, including the unique idempotency key (50 minutes). Add a stale-job reaper and prove with a killed worker that the job is reclaimed and completed once (45 minutes).

quiz.question: Which properties make work a good candidate for a background job rather than inline execution?
choices: Work is a good background job if it is slow, external, retryable, or fan-out. Keep quick validation, authorization, and…
At-least-once delivery means a job may be delivered or run more than once. Without an idempotency key under a unique…
Retry only transient failures such as timeouts, 429, and 5xx. Validation errors or 404s should fail immediately with a…
A stale locked_at timestamp indicates a worker died or crashed while running the job, allowing a supervisor or reaper to…
quiz.explanation: Work is a good background job if it is slow, external, retryable, or fan-out. Keep quick validation, authorization, and writing the intent in the request.

outcomes: Decide which work belongs in the request and which becomes a background job.
Design an idempotent job with persisted status, a retry policy, and progress records.
Detect stuck, duplicated, and poisoned jobs before users report them.
lessons.mental_model: A background job is a receipt, not a promise: the user gets an identifier now, and the system must later say exactly what happened to it.
worked_example: A claims portal generates a 60-page PDF summary on demand. The original endpoint built it inline, so p95 was 52 seconds and a client retry after 30 seconds produced two documents. The team writes a jobs row with a unique key on (tenant_id, claim_id, 'summary'), returns 202 with /v1/jobs/{id}, and workers claim rows where state is queued using FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. Rendering averages 38 seconds, and a reaper resets rows running longer than 10 minutes. Attempts cap at four with 30, 120, 480, and 960-second backoff. Duplicate submissions now return the existing job, and support can see which of 940 nightly jobs failed.
common_mistakes: Running a 40-second job inside the request handler and assuming the client will wait without retrying.
Retrying every exception, including validation errors, until the table fills with jobs that can never succeed.
Sending email or issuing a refund without an idempotency key, so a redelivery charges the customer twice.

key_terms.definition: A stable identifier for a unit of work, stored under a unique constraint so a repeat delivery changes nothing.
A retry delay that grows between attempts, usually with random jitter, so a failing dependency is not hammered.
A stored failed job with its error and attempt count, kept for inspection or replay instead of being discarded.

checkpoint.question: Which properties make work a good candidate for a background job rather than inline execution?
checkpoint.answer: Work is a good background job if it is slow, external, retryable, or fan-out. Keep quick validation, authorization, and writing the intent in the request.

checkpoint.question: Why does at-least-once delivery force every job to be idempotent?
checkpoint.answer: At-least-once delivery means a job may be delivered or run more than once. Without an idempotency key under a unique constraint, a repeat can create a duplicate record or charge the customer twice.

checkpoint.question: What does a stale locked_at timestamp tell you about a worker?
checkpoint.answer: A stale locked_at timestamp indicates a worker died or crashed while running the job, allowing a supervisor or reaper to reclaim the work.

checkpoint.question: Which errors deserve a retry, and which should fail immediately with a reason?
checkpoint.answer: Retry only transient failures such as timeouts, 429, and 5xx. Validation errors or 404s should fail immediately with a reason because they will fail identically forever.

checkpoint.question: How does SKIP LOCKED change the behaviour of twenty workers polling one table?
checkpoint.answer: With a plain lock, twenty workers would wait on each other. With SKIP LOCKED, twenty workers can claim twenty different queued rows without contention.

lessons.title: Queues
lessons.goal: Compare at-most-once, at-least-once, and exactly-once claims with the behaviour they actually deliver.
lessons.takeaway: A queue is a conveyor belt with a receipt: the belt moves work, but someone must confirm each item and set aside the ones that jam.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: A queue decouples a producer from a consumer, which buys burst absorption, independent scaling, and retry. It also introduces delivery semantics you cannot ignore: a message may arrive twice, arrive late, or never arrive if the consumer acknowledges too early. Most queue incidents are configuration mistakes around acknowledgement and timeouts, not broker capacity.
A queue is a conveyor belt with a receipt: the belt moves work, but someone must confirm each item and set aside the ones that jam.

sections.heading: Delivery semantics in practice At-most-once acknowledges before processing and c
body: Delivery semantics in practice At-most-once acknowledges before processing and can lose work. At-least-once acknowledges after processing and can duplicate it, so consumers must be idempotent; this is the default for SQS, RabbitMQ, and Redis Streams.

Exactly-once is a property of a system boundary, achieved with idempotent writes and a transactional outbox, not a flag on the broker. Choose the weakest guarantee your correctness permits and compensate inside the consumer.

Ack, visibility, and prefetch A consumer receives a message with a visibility timeout; if it does not acknowledge within that window, the broker redelivers. Set the timeout above p99 processing time, or long jobs run twice while still in flight.

Prefetch caps in-flight messages per consumer: too high and one slow consumer hoards work while others idle, too low and throughput is bound by round-trip latency. Measure both before tuning, because the right value changes with message size.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Alert on consumer lag in seconds rather than queue depth, because depth looks healthy when producers also stop.
Use a transactional outbox so the database write and the publish commit together; publishing after commit can be lost.
Give dead-letter depth a paged alert with an owner, a documented replay command, and a limit on automatic redrive.

lessons.task: Write a delivery contract for two queues in your system covering duplicates, ordering, max age, and failure handling (35 minutes). Build a consumer with XREADGROUP, kill it mid-message, and demonstrate redelivery plus deduplication (50 minutes).

quiz.question: Why can a broker not simply provide exactly-once delivery across a database and a queue?
choices: The window after delivery during which a message is hidden from other consumers; expiry causes redelivery.
Design partitioning, backpressure, and ordering rules for a queue that must scale.
Compare at-most-once, at-least-once, and exactly-once claims with the behaviour they actually deliver.
Configure acknowledgement, prefetch, visibility timeout, and dead-letter routing for a consumer.
quiz.explanation: Compare at-most-once, at-least-once, and exactly-once claims with the behaviour they actually deliver.

outcomes: Compare at-most-once, at-least-once, and exactly-once claims with the behaviour they actually deliver.
Configure acknowledgement, prefetch, visibility timeout, and dead-letter routing for a consumer.
Design partitioning, backpressure, and ordering rules for a queue that must scale.
lessons.mental_model: A queue is a conveyor belt with a receipt: the belt moves work, but someone must confirm each item and set aside the ones that jam.
worked_example: A media pipeline ingests 240,000 images a day and fans them into thumbnail, moderation, and metadata queues. Thumbnail workers used a 30-second visibility timeout while p99 rendering took 48 seconds, so 6% of images were rendered twice and billed twice. The team raises the timeout to 120 seconds, adds a heartbeat that extends it during long renders, and sets prefetch to 5 per worker. One image that crashes the decoder is retried three times, then routed to a dead-letter queue with its S3 key and error. Throughput rises from 180 to 260 images per minute because workers no longer duplicate the slowest work.
common_mistakes: Acknowledging a message before the work succeeds, so a crash loses the job with no record anywhere.
Using one global ordering key for every event, which forces a single consumer and removes all parallelism.
Leaving a poison message in the queue, where it is redelivered forever and blocks everything behind it.

key_terms.definition: The window after delivery during which a message is hidden from other consumers; expiry causes redelivery.
A separate queue receiving messages that failed too often, so they can be inspected without blocking traffic.
The gap between the newest message produced and the newest one processed, measured in messages or seconds.

checkpoint.question: What is the goal of Queues?
checkpoint.answer: Compare at-most-once, at-least-once, and exactly-once claims with the behaviour they actually deliver.

checkpoint.question: Why does queues matter in practice?
checkpoint.answer: A queue is a conveyor belt with a receipt: the belt moves work, but someone must confirm each item and set aside the ones that jam.

lessons.title: Async Backend Architecture
lessons.goal: Trace concurrency through an async request path and identify every blocking call.
lessons.takeaway: The event loop is one waiter serving every table: fast when each task is a short order, disastrous when one table asks for a forty-minute tasting menu.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: Async Python buys concurrency only when every awaited call actually yields. One synchronous database driver or a CPU- heavy PDF parse inside a coroutine blocks the loop and stalls every other request on that worker. An async backend is therefore an architecture decision: which work shares an event loop, which runs in a thread or process pool, and where a request gives up.
The event loop is one waiter serving every table: fast when each task is a short order, disastrous when one table asks for a forty-minute tasting menu.

sections.heading: One loop, many coroutines A worker process runs one event loop and interleaves t
body: One loop, many coroutines A worker process runs one event loop and interleaves thousands of coroutines at await points. Concurrency is bounded by whatever each coroutine waits on: sockets, a connection pool, or a semaphore you add. CPU work and blocking libraries hold the loop and serialise everything behind them.

Run uvicorn with workers equal to cores minus headroom, and limit each worker's outbound concurrency explicitly rather than trusting demand to stay polite. Push blocking work out of the loop Use async drivers end to end: asyncpg with SQLAlchemy's async engine, redis.asyncio, httpx.AsyncClient.

A library without async support runs in a bounded thread pool through anyio.to_thread.run_sync, and genuinely CPU-bound work such as parsing or image resizing belongs in a process pool. Cap the pool so 500 requests cannot spawn 500 threads. Watch event-loop lag: sustained values above 50 ms mean something is blocking and must be found.

Deadlines, cancellation, and pools Give the whole request one deadline with asyncio.timeout and pass the remaining time to each dependency; per-call timeouts that ignore the total still exceed the user's patience. On client disconnect, cancel the task so you stop paying for work nobody receives.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Run four workers per container rather than forty, because each worker has its own loop, pool, and memory footprint.
Expose event-loop lag, pool wait time, and in-flight request count as metrics; together they explain most latency spikes.
On shutdown, stop accepting requests, wait for in-flight work with a deadline, then close pools in reverse order.

lessons.task: Instrument one endpoint with event-loop lag, pool wait time, and p99 latency, then reproduce a block with time.sleep (50 minutes). Move a blocking library into a bounded thread pool and measure throughput before and after under 100 concurrent requests (45 minutes).

quiz.question: Why does one blocking call slow down every request handled by that worker?
choices: Use a thread pool for a slow library that waits on outside resources but lacks async support; use a process pool for…
A worker has one event loop, a single scheduler. If one request blocks it, no other request on that worker can run until…
One overall deadline caps the whole request and shrinks as time is spent. Per-call timeouts that ignore the total can add…
Event-loop lag shows how late scheduled work runs, exposing blocking code on the loop. CPU use can look normal while the…
quiz.explanation: A worker has one event loop, a single scheduler. If one request blocks it, no other request on that worker can run until the blocking call finishes.

outcomes: Trace concurrency through an async request path and identify every blocking call.
Size connection pools, thread pools, and worker counts from measured limits rather than guesses.
Set deadlines and cancellation so slow dependencies cannot exhaust the service.
lessons.mental_model: The event loop is one waiter serving every table: fast when each task is a short order, disastrous when one table asks for a forty-minute tasting menu.
worked_example: A FastAPI service handles 600 requests per second across four uvicorn workers. A feature adds inline PyMuPDF parsing and p99 jumps from 180 ms to nine seconds while health checks start failing. Event-loop lag reads 2.4 seconds. The team moves parsing to a process pool of four with a queue depth of 32, switches the reporting endpoint from psycopg2 to asyncpg, and sets a 2.5-second request deadline that returns 504 with a trace id. They cut each worker's database pool from 20 to 8, so 32 connections replace the 80 that were exhausting Postgres. p99 settles at 240 ms and lag stays under 12 ms.
common_mistakes: Calling a synchronous database or HTTP library inside a coroutine and assuming the loop will handle it.
Setting generous per-call timeouts with no overall deadline, so four slow calls add up to thirty seconds.
Sizing each worker's pool independently, then exceeding max_connections when the service scales out.

key_terms.definition: A single-threaded scheduler that runs ready coroutines and switches between them at await points waiting on I/O.
The delay between a callback's due time and its execution, revealing blocking code on the loop.
A limit that makes producers slow or fail at capacity instead of queueing work without bound.

checkpoint.question: Why does one blocking call slow down every request handled by that worker?
checkpoint.answer: A worker has one event loop, a single scheduler. If one request blocks it, no other request on that worker can run until the blocking call finishes.

checkpoint.question: How do you decide between a thread pool and a process pool for a slow library?
checkpoint.answer: Use a thread pool for a slow library that waits on outside resources but lacks async support; use a process pool for genuinely CPU-heavy work like parsing or image resizing.

checkpoint.question: What does event-loop lag reveal that CPU utilisation does not?
checkpoint.answer: Event-loop lag shows how late scheduled work runs, exposing blocking code on the loop. CPU use can look normal while the loop is stalled.

checkpoint.question: How does an overall request deadline change the value of per-dependency timeouts?
checkpoint.answer: One overall deadline caps the whole request and shrinks as time is spent. Per-call timeouts that ignore the total can add up past the user's patience.

checkpoint.question: Why can scaling workers increase database connection pressure instead of reducing it?
checkpoint.answer: Each worker has its own database pool, so more workers multiply connections. Eight workers with pool size 20 request 160 connections, which most Postgres instances refuse.

outcomes: Automate tests and checks in a repeatable CI pipeline
Debug systematically with hypotheses, logs and minimal reproductions
Integrate linters, formatters and editors into one coherent workflow

modules.title: API and Backend Foundations

lessons.title: HTTP Fundamentals
lessons.goal: Read an HTTP exchange like a document: method, path, headers, status, body — and diagnose failures with curl.
lessons.takeaway: HTTP is a text protocol with intent in the method and outcome in the status code; curl makes both visible.

sections.heading: The request and the response
body: An HTTP request is one text block: METHOD PATH HTTP/1.1, headers (Host, Content-Type, Authorization), blank line, optional body. The response mirrors it: status code, headers, body. Every web interaction you have ever made is this shape.

Methods carry intent: GET reads (safe, idempotent, cacheable), POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH partially updates, DELETE removes. Status codes carry meaning at a glance: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx your fault, 5xx my fault (the server).

curl is the universal HTTP microscope: curl -i shows the response with headers; curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"a": 1}' sends a JSON POST. If you cannot curl it, you do not yet understand it.

sections.heading: Headers that matter
body: Content-Type declares what the body is (application/json, text/html); Content-Length frames it; Authorization carries credentials (Bearer tokens, Basic auth); Accept tells the server what you can consume; Cache-Control governs freshness.
Cookies are state that rides along: Set-Cookie on response, Cookie on request. They are why HTTP feels stateful when it is fundamentally stateless — and why sessions work at all.
Every hop may add headers: proxies, load balancers, CDNs. X-Request-Id style correlation headers let you trace one user request through five services.

sections.heading: Status codes you actually meet
body: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content. 301/302 redirects (GET location). 304 Not Modified (cache). 400 Bad Request (malformed), 401 Unauthenticated (who are you?), 403 Forbidden (no), 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 422 Unprocessable. 500 Internal, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Unavailable, 504 Timeout.
Idempotency: GET/PUT/DELETE are idempotent (same call N times = same effect); POST is not. This is why safe retries exist for the former and dangerous replays are avoided for the latter.
Latency lives in the network too — DNS, TLS handshake, time to first byte. A 200 in 50ms vs 5s tells different stories even with identical bodies.

lessons.task: Use curl against a public endpoint (e.g., https://api.github.com/zen or your own local server). Record: the exact command, the status code, three interesting headers, and the body. Then POST to any endpoint that echoes JSON (httpbin.org/anything) with a small payload and capture the response.

quiz.question: A client receives HTTP 401. What does it mean and what should it do?
choices: The server crashed — retry
Authentication missing or invalid — obtain or fix credentials
The resource does not exist
The request was malformed — fix the JSON
quiz.explanation: 401 means "who are you?" — authenticate with valid credentials (or sign in), then retry. 403 means "I know you and you still cannot have it"; 404 means the thing is not there.

outcomes: Break an HTTP/1.1 exchange into request line, headers, body, and status line, and explain what each part controls.
Choose status codes and methods that tell clients whether to retry, cache, or surface an error.
Diagnose a production issue using status codes, headers, and connection reuse evidence from logs and curl.
lessons.mental_model: HTTP is a typed letter, not a phone call: the envelope's method, status, and headers tell every handler how to route, retry, and cache it.
worked_example: A client retries POST /v1/summaries after a 30-second gateway timeout. The service had already stored the summary and charged the account, so the retry generates a second summary and a duplicate invoice line. Review finds no idempotency key and a 504 returned by the gateway after the backend committed. The team adds an Idempotency-Key header stored with a 24-hour unique constraint, returns the original result for a repeat key, and changes the gateway to return 202 for jobs exceeding 25 seconds. The decision: never retry non-idempotent calls without a key the server recognises.
common_mistakes: Returning 200 with an error body so clients, retries, and dashboards all treat failure as success.
Retrying POST requests on timeout without an idempotency key, then duplicating charges or records.
Sending Content-Type: application/json with a form-encoded body and blaming the framework for the 422.

key_terms.definition: The property that repeating a request produces the same state as sending it once, which makes safe retries possible.
A persistent connection reused for multiple requests, avoiding a new TCP and TLS handshake each time.
A response header that tells browsers and proxies how long a response may be stored and reused.

checkpoint.question: Why is POST not idempotent, and what does that imply for retries?
checkpoint.answer: POST creates or triggers an action, so repeating it can create duplicate records or charges. Retrying a POST safely requires an idempotency key that the server recognizes and stores with the result.

checkpoint.question: When should a service return 409 rather than 422, and why?
checkpoint.answer: Return 409 when the request conflicts with the resource's current state; return 422 when fields are semantically invalid. The codes tell the client whether to resolve a conflict or fix invalid data.

checkpoint.question: What breaks when an API returns 200 for a validation failure?
checkpoint.answer: Returning 200 with an error body treats failure as success, which breaks retries, monitoring, and intermediaries. Clients and dashboards may not notice the validation failure.

checkpoint.question: How does Cache-Control change the load a proxy places on your origin?
checkpoint.answer: Cache-Control tells browsers and proxies how long they may store and reuse a response. Caching reduces requests to your origin; a missing cache header makes every request pay full price.

checkpoint.question: Why do browsers and gateways treat 503 differently from 500?
checkpoint.answer: 503 explicitly means temporary unavailability, so clients and gateways can back off and retry. 500 is a generic server-side failure, so it does not signal that the service is temporarily unavailable.

lessons.title: API Design
lessons.goal: Design REST endpoints that are predictable to consume: resources, verbs, status codes, pagination, versioning.
lessons.takeaway: A good API is boring: resource-shaped paths, consistent verbs and status codes, and responses that never surprise the caller.

sections.heading: Resources and nouns, not verbs
body: URLs name resources: /users, /users/42, /users/42/orders. The method says what you do to them: GET /users (list), POST /users (create), GET /users/42, PATCH /users/42, DELETE /users/42. No /getUser?id= or /deleteUser endpoints.

Nest only one level deep: /users/42/orders is fine; /users/42/orders/7/items/3/notes is a design smell — flatten to /order-items/3 or /orders/7/notes. Deep nesting encodes navigational structure, not meaning.
Collections return arrays; single items return objects. A collection of one is still an array — clients that special-case it write bugs.

sections.heading: Predictable responses
body: Errors are part of the contract: a consistent error body {"error": {"code": "VALIDATION_FAILED", "message": "...", "details": [...]}} lets clients handle failures programmatically. Empty 500s with no body are hostile.
List endpoints paginate: limit/offset or cursors, always with a stable sort. Unbounded lists become 30-second responses — and keep users (and your database) honest.
Validation failures are 422 with the offending fields listed — not "invalid input". Partial success (207) exists for batches but use it only when partial really is the intent.

sections.heading: Versioning and change management
body: Never break existing clients mid-flight. Version in the path (/v1/, /v2/) so old and new can coexist; deprecate loudly with sunset headers and changelogs; remove nothing without notice.
Additive changes are free; subtractive changes are expensive. Add new fields; never remove or retype old ones — there are clients you cannot see.
Rate limiting is part of availability: 429 with Retry-After tells well-behaved clients exactly what to do. Unbounded public APIs exhaust themselves.

lessons.task: Design the JSON API for a minimal "team task tracker": list/create tasks, comment on a task, assign a task. Write the routes, example request/response bodies (including one error case and one paginated list), and name the status code for each. No code — the design is the deliverable.

quiz.question: Which endpoint pair best follows REST conventions?
choices: GET /getUsers and POST /createUser
GET /users and POST /users
POST /users/list and GET /users/add
GET /users/fetchAll and POST /users/save
quiz.explanation: URLs name resources; the HTTP method names the action. /users + GET lists, /users + POST creates — nothing else should be in the URL.

outcomes: Produce a consistent naming, filtering, pagination, and error convention that every endpoint follows.
Choose offset or cursor pagination based on data size, mutation rate, and client needs.
Write a versioning and deprecation policy with concrete signals and removal dates.
lessons.mental_model: An API is a contract with every client you will never meet; design for the support ticket six months after the author has left.
worked_example: A B2B reporting API lists model runs with offset and limit parameters. At 40,000 runs, page 400 takes 3.2 seconds because Postgres must scan 8,000 rows. The team replaces it with a cursor over (created_at, id), indexes that pair, and returns next_cursor plus has_more. They cap limit at 100, default to 25, and reject offsets above 1,000 with a 400 that links to migration docs. Old clients keep working for 90 days: responses carry a Deprecation header and the team emails the top five integrators. After migration, p95 list latency falls from 3.2 seconds to 90 milliseconds and duplicate-row tickets stop.
common_mistakes: Returning arrays at the top level, leaving no place for pagination metadata without a breaking change.
Using offset pagination on a fast-changing table and shipping duplicate rows to the client.
Renaming a field inside v1 because the mobile app can be updated in the same sprint.

key_terms.definition: Pagination that returns a token encoding the last seen sort position, giving stable pages while data changes.
The RFC 9457 JSON error format with type, title, status, detail, and instance fields that clients can parse consistently.
A response header announcing when an endpoint or version will be withdrawn, used with deprecation notices.

checkpoint.question: Why does cursor pagination avoid the duplicate rows that offset pagination produces?
