checkpoint.question: What makes object-level checks different from a role check on the route?
checkpoint.answer: A role check on the route only asks what kind of user is calling. An object-level check compares ownership or tenant on the specific loaded row, so one user cannot reach another user's item. This prevents BOLA, which is first on the OWASP API list.

checkpoint.question: Why is scoping the SQL query stronger than filtering results after the fetch?
checkpoint.answer: If the query itself includes the tenant restriction, an unscoped read cannot run at all. Filtering results after the fetch still loads the row first, so a forgotten filter leaks it.

checkpoint.question: When would attribute-based rules be necessary instead of a simple role check?
checkpoint.answer: When roles are too coarse to express the rule, like an approver allowed to release invoices only below GBP 10,000 in their own region. Attributes describe those finer conditions.

checkpoint.question: What does returning 404 for a foreign object protect against?
checkpoint.answer: It prevents identifier enumeration. A 404 means missing and foreign rows look identical, so the API never confirms an ID exists in another tenant.

outcomes: Read and diagnose HTTP requests and responses with curl
Design predictable REST endpoints with sensible status codes
Explain the responsibilities of a backend and its data store

modules.title: Data and Computational Thinking
modules.description: Algorithms, data structures, and computational thinking

lessons.title: Algorithmic Thinking
lessons.goal: Decompose a problem into a correct, verifiable algorithm before writing code: specification, invariant, walkthrough, then implementation.
lessons.takeaway: An algorithm is a precise recipe; state its inputs, outputs and invariants before you write a single line of code.

sections.heading: Start from the specification, not the keyboard
body: Every good algorithm starts as a precise statement: given X (inputs), produce Y (outputs), satisfying Z (constraints). "Find duplicates" is vague; "given a list of ≤10⁶ ids, return all values appearing ≥2 times, order-preserving" is buildable.
Identify the decision procedure: for each output element, what rule decides it? If you can say the rule in one sentence, you are ready to implement. If not, you are still defining the problem.
Work a tiny example by hand first — three to five cases — and write down each step. The hand-solved example becomes your first unit test and your spec.

sections.heading: Invariants and walkthroughs
body: An invariant is a statement true before, during and after the algorithm: "every value before index i is already known to be smaller than everything after". Correctness is mostly preserving the invariant.

Walk through your example in slow motion: track the state after each step. If the state matches your intuition at step k, the invariant holds; if it breaks, your algorithm is wrong — not your intuition.

Greedy solutions (take the locally best choice) work only when local optima compose into global ones — e.g., scheduling by earliest finish. When in doubt, prove a tiny counterexample or choose the exact approach.

sections.heading: From algorithm to code
body: Translate mechanically: inputs → arguments, spec → assert/comment, invariant → comment at the loop head. The code should look like your walkthrough, not a clever re-derivation.
Pick boring data structures first: list and dict cover 90% of problems. Fancy structures exist for the remaining 10% and carry their own complexity.
Decompose into named pieces: half the time "the algorithm" is three functions: normalize, decide, emit. Each becomes independently testable.

lessons.task: Design (on paper) an algorithm that, given a stream of support tickets with timestamps, returns the longest silence gap and its start/end. Write the spec, the invariant, a hand-worked example (or two), then implement it in Python with tests for empty, one-ticket, and out-of-order input.

quiz.question: What does an "invariant" buy you?
choices: Faster code
A property you can lean on at every step to reason about correctness
Better error messages
Shorter functions
quiz.explanation: The invariant is the backbone of the correctness argument: it is what you assume going in and what you guarantee going out, at every iteration.

outcomes: Explain the difference between the mean and the median and when each misleads.
Read a percentile such as p95 and say in one sentence what it means.
Estimate the daily cost of an API from tokens, request volume, and price.
Recognise why slow tails, not averages, drive user complaints.
lessons.mental_model: Think of a shop checkout queue. The average wait hides the truth: one stalled lane can make ninety shoppers wait while ten breeze through. The p95 is 'the wait nine out of ten shoppers beat'; the median is the middle person in line. Averages flatter you, percentiles tell you when to fix things.
worked_example: Dami logs ten request latencies in milliseconds: 120, 95, 300, 110, 105, 500, 118, 112, 108, 115. Her dashboard says 'average 168 ms' and the product seems fine. She sorts them, finds a median near 113 ms, and a p95 of about 380 ms, and realises nine requests are quick while two stall. She sets an alert on p95 instead of the mean, so the next stall pages her before users notice. The decision: report the tail, not the average.
common_mistakes: Reporting only the average and concluding the service is healthy while the p99 doubles.
Confusing throughput (requests per second) with latency (time per request); one is a rate, the other a duration.
Forgetting to divide tokens by one million when the price is quoted per million, so the bill looks 1,000 times smaller.

key_terms.definition: Add every value, divide by the count; sensitive to outliers.
The middle value once sorted; ignores extreme outliers.
The value a given share of results fall under, e.g. p95 = 95% are at or below it.
The 99th percentile; the slowest 1% of requests are above it. Watch it for tail latency.
How many requests you finish per second; a count, not a speed.
Price for one thing (e.g. USD per million tokens) so totals scale cleanly.

checkpoint.question: Why can two services with the same mean latency feel very different to users?
checkpoint.answer: Because the mean hides the tail: one service has every request around the average, the other has many quick ones and a few very slow ones that users actually notice.

checkpoint.question: What does a p99 of 1200 ms tell you that a p50 of 200 ms does not?
checkpoint.answer: p99 = 1200 ms means the slowest 1% of requests take about 1.2 seconds or more, revealing a tail that the p50 of 200 ms never shows.

checkpoint.question: If a price is quoted per million tokens, what mistake makes your cost estimate 1000 times too small?
checkpoint.answer: Multiplying by the per-million price but forgetting to divide the token count by one million makes the estimate a thousand times too big (reading it the wrong way round makes it a thousand times too small).

checkpoint.question: When would you deliberately report the median instead of the mean?
checkpoint.answer: When a few extreme outliers would distort the mean, the median gives the more honest "typical" value.

lessons.title: Data Structures
lessons.goal: Know the workhorse structures beyond list and dict — stacks, queues, linked lists, trees, and graphs — and when to reach for each.
lessons.takeaway: The right structure makes the common operation cheap; the wrong one hides cost in every loop.

sections.heading: Stacks and queues: order disciplines
body: A stack is last-in-first-out: push/pop from one end. Uses: undo history, expression parsing, DFS, call stacks themselves, matching brackets. In Python, a list with append/pop(-1) is a stack.

A queue is first-in-first-out: push one end, pop the other. Uses: BFS, task scheduling, producer-consumer buffering. collections.deque is the O(1) implementation; list.pop(0) is O(n) and will hurt at scale.
Deques (double-ended) let you push/pop at both ends — the right tool for sliding-window problems and palindrome checks.

sections.heading: Trees and hash tables under the hood
body: A tree is a connected, acyclic, parent-child structure: filesystems, the DOM, org charts, the parse tree of this sentence. Traversals: depth-first (pre/in/post) and breadth-first. Binary search trees give log(n) search/insert — when balanced (self-balancing variants).
A hash table maps keys to values in expected O(1) by hashing keys into buckets and handling collisions (chaining or open addressing). Everything in your dict and set internals is this.
Load factor (items/buckets) controls collision rate; resize doubles buckets to keep amortized O(1). Understanding this demystifies why dict is fast and why iteration order survived 3.7+.

sections.heading: Graphs: relationships everywhere
body: A graph is nodes and edges — everything is a graph: dependencies (lessons), social networks, road routes, package imports. Represent with adjacency list (dict of lists) for sparse graphs; adjacency matrix only when dense.
BFS (queue) finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs and spreads level-by-level; DFS (stack/recursion) explores depth first: cycle detection, topological sort, connected components.
Cycles matter: software builds must be acyclic in dependencies; a cycle means impossible task order. Topological sort exists precisely for this.

lessons.task: Implement a small "dependency resolver" print order: given a dict of lesson -> list of prerequisite lessons, output a valid order (Kahn's algorithm or DFS). Handle a cycle of your choosing and print a clear error naming the lessons in the cycle. Provide three example graphs: valid chain, diamond, cycle.

quiz.question: Which structure finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph fastest and simplest?
choices: DFS
BFS
Binary search
Union-find
quiz.explanation: BFS expands level by level, so the first time it reaches a node determines its shortest distance in edges — the correct tool for unweighted shortest paths.

outcomes: Decide whether a problem needs a class or a set of functions, using state, invariants, and call-site clarity as the test.
Write a client class with a constructor, private helpers, a factory, and a useful __repr__.
Replace inheritance with composition so transport, retries, and parsing can be tested and swapped independently.
lessons.mental_model: A class is a small machine with dials set at construction: the dials must stay in valid positions, and the machine should expose buttons, not its wiring.
worked_example: A client class grows to 780 lines covering chat, embeddings, uploads, retries, and CSV export. Every new endpoint copies the same header logic, and mocking a call requires patching three module globals. In a design review, the team keeps ModelClient for configuration and one request() method, moves endpoint-specific payloads into functions, and injects a transport callable. Retries become a wrapper around transport; tests use a fake that returns a 429 once, then a valid body. The class drops to 90 lines, and coverage of the retry path goes from zero to four tests. The decision: a class owns state and one job; everything else is a function or a collaborator.
common_mistakes: Subclassing the client for each provider, then duplicating header and error logic across five fragile children.
Doing network calls in __init__, so constructing the object fails in tests and at service startup.
Making every attribute public and mutable, so any caller can change the base URL mid-request.

key_terms.definition: A condition that must remain true for an object to be valid, such as a base URL with no trailing slash.
Building behaviour by holding a collaborator and delegating to it, instead of inheriting its methods through a class hierarchy.
An alternative constructor declared with @classmethod that builds an instance from configuration, a file, or another object.

checkpoint.question: What test tells you that a group of functions should become a class?
checkpoint.answer: A group of functions should become a class when they share state that must remain valid together and that state requires an invariant to be protected.

checkpoint.question: Why is a network call inside __init__ a problem for tests and for startup?
checkpoint.answer: Network calls in __init__ cause problems because tests cannot construct the object without hitting the real network, and service startup fails if the network is down. Keep __init__ cheap: just store the settings, don't do work.

checkpoint.question: How does injecting a transport change the way you test a 429 retry?
checkpoint.answer: Injecting a transport allows you to pass a fake version that returns a 429 error first, then a success response, enabling you to test retry logic without touching the real network.

checkpoint.question: When is inheritance a better choice than composition, and what must remain true?
checkpoint.answer: Inheritance is better than composition only when the child class is usable anywhere the parent is and adds no surprising behavior—genuine substitution. Otherwise, pass collaborators in as parameters.

checkpoint.question: What belongs in __repr__, and what must never appear there?
checkpoint.answer: __repr__ should show identifying information like the host and request count so logs are readable. Never include headers, tokens, keys, or personal data that could leak secrets.

lessons.title: Complexity Analysis
lessons.goal: Reason about how an algorithm scales: O-notation, best/average/worst cases, time vs space trade-offs, and what actually matters at your data sizes.
lessons.takeaway: Big-O describes how work grows, not how fast a machine is; use it to compare approaches before optimising details.

sections.heading: Big-O in plain terms
body: Big-O is an upper bound on growth, not a stopwatch: O(n) means the work grows at most linearly with input size n. Constant factors fall away: O(2n) is O(n); O(n + log n) is O(n).
The ladder: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ) < O(n!). At n = 10⁶, O(n) is fine, O(n log n) is fine, O(n²) is 10¹² steps — hours; O(2ⁿ) is heat death of the universe.
Notation drops constants and lower-order terms deliberately so you compare shapes, not nanoseconds. Hardware is constant; scale is the variable.

sections.heading: Time vs space, best/average/worst
body: Big-O hides two stories: time and space. Memoization buys speed with memory (naive recursion → DP). Choose deliberately: linear space for log-time beats quadratic time for constant space when memory is free.

Average vs worst: hash tables are expected O(1) but O(n) at pathological collision chains; quicksort averages O(n log n) but degrades to O(n²) — which is why implementations shuffle or switch to heapsort.
Amortized: a list append is O(1) on average across resizes even though individual resizes are O(n); an expensive operation every k-th call can still be O(1) amortized.

sections.heading: What matters in practice
body: Profile before optimizing: 80% of time is usually in 20% of code. Big-O guides where to look; benchmarks tell you what to fix.
Constant factors and IO dominate real systems: a hash lookup vs. an SQL row fetch is nanoseconds vs. milliseconds — algorithmic purity loses to cache locality and round trips.
Choose the right tool: the gap between O(n²) piped code and O(n log n) algorithm is irrelevant at n = 100 but decisive at n = 10⁸. Know your n.

lessons.task: Given a list of 100,000 order dicts with customer ids, compute (a) customers with more than one order and (b) the id with the highest total spend. First do it the naive way and time it; then do it with a dict and time it again. Report both timings and the theoretical comparison.

quiz.question: A nested loop over the same list is typically:
choices: O(n)
O(log n)
O(n²)
quiz.explanation: Two independent traversals of an input of size n multiply: n × n = O(n²) work in the worst case.

outcomes: Calculate whether a cache pays for itself using hit rate, latency, and tolerated staleness.
Implement cache-aside with TTL jitter, negative caching, and single-flight protection.
Invalidate safely on write and measure hit ratio, entry age, and origin load.
lessons.mental_model: A cache is a photocopy left on the counter: fast to grab, occasionally out of date, and useless if nobody agrees which copy is current.
worked_example: A tenant-config endpoint serves 1,800 requests per second from Postgres at 62 ms p95. The team caches 4,100 tenant documents for 300 seconds. Their first version expires every key together every five minutes, so the database sees 4,000 queries in 800 ms and connection waits spike. They add 15% TTL jitter, a 2-second single-flight lock, and a config_version in the key that is bumped on write. Hit ratio settles at 98.7%, p95 falls to 3 ms, and database CPU drops from 71% to 9%. They never cache the permissions table, which changes on every login.
common_mistakes: Caching a query before checking its hit rate, then maintaining invalidation code for data read once a day.
Caching per-user responses under a key that omits the tenant, leaking one customer's data to another.
Deleting the key inside a slow transaction, so readers repopulate it with pre-commit data.

key_terms.definition: The share of reads served from the cache, computed as hits divided by hits plus misses over a window.
A burst of concurrent misses on the same expired key, all recomputing and loading the origin at once.
Storing a short-lived record that something does not exist, so repeated lookups for missing ids skip the database.

checkpoint.question: How do you compute whether a cache will reduce average latency at a given hit ratio?
checkpoint.answer: Multiply the hit rate by the cache latency and the miss rate by the origin latency, then add the two. At 50% hits with a 40 ms origin query and a 2 ms cache read, average latency is 0.5 × 2 + 0.5 × 40 = 21 ms, down from 40 ms. At a 5% hit rate you have added a dependency while keeping almost all the origin load.

checkpoint.question: What causes a stampede, and which two controls reduce it without changing the data model?
checkpoint.answer: A stampede happens when a hot key expires and every concurrent request misses at once, so 2,000 requests per second become 2,000 queries against the database. The two controls are TTL jitter of ten to twenty percent (varied per write, not per process, so a whole fleet does not expire in lockstep) and a short single-flight lock so one worker recomputes while others wait or serve stale data.

checkpoint.question: Why is deleting a key on write not sufficient on its own to prevent stale reads?
checkpoint.answer: Delete-on-write can race with an in-flight read: the reader misses, fetches the old value, and stores it back into the cache after your delete completes. Version the key by config_version or updated_at so a stale entry becomes unreachable instead of merely wrong, and old entries age out without a delete storm.

checkpoint.question: When is caching a negative result better than caching nothing at all?
checkpoint.answer: When the same missing id is looked up repeatedly. Without negative caching, every retry for a nonexistent id hits the database; storing a short-lived record that the item does not exist lets those repeated lookups skip the origin.

checkpoint.question: What makes a per-tenant cache key safe, and what happens when the tenant id is omitted?
checkpoint.answer: The key must include the tenant id, and the user or permission scope where data is not public — never cache a permission decision without the permission set in the key. If the tenant id is omitted, one customer's cached data can be served to another tenant, leaking data across tenants.

lessons.title: Reading numbers: averages, percentiles, and cost
lessons.goal: Explain the difference between the mean and the median and when each misleads.
lessons.takeaway: Think of a shop checkout queue. The average wait hides the truth: one stalled lane can make ninety shoppers wait while ten breeze through. The p95 is 'the wait nine out of ten shoppers beat'; the median is the middle person in line. Averages flatter you, percentiles tell you when to fix things.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: Later lessons ask you to 'watch the p99', 'budget tokens', and 'report percentiles' as if these are obvious. They are not obvious yet, and no earlier lesson teaches them. This primer fills that gap in one sitting so the performance and cost language from Module 2 onward reads clearly instead of guessing.

Think of a shop checkout queue. The average wait hides the truth: one stalled lane can make ninety shoppers wait while ten breeze through. The p95 is 'the wait nine out of ten shoppers beat'; the median is the middle person in line. Averages flatter you, percentiles tell you when to fix things.

sections.heading: Mean, median, and why both matter
body: An average is not one number. The mean adds everything and divides by the count, so one huge outlier pulls it up. The median is the middle value once you sort, so it ignores the outliers and tells you what a typical request feels like.
When the mean is much larger than the median, a few bad events are doing most of the damage.

sections.heading: Percentiles and the slow tail
body: Sort your numbers, then ask what value a given share of them falls under. The 50th percentile (p50) is the median: half of requests are faster. The 95th percentile (p95) is the value 95% of requests beat, and p99 is the same idea for 99%.
Users rarely complain about the average; they feel the percentiles at the top, the slow tail, so engineers report p95 and p99 rather than a single average.

sections.heading: Turning usage into cost
body: Models are billed by tokens, and tokens are counted per request, so cost is simple arithmetic you can always sanity-check: tokens per request times requests per day, divided by one million, times the price per million. Add retries and fans-out on top.
If you cannot sketch the monthly bill on the back of an envelope, you cannot spot the request pattern that triples it.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Alert on percentiles you can defend, usually p95 or p99, not the mean, because a single request cannot wreck a percentile the way it wrecks an average.
Keep the unit-cost formula in one place so a price change is a single edit, not a hunt through notebooks.

lessons.task: Add a p99 line to the example and run it on your own ten-number list; write the two sentences explaining mean versus p99 (15 minutes). Estimate the monthly cost of your capstone's model calls from tokens per request, expected requests per day, and a per-million price (15 minutes).

quiz.question: Why can two services with the same mean latency feel very different to users?
choices: When a few extreme outliers would distort the mean, the median gives the more honest "typical" value.
p99 = 1200 ms means the slowest 1% of requests take about 1.2 seconds or more, revealing a tail that the p50 of 200 ms…
Multiplying by the per-million price but forgetting to divide the token count by one million makes the estimate a thousand…
Because the mean hides the tail: one service has every request around the average, the other has many quick ones and a few…
quiz.explanation: Because the mean hides the tail: one service has every request around the average, the other has many quick ones and a few very slow ones that users actually notice.

outcomes: Explain the difference between the mean and the median and when each misleads.
Read a percentile such as p95 and say in one sentence what it means.
Estimate the daily cost of an API from tokens, request volume, and price.
Recognise why slow tails, not averages, drive user complaints.
lessons.mental_model: Think of a shop checkout queue. The average wait hides the truth: one stalled lane can make ninety shoppers wait while ten breeze through. The p95 is 'the wait nine out of ten shoppers beat'; the median is the middle person in line. Averages flatter you, percentiles tell you when to fix things.
worked_example: Dami logs ten request latencies in milliseconds: 120, 95, 300, 110, 105, 500, 118, 112, 108, 115. Her dashboard says 'average 168 ms' and the product seems fine. She sorts them, finds a median near 113 ms, and a p95 of about 380 ms, and realises nine requests are quick while two stall. She sets an alert on p95 instead of the mean, so the next stall pages her before users notice. The decision: report the tail, not the average.
common_mistakes: Reporting only the average and concluding the service is healthy while the p99 doubles.
Confusing throughput (requests per second) with latency (time per request); one is a rate, the other a duration.
Forgetting to divide tokens by one million when the price is quoted per million, so the bill looks 1,000 times smaller.

key_terms.definition: Add every value, divide by the count; sensitive to outliers.
The middle value once sorted; ignores extreme outliers.
The value a given share of results fall under, e.g. p95 = 95% are at or below it.
The 99th percentile; the slowest 1% of requests are above it. Watch it for tail latency.
How many requests you finish per second; a count, not a speed.
Price for one thing (e.g. USD per million tokens) so totals scale cleanly.

checkpoint.question: Why can two services with the same mean latency feel very different to users?
checkpoint.answer: Because the mean hides the tail: one service has every request around the average, the other has many quick ones and a few very slow ones that users actually notice.

checkpoint.question: What does a p99 of 1200 ms tell you that a p50 of 200 ms does not?
checkpoint.answer: p99 = 1200 ms means the slowest 1% of requests take about 1.2 seconds or more, revealing a tail that the p50 of 200 ms never shows.

checkpoint.question: If a price is quoted per million tokens, what mistake makes your cost estimate 1000 times too small?
checkpoint.answer: Multiplying by the per-million price but forgetting to divide the token count by one million makes the estimate a thousand times too big (reading it the wrong way round makes it a thousand times too small).

checkpoint.question: When would you deliberately report the median instead of the mean?
checkpoint.answer: When a few extreme outliers would distort the mean, the median gives the more honest "typical" value.

lessons.title: PostgreSQL
lessons.goal: Explain MVCC snapshots, the default read-committed isolation, and when a serialisable retry is required.
lessons.takeaway: PostgreSQL is a busy library: snapshots are the reading rooms, backends are the staff, and autovacuum is the cleaner who must not be locked out.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: PostgreSQL will happily accept a schema and then fail under concurrency in ways SQLite never showed you. Connection exhaustion, long transactions holding vacuum back, and a sequential scan on a 40-million-row table all look like the API is slow. Knowing the server's model, snapshots, backends, WAL, and autovacuum, turns those incidents into measurements instead of guesses.
PostgreSQL is a busy library: snapshots are the reading rooms, backends are the staff, and autovacuum is the cleaner who must not be locked out.

sections.heading: MVCC: readers do not block writers Every statement sees a snapshot of committed
body: MVCC: readers do not block writers Every statement sees a snapshot of committed rows, so a long SELECT never blocks an INSERT. The cost is dead tuples: an update writes a new row version and marks the old one for vacuum.

A transaction left open, even idle, holds the oldest snapshot and prevents cleanup of everything newer, which is how a forgotten BEGIN becomes table bloat. Monitor pg_stat_activity for idle in transaction and set a timeout.

Connections are processes, not threads Each backend is an operating-system process with several megabytes of memory, so max_connections = 500 is a memory and context-switch decision, not a free knob. A pool of ten connections per API replica multiplied by forty replicas is four hundred backends before traffic arrives.

Size the pool from concurrent query slots, not request rate; put PgBouncer in transaction mode in front as replicas grow, and set statement_timeout so one bad query cannot hold a slot forever. The planner needs statistics PostgreSQL chooses between sequential and index scans using row estimates from pg_statistic, refreshed by autovacuum's analyse phase.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Cap the connection budget per service in configuration and alert when total backends on every primary exceed 70% of max_connections.
Monitor replication lag, disk usage, and the age of the oldest snapshot; each predicts a different class of outage.
Test restore from a base backup on a schedule into a scratch environment, because a backup that has never been restored is only a hypothesis.

lessons.task: Calculate the connection budget for a hypothetical 30-replica service and write the pool settings you would ship. Create a 1-million-row table, run a filtered query, and compare the plan before and after ANALYZE.

quiz.question: Why does an idle transaction prevent autovacuum from reclaiming newer rows?
choices: Read EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) and identify a missing index, stale statistics, or table bloat.
Multi-version concurrency control; each transaction reads a consistent snapshot while writers create new row versions.
Size a connection pool against max_connections and put PgBouncer in front of a growing fleet.
Explain MVCC snapshots, the default read-committed isolation, and when a serialisable retry is required.
quiz.explanation: Explain MVCC snapshots, the default read-committed isolation, and when a serialisable retry is required.

outcomes: Explain MVCC snapshots, the default read-committed isolation, and when a serialisable retry is required.
Size a connection pool against max_connections and put PgBouncer in front of a growing fleet.
Read EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) and identify a missing index, stale statistics, or table bloat.
lessons.mental_model: PostgreSQL is a busy library: snapshots are the reading rooms, backends are the staff, and autovacuum is the cleaner who must not be locked out.
worked_example: An API on 400 Fargate tasks, each with a ten-connection pool, starts returning FATAL: too many clients already at 09:10 on a Monday. The database allows 500 connections. Latency had already risen because analytics queries hold snapshots for minutes, blocking autovacuum. The team adds PgBouncer in transaction mode with 40 server connections, caps each service at a quarter of that, sets statement_timeout to 3s and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout to 10s, and moves reporting to a read replica. The decision to pool at the server rather than shrink every client pool keeps request code unchanged while making the ceiling explicit.
common_mistakes: Raising max_connections to 2,000 instead of pooling, which multiplies memory and context switching under load.
Leaving transactions open while calling a model API, so vacuum cannot reclaim rows for the duration.
Adding an index for every slow query without checking whether statistics are simply stale.

key_terms.definition: Multi-version concurrency control; each transaction reads a consistent snapshot while writers create new row versions.
The background process that removes dead row versions and refreshes planner statistics after enough changes.
A lightweight connection pooler that multiplexes many client connections onto a small number of PostgreSQL backends.

checkpoint.question: What is the goal of PostgreSQL?
checkpoint.answer: Explain MVCC snapshots, the default read-committed isolation, and when a serialisable retry is required.

checkpoint.question: Why does postgresql matter in practice?
checkpoint.answer: PostgreSQL is a busy library: snapshots are the reading rooms, backends are the staff, and autovacuum is the cleaner who must not be locked out.

lessons.title: SQL
lessons.goal: Replace per-row application loops with joins, aggregates, and window functions that return one result set.
lessons.takeaway: SQL is a specification, not a recipe: describe the set you want, then let the planner choose how to walk it.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: Most slow endpoints are not slow because PostgreSQL is slow; they are slow because the application asks it 200 times. SQL rewards thinking in sets: one query can join, group, rank, and filter what a loop does in 200 round trips. The same language also has sharp edges, including NULL comparisons, implicit casts, and read-modify-write races, that produce wrong answers silently rather than errors.
SQL is a specification, not a recipe: describe the set you want, then let the planner choose how to walk it.

sections.heading: Think in sets A query describes the result you want, not the steps to build it
body: Think in sets A query describes the result you want, not the steps to build it. Instead of fetching fifty invoices and then querying each customer, join the tables and return fifty rows in one round trip. Aggregates collapse rows; window functions add a ranking or running total without collapsing them.

The test is simple: count the queries your endpoint issues. If that count depends on the number of rows returned, you have an N+1 problem. NULL is unknown, not empty NULL = NULL evaluates to unknown, so WHERE deleted_at = NULL returns nothing; use IS NULL.

An inner join drops rows with no match, while LEFT JOIN keeps them and fills columns with NULL, which is why COUNT(*) counts preserved rows and COUNT(c.id) does not. COALESCE supplies a fallback, but putting a nullable column inside NOT IN can silently empty the result because unknown propagates.

Writes need a concurrency story Read-modify-write in application code loses updates when two requests overlap: both read 10, both write 9. Prefer a single statement such as UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = %s AND qty >= 1 RETURNING qty, and treat zero returned rows as a conflict. ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE makes ingestion idempotent.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Set a statement timeout on the API role so a pathological query cannot occupy a connection for minutes.
Log query counts per request and alert when an endpoint's count grows after a deploy; N+1 regressions are otherwise invisible.
Keep analytical queries on a read replica, and design indexes from actual plans rather than from column names.

lessons.task: Take a loop-based data fetch in your code and rewrite it as one join, recording query count and latency before and after. Write an upsert for an event table and prove that running it twice leaves exactly one row.

quiz.question: How can you tell from query logs that an endpoint has an N+1 problem?
choices: Replace per-row application loops with joins, aggregates, and window functions that return one result set.
Write concurrent-safe updates with transactions, ON CONFLICT, and RETURNING, using bound parameters.
Predict how inner and outer joins treat NULLs and use COUNT(*) and COALESCE correctly.
A pattern where one query fetches a list and one additional query runs per row, multiplying round trips with result size.
quiz.explanation: Replace per-row application loops with joins, aggregates, and window functions that return one result set.

outcomes: Replace per-row application loops with joins, aggregates, and window functions that return one result set.
Predict how inner and outer joins treat NULLs and use COUNT(*) and COALESCE correctly.
Write concurrent-safe updates with transactions, ON CONFLICT, and RETURNING, using bound parameters.
lessons.mental_model: SQL is a specification, not a recipe: describe the set you want, then let the planner choose how to walk it.
worked_example: A finance dashboard takes 6.8 seconds and issues 1,204 queries: one for the invoice list and one per invoice for its payments. The rewrite uses a single LEFT JOIN with COALESCE(SUM(p.amount_cents), 0) grouped by invoice, plus a LATERAL subquery for the latest payment, and drops the endpoint to 38 ms. A second bug appears in review: the old query used WHERE p.status != 'void', which silently excluded invoices with no payments because the comparison was unknown. The fix moves the predicate into the join condition. The team adds a query-count assertion to the endpoint test so a future ORM shortcut cannot reintroduce the loop.
common_mistakes: Looping in Python to fetch related rows, turning a 40 ms query into 1,200 network round trips.
Writing WHERE column = NULL or NOT IN with a nullable subquery and accepting an empty result as correct.
Building SQL with f-strings and user input, which is both an injection risk and a plan-cache problem.

key_terms.definition: A pattern where one query fetches a list and one additional query runs per row, multiplying round trips with result size.
A function that computes across related rows while keeping each row, such as ROW_NUMBER() partitioned by tenant.
An insert that updates the existing row when a specified conflict target is violated, expressed with ON CONFLICT.

checkpoint.question: What is the goal of SQL?
checkpoint.answer: Replace per-row application loops with joins, aggregates, and window functions that return one result set.

checkpoint.question: Why does sql matter in practice?
checkpoint.answer: SQL is a specification, not a recipe: describe the set you want, then let the planner choose how to walk it.

lessons.title: Database Design
lessons.goal: Translate a domain description into entities, relationships, and keys normalised to third normal form.
lessons.takeaway: A schema is a contract with every future writer: the database should make the wrong shape impossible, not rely on everyone remembering the rules.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: A schema outlives the code that first wrote it. Renaming a column is easy; removing a duplicated fact that three services update is not. Design decisions encode trust: if the database does not enforce tenant ownership and positive quantities, every service must, and one will forget. An hour on keys, constraints, and delete rules prevents months of reconciliation and corrupted reports.
A schema is a contract with every future writer: the database should make the wrong shape impossible, not rely on everyone remembering the rules.

sections.heading: Model the invariant, not the screen Start from the nouns the domain reasons abou
body: Model the invariant, not the screen Start from the nouns the domain reasons about and the rules that always hold: an invoice belongs to one tenant, a line item to one invoice, a payment never exceeds the balance. Draw cardinality before naming columns. Third normal form removes duplicated facts so an address change happens once.

Denormalise only with a measured read cost and a plan for keeping the copy correct, such as a trigger or outbox job. Constraints are cheapest validation NOT NULL, UNIQUE, FOREIGN KEY, and CHECK run inside the database, cover every writer including scripts and migrations, and cannot be forgotten by a new service.

Pydantic protects one API; constraints protect the data. Choose delete behaviour explicitly: ON DELETE CASCADE for owned children, RESTRICT for referenced records such as a product on an open order, and SET NULL only when the reference is optional.

Types, time, and delete policy Use timestamptz for instants and run sessions in UTC; a naive timestamp is a bug waiting for a daylight-saving boundary. Store money as integer minor units or numeric, never double precision. Prefer text with a CHECK for small closed sets and a lookup table when labels, ordering, or translations matter.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Add the constraint as NOT VALID during the migration, then run VALIDATE CONSTRAINT separately on the table to avoid a long lock.
Document the delete policy for every foreign key; an accidental cascade can erase audit history in one statement.
Keep a reconciliation query for every derived total and run it on a schedule, alerting on any mismatch.

lessons.task: Model a document-ingestion domain with sources, chunks, and permissions, then list the constraints each table needs. Write a migration adding a foreign key to a populated table and explain how to validate it safely.

quiz.question: Why does third normal form make an address change safer than a duplicated copy?
choices: A schema where every non-key column depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.
Choose constraints, delete behaviour, and column types that make invalid rows impossible rather than unlikely.
Translate a domain description into entities, relationships, and keys normalised to third normal form.
Decide deliberately between normalisation, JSONB, soft deletes, and denormalised counters, with a recorded reason.
quiz.explanation: Translate a domain description into entities, relationships, and keys normalised to third normal form.

outcomes: Translate a domain description into entities, relationships, and keys normalised to third normal form.
Choose constraints, delete behaviour, and column types that make invalid rows impossible rather than unlikely.
Decide deliberately between normalisation, JSONB, soft deletes, and denormalised counters, with a recorded reason.
lessons.mental_model: A schema is a contract with every future writer: the database should make the wrong shape impossible, not rely on everyone remembering the rules.
worked_example: A billing design review finds line items stored as a JSONB array on invoices, because it shipped faster. Finance needs revenue by SKU, and each report parses every invoice in application code; a 90-day query takes 40 seconds. The team introduces invoice_items with a foreign key, CHECK (quantity > 0), and unit_cents bigint, backfills from JSONB, and keeps the payload in a provider_payload column. They choose CASCADE for items and RESTRICT on the tenant reference. Normalising costs one migration and removes the report's dependency on parsing; a nightly reconciliation test compares totals for two weeks.
common_mistakes: Storing a list of child records in a JSONB column and later needing to join, index, or aggregate them.
Using a nullable column to mean both unknown and not applicable, then guessing which in reports.
Denormalising a total without a trigger, job, or reconciliation test, so it drifts from the line items.

key_terms.definition: A schema where every non-key column depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.
A constraint that requires a column's value to exist in another table's key, protecting referential integrity.
Marking a row as deleted with a timestamp instead of removing it, preserving history at the cost of query complexity.

checkpoint.question: What is the goal of Database Design?
checkpoint.answer: Translate a domain description into entities, relationships, and keys normalised to third normal form.

checkpoint.question: Why does database design matter in practice?
checkpoint.answer: A schema is a contract with every future writer: the database should make the wrong shape impossible, not rely on everyone remembering the rules.

lessons.title: SQLAlchemy
lessons.goal: Define mapped classes with typed columns, relationships, and a session factory bound to one engine.
lessons.takeaway: A session is a shopping basket for one trip to the database: fill it, commit once, throw it away. The engine is the shop that stays open all day.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: The ORM is a productivity layer over SQL, not a replacement for knowing SQL. Used carelessly it emits hundreds of queries behind one endpoint, holds a transaction open across a network round trip, and hides the difference between a session and a connection. Used deliberately it gives typed models, parameterised queries, and one clear unit of work per request.
A session is a shopping basket for one trip to the database: fill it, commit once, throw it away. The engine is the shop that stays open all day.

sections.heading: Engine, session, and unit of work The engine owns the connection pool and is cre
body: Engine, session, and unit of work The engine owns the connection pool and is created once per process. A session is short-lived: it tracks loaded objects, batches their changes, and commits or rolls back one transaction. Build it with async_sessionmaker(engine, expire_on_commit=False) and open one per request through a dependency.

Never share a session between concurrent tasks, because it is not task-safe; a leaked session holds a pooled connection until the pool is exhausted. Loading is a query decision A relationship using lazy='select' fetches related rows on first attribute access, so serialising 50 orders with their customers issues 51 queries.

That N+1 is invisible in a test with two rows. Choose loading per query: selectinload for collections, which costs one extra query per relationship, joinedload for many-to-one when the parent set is small, and lazy='raise_on_sql' so an accidental load fails in tests instead of in production.

Transactions and readable SQL Keep a transaction open only as long as correctness requires: never across a model call or an outbound HTTP request. Writes that must be atomic share one session and commit once, and a failure rolls the whole unit back.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Size the pool as database max_connections divided by process count; a larger pool turns overload into connection timeouts.
Set statement_timeout on the role and a request timeout in the app, so a slow query cannot hold a connection indefinitely.
Use READ COMMITTED with explicit SELECT ... FOR UPDATE for contended rows, and put retries outside the session.

lessons.task: Instrument the query count of one list endpoint, record the SQL it emits, and write before-and-after numbers in notes (45 minutes). Rewrite a lazy relationship with selectinload and joinedload, then compare query count and p95 latency (40 minutes).

quiz.question: Why is a session unsafe to share between two concurrent request handlers?
choices: A short-lived unit of work that tracks loaded objects and turns their changes into one transaction on commit.
Choose transaction boundaries and pool settings that survive concurrent async requests.
Diagnose N+1 queries and fix them with selectinload, joinedload, or an explicit select of columns.
Define mapped classes with typed columns, relationships, and a session factory bound to one engine.
quiz.explanation: Define mapped classes with typed columns, relationships, and a session factory bound to one engine.

outcomes: Define mapped classes with typed columns, relationships, and a session factory bound to one engine.
Diagnose N+1 queries and fix them with selectinload, joinedload, or an explicit select of columns.
Choose transaction boundaries and pool settings that survive concurrent async requests.
lessons.mental_model: A session is a shopping basket for one trip to the database: fill it, commit once, throw it away. The engine is the shop that stays open all day.
worked_example: Aleks supports a 12-person team running an admin API over 480,000 orders. The order-list endpoint takes 4.8 s at p95, and the database logs 1,204 queries for a 250-row page, because each order's customer and three line items loaded lazily during JSON serialisation. Aleks adds selectinload(Order.customer) and selectinload(Order.lines), cuts the page size to 50, and selects only the twelve columns the table renders. Queries fall to 3, p95 to 210 ms, and the 20-connection pool stops saturating at 40 requests per second. The decision: ORM objects stay, but every list endpoint must declare its loading strategy, and a test asserts query count.
common_mistakes: Leaving relationships lazy and discovering N+1 queries only when the production table holds thousands of rows.
Holding one global session across requests, so concurrent handlers see each other's uncommitted objects.
Calling commit inside a loop, producing thousands of transactions and partial writes when one iteration fails.

key_terms.definition: A short-lived unit of work that tracks loaded objects and turns their changes into one transaction on commit.

One query for a parent set plus one per row for a relationship, so cost grows with result size. selectinload A loader that fetches a whole collection in one extra query using WHERE id IN (...), avoiding per-row round trips.

checkpoint.question: What is the goal of SQLAlchemy?
checkpoint.answer: Define mapped classes with typed columns, relationships, and a session factory bound to one engine.

checkpoint.question: Why does sqlalchemy matter in practice?
checkpoint.answer: A session is a shopping basket for one trip to the database: fill it, commit once, throw it away. The engine is the shop that stays open all day.

lessons.title: Database Migrations
lessons.goal: Generate an Alembic revision, review the autogenerated diff, and write an explicit downgrade or forward fix.
lessons.takeaway: A migration is a bridge between two versions of the code: both ends must be able to stand on it while traffic crosses.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: A schema change is a deployment to a shared stateful system and the change most likely to take an API down. Autogenerate hides decisions: it will happily add a NOT NULL column to a 40-million-row table and hold an exclusive lock while it rewrites. Migrations stay safe only when they are reviewed, versioned, applied by one runner, and rehearsed against realistic data volume.
A migration is a bridge between two versions of the code: both ends must be able to stand on it while traffic crosses.

sections.heading: A migration is versioned code Alembic records applied revisions in alembic_versi
body: A migration is versioned code Alembic records applied revisions in alembic_version, and each revision declares upgrade and downgrade steps. Revisions are applied in order by alembic upgrade head, which must be the same command in every environment.

Autogenerate diffs models against the live database and writes a draft; treat that draft as a proposal, because it misses data backfills, extensions, triggers, and index options it cannot infer. Once a revision has run anywhere shared, it is immutable.

Expand, then contract A column rename is three deployments: add the new column and dual-write, backfill and verify, then switch reads and drop the old column. Old and new application versions must both work during rollout, because containers restart at different times.

Tightening constraints follows the same shape: allow nulls, backfill, then add NOT NULL and CHECK once no row violates them. The destructive step waits at least one release after the last reader moves.

sections.heading: Production notes
body: Run migrations as an explicit deploy step with a single runner; replica startups applying head concurrently cause races and duplicate work.
Log revision, duration, and lock wait for every migration, and alert when deploy time exceeds the previous baseline.
Take a verified snapshot before destructive steps and rehearse the restore, not just the upgrade, in a staging environment.

lessons.task: Create two revisions that add, backfill, and constrain a column, then run both against a seeded million-row table (60 minutes). Time upgrade head on a restored snapshot, record lock waits from pg_stat_activity, and write the before-and-after table (45 minutes).

quiz.question: Why can one commit not safely rename a column and update every reader at once?
choices: One versioned Alembic file with upgrade and downgrade functions, identified by a hash in an ordered graph.
Measure lock impact and choose CONCURRENTLY, batching, or a maintenance window for large tables.
Apply expand-and-contract to rename or tighten a column while old and new code serve traffic.
Generate an Alembic revision, review the autogenerated diff, and write an explicit downgrade or forward fix.
quiz.explanation: Generate an Alembic revision, review the autogenerated diff, and write an explicit downgrade or forward fix.

outcomes: Generate an Alembic revision, review the autogenerated diff, and write an explicit downgrade or forward fix.
Apply expand-and-contract to rename or tighten a column while old and new code serve traffic.
Measure lock impact and choose CONCURRENTLY, batching, or a maintenance window for large tables.
lessons.mental_model: A migration is a bridge between two versions of the code: both ends must be able to stand on it while traffic crosses.
worked_example: A team must rename customers.name to full_name on a 40-million-row table taking 900 writes per second. Their first attempt is one revision with alter_column; 40 seconds into the deploy it holds an exclusive lock and checkout starts timing out. They split it. Revision one adds full_name as nullable and the ORM dual-writes. A separate job backfills 5,000 rows per batch with a sleep between batches and logs progress. Revision two, two releases later, sets NOT NULL after a gap query returns zero and drops name. Reads move behind a feature flag. Downtime is zero and the work finishes across four 14-minute windows.
common_mistakes: Editing a migration that already ran in staging or production, so environments disagree about the schema.
Letting autogenerate decide the plan, then discovering it dropped an index or ignored a data backfill.
Adding a NOT NULL column with a default to a large table in one step and locking writes for minutes.

key_terms.definition: One versioned Alembic file with upgrade and downgrade functions, identified by a hash in an ordered graph.
A rollout that adds compatible schema first, migrates data, then removes old structures after clients stop using them.
A PostgreSQL index-build option that avoids blocking writes, at the cost of a longer build outside a transaction.

checkpoint.question: What is the goal of Database Migrations?
checkpoint.answer: Generate an Alembic revision, review the autogenerated diff, and write an explicit downgrade or forward fix.

checkpoint.question: Why does database migrations matter in practice?
checkpoint.answer: A migration is a bridge between two versions of the code: both ends must be able to stand on it while traffic crosses.

outcomes: Turn a vague problem into a precise algorithm
Pick data structures that fit the access pattern
Compare solutions with complexity analysis rather than guesswork
